MR. HENRY A. BRIGHT. lAuthor of that delightful book, "In a Lancashire G;u•clen:l Yet again another; ere his crowning year, Gone from friends, that here may look for him no more. Never now for him shall hope set wide the door, Hope that hailed him hither, fain to greet him here. All the gracious garden-flowers he held so dear, Old-world English blossoms, all his homestead store, Old-world grief had strewn them round his bier of yore. Bidding each drop leaf by leaf as tear by tear; Barer lutes than mine had borne more tuneful token, Touched by subtler hands than echoing time can

wrong, Sweet as flowers had strewn his graveyard path along. Now may no such old sweet dirges more be spoken, Now the Sowers whose breath was very song are broken, Nor may sorrow find again so sweet a song. From "A Midsummer Holiday and other Poems." By Alger- non Charles Swinburne.

GRANDMA'S ANGEL. "Mamma said: Little one, go and see If Grandmother's ready to come to tea;' I knew. I mustn't disturb her, so I stepped as gently along, tip-toe, And stood a moment to take a peep— And there was Grandmother fast asleep! " I knew it was time for her to wake; I thought DI give her a little shake, Or tap at her door, or softly call; But I hadn't the heart for that at all— She looked so sweet and so quiet there, Lying back in her high arm chair, With her dear white hair, and a little smile, That means she's loving you all the while. "I didn't make a speck of a noise; I knew she was dreaming of little boys And girls who lived with her long ago, And then went to Heaven—she told me so. "I went up close, and I didn't speak One word, but I gave her on her cheek The softest bit of a kiss. Just in a whisper, and then said this: Grandmother, dear, it's time for tear' I "She opened her eyes, and looked at me, And said: Why, Pet, I have just now dreamed Of a little angel who came and seemed To kiss me lovingly on my face.' She pointed right at the very place! "I never told her 'twas only me; I took her hand, and we went to tea." SYDNER DAYRIL

"No, ma'am; she only said I was to ask you to come, and then it would be off her mind." A fellow lately contracted in writing with a wood- dealer for a quantity of "tip-top wood.' The man be- gan to deliver it, but it was so full of limbs that the purchaser demurred, saying that it was not good. The wood-man replied, "It was just what I agreed to de- liver, tip-top wood,' and I believe this grew on that part of the tree." • The wrongs of man to man but make The love of God more plain; As through the shadowy lens of even The eye looks farthest into heaven On gleams of star and depths of blue The glaring sunshine never knew !—Whittier. "Plass ON AND DO WHAT'S RIGHT."—A significant little story, which is now being told of the late Mr. Fawcett, gives an indication of the solid moral ground on which his political views were built, and thus helps to explain the enthusiasm felt for him at least by those Englishmen who retain something :of the old Puritan leaven. It, was a year ago; a party were;talking about the endless problem of Irish Government. How was the hostility of the Irish to be disarmed or overcome? How was_their national hatred to Englantl to be made to give way? The answers were mostly despairing; but Fawcett, quietly beating one hand against the other, kept, repeating in a low voice, as it were to himself, "You must press on and do what's right !—Times. As An "SALLY IN OUR Aktary.."—A Derby Day with the Arabs has been humourously described by John Ormsby, Esq., of the Middle Temple, in his book entitled "Autumn Rambles in North Africa." "Gathered to- gether to witness the sport and make a harvest- of the spectators were to be seen," he tells us, "the analogues of the Ethiopian serenader, the barrel-organ, the comic orator, and the other humorous features of our Derby Day. It must be confessed, however, that any com- parison between our nigger melodist and the gentlemen who perform the corresponding services for the Bedouin sporting world would be very much to the disadvantage of the London Arab. Owing, perhaps, to the fact that the Moslem wind has not a keen sense of humour, the performer is not a pure creature with a smudged face, limp white hat, and enormous shirt collar; but a grave, decorous, almost venerable—at any rate, highly pic- turesque—individual; and round him is a circle, from one to four deep, according to his merits, of ergs-legged listeners, whose demeanour and attitude of respectful attention would make a street-preacher envious. . . . In nine cases outof ten the theme of the Arab lyrist is the Sally of his Alley,' her attractions and his affection for her, a subject which has been rather frequently treated of by lyrical poets. But the mode in which it is administered to a7istening public is at least peculiar. The singer (generally a grave gray-bearded old fellow, who ought to know better than sing amatory ditties), ignoring his audience, and looking into ,hisZtambourine for encouragement, sings: "Among the maidens of the tribe there's none like little Sara." Here the flutes repeat the notes of the air—if air it can be called—while he beats time on the tambourine. " She Is the darling of my heart, and she dwells in the Sahara." Flutes and tambourine as before. "Hem' mother is a skilful weaver of hails, H,er father makes horseshoes for the warriors of the tribe."
Flutes and tambourine again. • But these persons are not really the parents of Bars.

I cannot believe it. - BM/3 i 9 the darling of my heart, and she dwells in the Sahara." Here comes in a double allowance of flute and tambour- ines; and so on to the end,A when he declares that as soon as Rhamadan is over, and he has money enough, he will marry Sara, and take her to his tent, but not in the Sahara.—London Society. Patcricar, Joicss.—My great chum was a man about -ten years older than myself, whom for distinction's sake I will call Pitt, and who was the most audacious prac- tical joker I ever met. Two of his exploits I remember well. At the corner of one of the streets running from -the Strand to the river, near St. Mary's Church, was a well-known Italian warehouse. One day, as Pitt and I were walking westward after office hours, we saw hang- ing at the shop door a bundle of bananas, with an in- scription—" The last bananas we shall receive this season." Pitt stopped and read the placard. "That is very curious," he said, "and must be inquired into!" I followed him up the shop, a long low addition to the original house, until we reached the counter at the far end, where two or three shopmen were busy serving cus- tomers. "Could I speak to Mr. —7" asked Pitt, men- tioning the name he had read on the shop door, and speaking with the greatest earnestness. "He's in, sir, but heik having his tea; but if you particularly want him I'll call him." "Thank you, Ido want a word with him." The proprietor came out of his parlour wiping his mouth, and, rounding the counter, was immediately laid hold of by Pitt, who took him by the elbow, and led him, astonished, to the door. Arrived there, Pitt pointed to the bananas. "Are these positively :the very last bananas that you will receive this season ?" "Yes, said the man, "they are." " What of it ?" "Is there no probability, then, of your having another batch ?" "No—not that I know of. What of it, said the man. "What of it? Well, I think it a most interesting circumstance! Deeply obliged to you! Good morning !" And he took off his hat with an air, and left the man, purple and speechless on his own threshold. Another of Mr. Pitt's practical jokes was even more audacious :—Middle-aged readers will possibly remember that the original shop for Holloway's patent medicines was at the extremity of the Strand a few doors west of Temple Bar. It was a long shop, with a narrow counter running the length of it, at which sat s number of men, occupied in rolling the pills, spreading the ointment, &c. Pitt had often told me he felt curiously attracted to that shop; and one day, as we were passing, he said, " Can you keep grave for five minutes ?" I told him I thought I could, little guessing to what test my gravity .was subjected. "Then come along !" And the next minute he sprang from my side into the shop, where in the open space before the counter he began leaping about and throwing up his legs with an agility i which, n these prx-Voke days, was unknown. The shopmen stared in wonder, and one of them was ad- vancing, when Pitt bounded in front of him and asked, "You don't know me ? you don't recognise me ?" The ahopman, evidently taking him to be a lunatic, was muttering something about not having the pleasure, when Pitt, pointing to the others. asked, "Do none of - those recognise me?" A general chorus of "No 1" "I don't wonder at it !" said Pitt. "When I was last in this shop, I was carried in on the cabman's back— couldn't walk a step—bad legs of fortyZearS' standing! But now, thanks to your invaluable p and ointment —look here! and here!" Once more he bounded and danced up and down the shop—and then we ran for our lives.—" Memoirs of a Man of the World," by Edmund Yates. Upward steals the life of man, As the sunshine from the wall; From the wall into the sky, - From the roof along the spire; Ah, the souls of those that die Are but sunbeams lifted higher.—Longfellow. A holy life is made up of a number of small things; little words, not eloquent speeches or sermons; little deeds, not miracles or battles, nor one great heroic act of mighty martyrdom,' make up the true Christian life. The little, constant sunbeam, not the lightning; the waters of Siloam "that go softly" in the meek mission of refreshment, not the "waters• of the river, great and many," rushing down in noisy torrents, are the true symbols of a holy life. The avoidance of little evils, little sins, little inconsistencies, little weaknesses, little follies, indiscretions and imprudences, little foibles, little indulgences of the flesh; the avoidance of such little things as these goes far, to make up, at least, the nega- tive of a holy life.—Bonar. The First Regiment of California has been camping out during the water-melon season, and the consequence was that between the bar rooms of Santa Rosa and the water-melon farms there were a large number of un- authorised absences. One evening the guard observed a private approaching, who was staggermg along under the combined load of much conviviality and an enor- mous water-melon under each arm. "Who goes there?" "Er—hic—er fren," responded the truant. "Advance, friend, and give the countersign." " Hain't got no— ble— countersign," amiably replied the private; abut er—hic—give yer er—warmellin." Pretty soon the officer of the day came round, and said to the sentinel, who was absorbed in munching a huge piece of water- melon stuck at the end of his bayonet, "Did Perkins pass you just now?" "Yes, sir.' "Did he give the countersign?" inquired the lieutenant, taking a bite himself, as the man presented arms. "Well, no, sir," said the sentinel, confidentially; "the password was cholera,' but he said water-melon,' so I passed him and put the other half in your tent." "Did, eh?" mused the officer. " Hum ! water-melon, eh ? Well, I guess that was near enough." AN AFFECTIONATE Doo.—Stories about the fidelity of dogs are without number, but a more pathetic one than this there could not well be :—A snowstorm once arose very suddenly in the Isle of Skye, and a shepherd and his dog set out on their duties to look after and collect , their flock. It was a hard task, with the chilly snow- flakes driving in their faces, and night set in before the sheep were housed. Still struggling to count and fold the helpless creatures, the poor shepherd became ex- hausted, and filially sank down on the cold ground to die. The dog went home, however, better able to find his way, and then a search was set on foot for the lost shepherd, but in vain. Suddenly some one noticed that the dog each morning carried off an oatcake in his mouth, not to eat, as it was thought, but to hide for a future occasion. Now, it was purposed to follow him wben he carried off the food, since a glimmer of the possible reason for this action came across the minds of his friends. lie was tracked on and on across the deso- late hillside to a lonely dell, and there, stiff and cold, lay the body of the dead shepherd, and on his breast the five oatcakes his faithful dog had brought him, in the vain hope of preserving his life. Hzs Picr.—A pigeon which was for six years a pet of the late Thurlow Weed for a low, time showed in a . .

touching way his appreciation of the loss of his master. Not long since a gentleman called at the house, and the pigeon alighted on his shoulder, cooed, peered into the stranger's face, and then flew into an adjoining room. "He has done that 0 every gentleman that has come into the house since father died," said Miss Weed, with a sigh. "He takes most kindly to General Bowen, who visits- me occasionally, who has been in feeble health some time, and walks slowly. The bird will coo and fly to the General's shoulder, but when he bees that it is not my father he will stop his cooing and find some other I perch. Since the day that father's remains were carried away the affectionate creature has been seeking for his master. He flies through every room in the house, and fairly haunts the library, where father spent most of his time with his pet. He will tread over every inch of space on the lounge and then go to the rug, over which i he will walk repeatedly, as if n expectation of his tlead ,master's cqming. He invariably does this at meal times, wiled our table is set in the :back parlour, of which we now make a dining-room. He can see our table from the rug." "Then you do not put him in a cage?" "0, never!" was the response. "The run of the house has been his since he came into it. Other pigeons come into ouryard frequently, and our pet some- times joins them. He seldom remains long with them, but comes back through one of the windows, and begins his search again 'through the house for my father. Our Dumb Animals.

A. GAME FOR LONG EVENINGS.—Those who learn draw- ing will find the game of "Positions" a particularly pleasant pastime for the long evenings. Any number can play the game—the more the merrier. All the players seat themselves round the table, and each one must be, supplied with small pieces of white paper, about two inches square, and a pencil—or, better still, a , pen and ink. All the players, except one, then silently resolve on some :position in life which it is possible for them to fill, andleach makes some sign of' their "Posi- tion" by sketching a little picture of some article con- nected with their supposed trade or business on one of the lllank pieces of paper. The name of each sketcher should be written on his paper. Five minutes are al- lowed for the sketching, the time being kept by the player who has not selected a "Position." All the illus- trated papers are then passed in order round the table so that each may view the other's pictures; but no one is supposed to criticise them aloud. Lastly they are handed to the "Guesser" (who, up to this point, has taken no active part in the game, except to time the five minutes), and he ranges them in order before him according to the order in which the players are seated at the table. He looks at them attentively and proceeds to guess from the pictures what are the intended posi- tions of each person. Supposing that there were three players, and each one drew a sketch, say of a house, a pear, and a crown respectively. The Guesser looking at them would have no difficulty in pronouncing (1) land- lord, (2) greengrocer, 3 (king). If she fail to guess any of the "Positions," the first person at whom he or she stopped is chosen Guesser for the next time; if there has been no failure, the player on the right hand of the Guesser fakes the privilege. The principal, object of this game is for each player to try who 'can make the best sketch in five minutes, and the next object is to puzzle the Guesser.—Little Folks Magazine for November. A PLEA FOR TIME TRADES.—I am at a lOSS to IMO", why so many persons send their children to be clerks and assistants. The world is simply glutted with such per- sons, and yet still they come. Is it because they do not like to dirty their hands or double up their sleeves? Is it because they like to assume the appearance of gentle- mail? Is it•because- they despise the anvil, the lathe, the chisel, the vice, or the shuttle? Is it because the desk and the counter are more profitable or more re- spectable? If sb' no greater mistake was ever made. A scholar can always become a clerk,, and a sharp man or woman can always be an assistant. These occupa- tions should be n last resort, and to know a useful handicraft trade should bd the first aiim of every youth. Parents should abandon false notions of gentility. A black coat in these days frequently hides a sad heart, and clean hands often mean starvation. 'A man who can turn his hand to a good trade is always independent, and need be the slave of no one. I sincerely trust that parents will discontinue sending their children to the desk or the Counter, and make, them useful mechanics or artisans of some kind; for in the latter case they may become prosperous manufacturers, but in the former they may probably be servilely poor all their lives, and die prematurely into the bargain. We shall soon be an educated nation, and we should, above all, see that the ' increased intelligence is rightly directed. The tenden- cies are unquestionably to avoid producing wealth, and to participate in its aistribution. The factories and , workshops—the real sources of wealth—are too often regarded as beneath the attention of persons whose parents have prospered therein. I beseech everyone having the custody of children to see that the education they possess is directed to the manipulating and , fashioning of the products of the earth for the use and en- joyment of man, and not to the connter and quill-driving:' Of course, there must always be, clerks and assistants, and I have no fear of the supply ever being inadequate to the demand. There are, however, grave reasons why the energies of young persons should be directed into healthier and more profitable channels." Thomas Suthurst, in "Death and Disease Behind the Counter." div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22. 1884. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI-

fore adding the rennet, as when that was right the cheese was half made. The cheesemaker had got to find that out for himself, as the milk worked differently on every change of soil. There were, in fact, a hundred pitfalls that the cheesemaker may fall into, and it required the greatest care and attention with experience and com- mon sense and skill to accomplish the desired end. He may do everything right and at the time but one; and because of that one thing he may have a faulty cheese. The active agents that affect the character of cheese in lits making and curing are heat, rennet, salt, moisture, lactic acid, and the alcoholic acid developed by the action of the air. The action of these various agents was de- scribed by Mr. Harris in detail. Heat up to 98 degs. seemed to hasten and stimulate the action of all the other active agents;. above 98 up to 140 it had a kill- ing effect. He then went on to lay down the principles of manufacture so as to produce the largest yields and the best quality. He used one-third more rennet and less salt in spring tan in summer. The heating of the curd should be slow at first, gradually increasing as the whey formed on the outside of the curd._ .98 was the usual heat in summer, but as the seasonjadvanced the milk became richer, and he had found it necessary to heat to 102 degs. in Scotland.. The great :secret of good cheesemaking was that means must be' used to expel the whey before acid is developed. Thist`was best done by stirring. Lactic acid should be allowed to i develop n a small degree only, so as to overcome the putrefactive ferment, and prevent the formation of gas in the cheese during the time of curing. The alcoholic acid, or the form of acid which develops by the exposure of the dry curd to the air at a temperature of 95 to 98 degrees, takes from [two to four hours' exposure of the curd to the free action of the air. This exposure is done by grinding the curd and stirring until it has the proper consistency, when it will feel soft and velvety. Curd should contain 35 per cent, of moisture when 'pressed, and 33 per cent. when cured. To determine and retain this proper proportion of moisture required good judg- ment in the operator, the only guide being observation and common sense. Mr. Hams expressed his preference for coarse over fine salt, as the latter dissolved too rapidly, but it must be the best salt that couldjbe got. It was unfortunate that a great many dairy buildings were not fit to make cheese in, but it was with pleasure he could say that the dairies of Scotland, with few exceptions, were scrupulously clean, and that the people had shown him every kindness he could desire, for which he returned them his heartfelt thanks.

THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION'S EXCUR- SION TO THE ROCKY MOUNTAINS. The following interesting letter, describing the recent scientific excursion from Montreal to the Rocky Mountains, is from the pen of a Blackburn gentleman, Mr. Harry Bragg, now of Montreal. Sin,—Perhaps some of your numerous circle of readers would like to hear a little of a journey across this vast country, which has lately become my home ; a journey taken in company with a present resident in Blackburn, and one which was made under circumstances so exceptional that they will hardly be repeated; I refer to the special excur- sion of the British Association from this city across Canada to the Rocky Moaatains, and over into British Columbia. This journey a limited number of the visiting members were enabled to take through the courtesy of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I was singularly fortunate in being able to accompany the party. So that since I bade farewell to my numerous friends in my native country I have travelled a considerable distance away from it. We left Montreal On Thursday morning the 4th Septem- ber, travelling up to Ottawa, but only got a view of the city crowded by the Government buildings from the other side of the river. The heat all day was very great, and the dust made travelling the reverse of pleasant; the continuous cars, however, made it more endurable, as we could move up and down and have a wash now and then to take off a few layers of dust. Although our train was an express, it was late at night before we reached Toronto, and we were all glad to find comfortable quarters at the Albion, where the charges, in spite of all that is said about the hotel rates on this side, was a dollar (four shillings) a day, and this for a comfortable bedroom and three substantial meals with plenty of variety and good service. Friday was spent in Toronto; the morning being free, at noon a civic address was presented, followed by a drive through all the principal streets, stopping at the public buildings, and conclu- ded with a reception and garden party at the Government House. The city is a very handsome one, and the wide, well paved streets and good shops made it very attractive looking; it has the great advantage over Montreal of being thoroughly English, instead of mainly French-Canadian as this city is. Friday night was spent in Toronto, and next morning we set off by the train for Owen Sound, on the eastern shore of Lake Huron, across which passengers are carried until the railway along the north shores of Huron and Superior is completed. This is a pleasant break in the journey, especially as the steamers of the line are beautiful boats, fitted up with every convenience, and having an ex- cellent table. In one of these boats, the sm. Alberto, we left Owen Sound on Saturday afternoon, with a sail of 567 miles before us, across Georgian Bay and Lake Huron, then no the St. Mary River and across part of Lake Superior. About noon on Sunday we were pasaing up the canal to avoid the rapids in the river, and had time to run ashore in the States for a few minutes. On Monday morning we were pas- sing Thunder Cape, a very imposing headland, but inferior to many on the Norwegian coast, as Sir Richard Temple told me; the day was misty and wet, and when we reached Port Arthur we found they had had a month's rain, with a downpour for the last four days. So heavy had been the rain that the line was washed out on the way to Winnipeg, and we found ourselves stopped, and for an indefinite time. However we had a botanical expedition, and for the first time I saw the curious pitcher plant in its wild state; man' were the fresh kinds of plants and mosses 'found in the bogs and woods, and quite a collection was brought back and served to furnish amusement for the evening, which we spent again on the Alberta. Next morning—Tuesday—was a delightful contrast, and we were not sorry to get on our way once more about nine o'clock. Here the special expe- dition really began its separate existence for we had only had additional cars on the express trains hitherto; from this point the company provided a special train composed of a baggage car, four of the new Palman sleepers, and the private car of Mr. Egan, superintendent of the Western Division,who courteously went with us all the way and did all he could to make the journey comfortable and pleasant. On Tues- day, then, we commenced the second part of the trip, and had still upwards of 1,300 miles before the end was reached. The day was lovely and the rain had laid all the dust and made it much pleasanter for travelling. The country was very diversified in some respects, but anything but level; low rocky hills, covered with timber, being divided by swamps or " muskeys," which are practically bottomless, and over which the railway is carried with difficulty, the embank- ments being laid on a beading of tail firs which gradually sink, the ends bending upwards at each side of the embank- ment. The enormous quantity of timber destroyed by fire all along is sad to see, the blackened trees forming a fringe all along the track for miles. At Savanne the first glimpse of Indians was obtained, a squaw and some papooses loung- ing round a wigwam on the banks of the Red River, or rather a branch of it, and beside them some of the remnants of the boats used by Sir Garnet Wolselev in the Red River expedition. We had supper at Rail Portage, about 300 miles from Port Arthur, and passed through Winnipeg during the night. About noon next day, a halt was made at Brandon, a town scarcely four years old, yet possessing good streets and stores, tasteful private houses, two or three good churches, a fire engine building, and a masonic hall. Hearing that another Blackburnian had come out to settle, I tried to find him and again on the return journey, but failed to do so. Vile were now fairly Out on the prairie, having been travelling across for 80 miles, and all that day and all the next, we passed rapidly along; it is easy to say that the land is as flat as a table, that the sky line all round Is perfectly straight, unbroken by a hill or a tree, but it is difficult, if not impossible to realise it, until one actually sees it. Well, all that day and the next, the 'outlook was the same, except here and there, a farmstead, or a patch of bush near a water course, or a sedgy mere, broke the mono- tony; but on Thursday evening, in a mist and rain whieh prevented any distant views, we passed Calgary and entered the foot-hllle; as our engine toiled upward and puffed and panted as if unused to such exertion, the rain turned to sleet, and, by-and-by, the upper slopes of the hills loomed through the deepening gloom, all white with snow. This was a cheerful look-oat for the next day, which we were to spend in rambling about among the mountains! We turned out for supper at Canmore, and had a capital meal in a veritable log cabin, after which we turned in to our berths and enjoyed a good night's rest, in the delightful mountain air, more than 5,000 feet above sea level. Next morning we were turned out early, and found our train had halted at Laggan, a place represented by a few board houses, some log cabins, and some tents; one of the latter was occupied by a "fashionable tailor," while in another we got a substantial breakfast. After this our special carried us on to the summit where the future city of Stephen is situated, fitly named after the headman of the line, and now consisting of three or four log cabins, appa- rently empty. We were now nearly 6,000 feet above the.. sea, and among mountains which rose some 5,000 feet higher still. The upper peaks were still veiled in mist, but the day promised to be lovely, and proved so. At Stephen the grind of the breaks began, as we descended the ridge, leaving the Atlantic behind us, and sliding swiftly downwards towards the Pacific. Our train could not go far, however' but pulled up beside the lively mirror-like expanse of Kicking Horse Lake, where we were all turned out to wander for the whole day at our own sweet will. And it was a day of thorough enjoyment, while the weather was as perfect as could have been wished. As the sun got higher, the mist gradually broke and circled round the summits as though reluctant to leave them, and the peaks themselves peered through the wreathing clondS, all pare with snow, though broken with many a rude scar and precipice; down below, the bases were covered by a thick growth of pines, and in the valley the Kicking Horse river fretted into white foam amid its rocky channel. Our party necessarily broke into sections, forming groups as they were interested in betany, geology, or other subjects. Part of the day I spent in climbing amid the debris of a slide, admiring the luxuriant mosses arid delicate ferns, and feasting on wild gooseberries and rasp- berries. A:can of chicken and biscuits were acceptable as refreshment at noon, and plenty of pure spring water was handy; then I went further down the line to a tunnel where a slight fall of rock had taken place, narrowly missing some of the party. From down below the view grew grander, and the great snow beds lying in the upper slopes, and the greenish white of the glacier., looked very lovely against the bright blue sky. I rambled back with Mr. Thomas, the artist of the Graphic, and as we stopped at a little stream and drank the toast of "Absent Friends," I was back once more where smoky chimneys are more common than snowy peaks, and rows of cottages than gloomy pine woods. Re- turning to Stephen, our special returned to Laggan and waited there all night, so next morning we had the pleasure of going down to the plain in daylight, and seeing wonder- ful retrospective views of the mountains we were leaving behind. At Gleidren we stopped to see a " Pow-wow," but the Indians did not turn up in as large numbers as was ex- pected; still the party, under the war chief, look very pic- turesque and proved, on near inspection, to be very dirty ; old Crowfoot, the head of the tribes in that locality, was at the station, and made a small fortune by selling various ar- ticles of his attire. Most of the party secured some memen- toes of the redskins at one or other of the stopping places, and the Indians must have felt pleased at the free use of money exhibited by the scientists. We reached Regina on Sunday morning, and stopped at the Mounted Police-Bar- racks, to join in the service there, and later on halted at Bell's Farm, an enormous property, consisting of nearly 70,000 acres; round this we drove,, and thus bad an' oppor- tunity of seeing the state of the crops and the way in' which the farm was managed. Agriculture is simplicity itself here, as the prairie simply needs ploughing. I met with a man from near Blackburn at Calgary, I think it was, who said he had been a butcher at home. He and his brothers came out here less than two years ego, without a cent, and with no knowledge of farming; now they have 320 acres of land, and implements and stock worth 2,000 dols.—say £400; I asked if he would not like to go back, but his answer was a decided negative. At Medicine Hat, on our return, / saw lovely asters and zinnias, grown on land only broken in the spring. I hope that no one will accuse me of trying to " boom " up the North-West, and tempt men out there by writing thus. Perhaps, some day, I may be able, with your permission, Mr. Editor, to say something further about emigration to-this country. We reached Brandon about eleven o'clock on Sunday night, and found supper provided by the Corporation, after which, when Monday had really come, an address was pre- sented and speeches made. Then we returned to our berths —to dream anything but pleasant dreams of the hospitality at Brandon. Early next morning we turned out at Portage la Prairie for breakfast and more speeches, and on arriving at Winnipeg, and more speechifying, giving 'votes of thanks to Mr. Egan and the committee who had managed the trip,

CRlLM—Persons not keeping cows may always have a little cream, provided the milk they purchase be pure and unadulterated. As soon as it comes in it should be poured into very shallow open pie dishes, and set by in a very cool place, and in seven or eight hours a nice cream should have arisen._

DAIRY COWS.—Oats and bran are the best food for dairy cows, by way of grain or meal. Pea and bean meal make the butter strong, at least if given liberally. vats and bran, on the other hand, produce rich cream, and thet butter proves of excellent quality, while the cow's condition is improved. Some carrots would be a good addition to the food, and then, witkplenty of sweet hay, the cow would not need cake. Swedes,. like bean meal, if not carefully given, cause a strong taste to the butter. A gallon of scalded bran may be given each end of the day with the chaff or pulp, and a gallon Of , crushed oats would be a fair feed. If no roots are pro- curable, increase the oats to two gallons. - - TH CATTLE RANCHMEN in the Calgary district in the Canadian North-West, are reported to be moving their herds further south, and stocking the old ranches with sheep and cattle which are better suited ,to that particu- lei:section of lands. Cattle raising is found to be a highly profitable business throughout the Macleod re- gion, the coulees runniqg from the mountains affording excellent ' shelter. British Columbia will also, it is thought, be found an excellent land for the sheep indus- try. The lands of the Upper Fraser river, as well as the Thompson, Nichols, and O'Kanagan districts, are admir- ably adapted for it, as well as for cattle ranching. there being an endless supply of rich bunch grass, while thp winters are mild and the water supply never-failing. CANADA'S FOOD Pitonucrs.—Canada's position as an important food-producing country is not sufficiently ap- preciated by the English public at large, although much has been done by the combined action of the Press, of late years, to dispel the popular ignorance that existed of the resources of that colony. In addition to the pro- vision for her home consumption, Canada, in 1883, ex- ported food products to the value of 59,537,377 dols., subdivided as follows :—Agricultural products, 21,165,418 dols.; animals and their products, 29,515,033 dols.; pro- duce of fisheries, 8,156,926 dols. A glance at the details of some of the more important articles exported will not be without interest and instruction. Wheat and barley, 11,000,000 and 9,000,000 bushels respectively; flour, 500,000 barrels; live stock-67,000 cattle; 312,000 sheep; dairy produce-63,340,9381b5. of cheese, 8,162,7291b5. of butter. Under fisheries, the more noteworthy are lob- sters, 15,000,000 cans; cod, 780,000 cwt. ; herrings, 5,000 tons and 123,000 barrels; salmon 11,000,000 cans and 500 tons. This for a country of barely 5,000,000 inhabit- ants, speaks well for the productiveness of the soil, and the industry and enterprise of its people. . _ .

Aconws.—l had some rather striking experience when a youth in regard to young pigs eating acorns. They were abundant that year, as they are this, and about 40 young pigs, three to four months of age, were allowed to run under a number of oak trees and help them- selves. They throve well, apparently, for a time, but at the end of a month ulcers about the throat were largely developed. Nearly all the pigs had one or more ulcers. Some of these were exactly under the gullet, others were closely behind the ears, and others under the lower jaw: This must have been the effect of the powerful astringent in the form of tannic acid which the acorn contained. I have no professional knowledge on the subject, as I was so satisfied with myNrst expe- rience that I took care that the same error of:judgment was not repeated. 'But my theory is this, that the powerful tannic acid neutralised or 'destroyed the fatty matter and glycerine which lubricate the muscles of a healthy animal; that congestion of the muscles was thereby caused, and, therefore, that the obstructed fluids, pressed on by the circulation of the blood, found vent in the form of the ulcers referred to. NORTH LANCASHIRE CATTLE FEEDING.—Now that most farmers, who are stock-holders, will be feeding for,the Christmas markets, it is to be hoped that, in accordance with the general depression, they will avoid sending to market the wasteful carcases of both beef and mutton that have been too common in past years, in which the preponderance of fat has been so large as to be in great part unfit for human food, and thus a direct loss—a loss to consumers, and a loss to the feeders for the price per pound is less, whereas the food to produce such fat is more costly. Especially this year, when the prices of grain are so low, does this come home to British farmers who are producers of flesh meat. Where it has been the custom to feed large quantities of oil-cake,"or other cakes, it will be found much more economicaltand pro- duce better flesh, to feed more with chopped hay, straw, and oatmeal, with half the quantities of cake, or even less, and neutralising the effect of the dry food by giv- ing either turnips, cabbages, or other vegetable food. There is no better food than oatmeal for building up firm flesh in beasts, and oats for the same purpose in sheep. Ground malt, for a change, is useful alike as a feeder and a condiment, and acts as a refresher to the appetite. Such fed animals will be certain to realise the best prices. HORSE BREEDING.—A GOOD SI7GGESTION.—There is society in Kent which, really, is a company formed for the improvement of cart horses. It is certainly upon a small scale, but the principle is so good that it Might well be imitated in every district in England. A first-class!shire horse, which cost a large sum of money, is owned by the company, which is composed of farmers. It travels the district during the summer, each farmer paying a stud . fee of two guineas and keeping the horse while he re- mains on his farnf, and also the man. Outsiders pay three guineas. 'ln this way, by means of the farmers taking Considerable interest in the work, very much good is done. Mr. Martin, of Rochester, recently read tb valuable paper upon this system to the Southern Conn- ties Veterinary Association. He was very strong upon the fact that so many farmers prefer to work young mares until they are too old for work and then breed from them, instead of breeding from young mares and working them when they are at a more advanced age. In too many cases badly bred unsound mares when used for breeding are put to weedy cart horses, or anything in the shape of a stallion that is travelling the district, at a 10s. "or £1 fee, the result being only too well known; instead of a high-class animal worth £BO or £Botas a five-year-old, the animal is worth less than half that sum. It appears that 5 per cent. has been realised upon the year's procceeding?. The company has £3OO or £4OO in the bank, and now intends extending its district and buying a Clydesdale for change of blood. Although it has made a working profit, the intention is to improve the rate of horses rather than to make money. The horse used by the Rochester Society is in charge of a man during the summer months and worked all the winter, when the man is discharged. BLACK-LEM—There is no trustworthy cure for this deadly attack. It occurs from an absence of serum in the blood. If the part be cut the calf would not flinch, as it is virtually dead and insensible to the knife. The blood that would drain from a piece scr cut out would not solidify, but remain liquid in the same way as the blood of a pig does when the serum is whipped out of it by a bunch of birch twigs, for the purpose of making it suitable for black puddings—an old-fashioned delicacy which is now not much in favour except in obscure country corners. The object of owners of' young cattle should he prevention. This, of course, can only be at- tained by supplying suitable food. The attack is gene- rally more prevalent when the animals have been on parched pastures or hillsides. They then need a little nitrogenous food, such as linseed cakes, ground beans, peas, or lentils. This will keep the serum of the blood up to its normal proportion, when there will be no dan- ger of black-leg or quarter-ill. If the weather be very dry, it is advisable to boil linseed in the proportion of one busher to 36 gallons of water, and, when boiling, to turn it on to a tub or tank in which a quantity of chaff and a little pulse meal has been mixed. This is a mix- ture that is not appreciated as it should be. For horses that are delicate it is a safe preventive against gripes, colic, and flatulence. The best arrangement I know of for producing it is where a farmer built a small cistern in a corner near the boiler of his engine. He has a small boiler for the linseed, with the tap over the cistern. When the linseed has been sufficiently boiled—which is accomplished by a steam pipe from the engine boiler— the tap is turned, and the chaff and meal in the cistern are scalded. As he has a numerous lot of live stock, he boils a bushel of linseed in 38 gallons of water daily, or twice duly, according to the season. The cistern is plain brickwork about 2ft. deep, with the inside well concreted. The farmer gives a small portion of this to his horses, cattle, and sheep daily, and they all eat it with sviclity, while, as he said,' I keep my horse for work, and for hard work, but I have never had one dis- abled from an internal attack since I have given them a little food daily scalded, as you see it, with linseed tea." The same, undoubtedly, might be said of young cattle in regard to black-leg, if the same practice was applied to them.—A FARMER. THE MERITS OE: THE OLD AND NEW' SYSTEMS OF CHEESE,MAKING.—At a meeting of the Scottish Dairy Association last week, Mr. Harris read a paper on the above subject. He said: There can be no doubt that the Cheddar system has been of great service to this country, but a feeling prevails that it is not at present meeting the requirements of the market. This is chiefly attributable to the way in which the system is practised in most of the dairies in Scotland. A want of know- ledge of much of its working has a great deal to do with the inferior quality of the goods produced. Many theories and suggestions have been written on the sub- ject of cheese-making, but I doubt if there ever can be a code of rules laid down so that the maker can fol- low them under all conditions of weather, &c. The cheese-maker must use his own judgment and vary his processes as often as the atmosphere changes. After explaining why good, well-ripened cheese helped diges- tion, while bad cheese injured it, Mr. Harris went on to speak of the causes of poor cheese, which, he said, were too many to be enumerated. Some of them were cows out of health, or having had access to bad water, want of cleanliness, setting the milk at night too thick or too thin, too high Or too low, heat- ing, too much or too little rennet, not cutting at the proper time, scalding too fast, drawing off the whey too soon or not soon enough, not getting the whey, properly out, allowing too much acid or not enough to develop before salting, putting to press too soon, putting on too much pressure, too much heat or not enough in the curing room, Src. It was of the utmost importance to have the milk in the right condition be-

div.head: EARLY MATURITY.
div.p: EARLY MATURITY.

Mr. William Parsons, a famous breeder of Hampshire Down sheep, recently gave a most ,practical lecture at the Farmers' Club upon early maturity of stock, and his remarks have such a direct bearing upon the success of stock-breeding farmers in the present unsatisfactory times that they should be known to everyone who wishes to do his best in the breeding and feeding yard. The burden of Mr. Parson's advice is that it is the height of folly for a stockfeeder to keep animals over a winter and well on to two years of Age, during the greater part of which time they are being prepared for the butcher; and he contends that by judicious, not to say forcing feeding, from birth upwards, they may be made fit for sale considerably within their first year. He adduces powerful arguments in support of his con- tention, more particularly with regard to sheep. As to stock, he shows from figures drawn from the catalogues of the large fat-stock shows that fat beasts under two years are infinitely to be preferred for the butcher to those which are kept on to three and even four. years of age. For instance, taking the Smithfield:show, we find that in the years 1880 and 1881 there were 67 beasts averaging 20 months and 3 weeks, with an aver- age weight of newt. lqr. 231 b. In J. 882 and 'lBB3 78 similar beasts 211 months old averaged 12cwt..0qr. 191 b. In these years the three-year-olds at 32 months only averaged 154 cwt. and 15-cwt. respectively, while those under 4 years average 18cwt. Oqr. 61b. and 18kewt. re- spectively, so that by keeping two-year-olds another year the gain was only 474. to 3iewt. ; if kept two years the further increase is only newt. to 3cwt. Mr. Parsons argues very justly that the extra cost:of keep- ing these beasts was not nearly met by their enhanced price, and that their increased weight was 'iot at all commensurate with that cost. This being the case it would appear, as all with advanced ideas are now will- ing to admit, that it is far more profitable to force for early maturity than to keep beasts for a long period be- fore they are disposed of and the money turned over. Mr. Richard Strattan' one of the most famous breeders of exhibition beasts, says than an animal approach- ing three years should weigh 15cwt. in order to pay. He prefers two summers at grass, with cake. If, however, the same animal can be made to pull down lliewt. a year sooner, no one will contend but that it is infinitely better to produce it. Now with regard to sheep. Mr. Parsons quotes the fact that for the years 1875 and 1877 the average weight of 76 pens of lambs was 4cwt. lqr. 161 b. at 9+ months, 187 pens of wethers a year older scaling *wt. In the next three years 90 pens of lambs scaled 11b. more, 187 pens of wethers reaching 6cwt. 2qr. 271 b., while in the last three years 162 pens of lambs scaled 4cwt. 2qr. 121 h each, and 204 pens of wethers 6cwt. 3qr. 51b. If good ripe mutton can be produced at three months under the year to such a weight, Mr. Parsons asks what possible advantage could be gained by keeping stotti)Sheep until they are a year old in order to make them scale from 10 to 13 stone during the next year, which is about the result bf present practice. In- deed, it is questionable whether the store animal at a year old is worth any more than the lamb at three or four months. The best judges land :breeders of sheep are too clever and too judicious to attempt winter fat- ting if they can possibly avoid it, but this is what they are in a great measure compelled to do under the pre- sent system. One of the best breeders of Hampshire Down sheep remarks that lambs born in January with him are weaned as soon as his water meadows are fed off, about the 13th of May; they then get tares, sanfoin, and oilcake till July. Tares are then next succeeded by rape, and their allowance of cake is slightly increased until they get lilb. daily, together with3lb. of split beans, the rape being subsequently followed by turnips. If lambs are matured, as they ought to be, in this man- ner, they can be cleared out in the autumn at much more liberal prices, and more time can be devoted to the breeding flock. Food which has been grown for winter use will then maintain a much larger number of ewes (at least a third more), in order to increase the supply,of lambs for the following year. They will also help to fill up gaps in the breeding flock, and to increase that as well for future use. Many farmers consider that this kind of feeding and breeding is over-stocking; 'but the old adage which says it is "better to be over-rented than over-stocked" was never meant to apply to a system like this, for the farmer who pursues it will naturally produce sufficient food for his extra number of fatting lambs. '

div.head: SAVAGE ASSAULT ON WIDNES
div.p: THE SAVAGE ASSAULT ON WIDNES
MEN. THE JUDGE ON FLOGGING.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Day, Patrick Ginley, aged 23, Michael Ginley aged 34, and Anthony Ginley, aged 28, Irish labourers, were indicted for having, on the 13th September last, maliciously wounded Robert Moores, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, and also with wounding George Stanley, Alfred Moore, and Philip Parkinson, of Widnes, with a similar intent, at Weol- ton, on the 13th September. Mr. Heywood prosecuted, and Mr. T. Swift appeared for the defence. It was stated that Moores and the other men were going from Hunt's Cross Stearin along Speke-road on the night of the 13th September last, towards Woolton, when shortly before ten o'clock they met a gang of about 15 men, to whom they said "Good night." The men answered, 'We will give you good night," , and then the gang rushed upon them and inflicted on all of them the most serious injury. Robert Moores received ' seven woancla on the head, his nose was smashed, and he recei-ed other injuries of a serious nature. These injuries, it was allegee, were inflicted upon him while he was lying on the ground by the clogs of the men who attacked him. Several witnesses were called to identify the prisoners, two of whom were apprehended at Speke ' the following morning, with Moores' hat in their poseession.—The jury found the first-named prisoner guilty of unlawfully wounding, and acquitted the other prisoners on the ground urged for the detmce, of mistaken identity. —Mr. Heywood then said that there were two other counts in the indictment on which he could proceed against pri- soners, and, sating on his privilege on behalf of the Crown, be should challenge the jury. A new jury was then sworn, and the prisoners were charged with wounding John Jack- son on the same night with intent to do grievous bodily harm.—Jackson was called, and stated he heard the cries of the other men, and went to their assistance. He was knocked down by the prisoners, and brutally kicked.—The prisoners were all found guilty of unlawfully wounding. Sentence was deferred until Tuesday, when his Lordship, addressing the prisoners, said : You have been convicted on the clearest possible evidence of a brutal and dastardly at- tack on these young men. A more cowardly piece of ruf- fianism I never conceived it possible there could be found in England. You ruffians formed part of a gang who set upon two or three harmless men in the road, and treated them in an outrageous manner. They gave you no provo- cation, and were proceeding along peaceably towards their homes, when you rushed upon them and then, after you had got them upon the ground, you kicked and ill-used them in a hideous manner. Such a dastardly, cowardly, brutal crime could not be found, in England if it were ndt found to be committed by men who are, unfortunately, im- ported into this country. I really don't ,know how to deal with you. If 1 had my way I would deal with you very effectively, and in a way which would prevent ye: or any- one else for some time to come committing a crime of this description. I don't see why men lik2 you should be main- tined by the country for a long time with too Much comfort. If the law only allowed ens to do what I think ought to be dune and what justice and the interests of society demand, I would not al- low you to be kept for any length of time by the honest tiapayers of the country. I would have you thoroughly well flogged, and more than once. And when you have sufficiently recovered I would have turned you out to earn your own living. But I cannot do that. The law does not allow me. It is a pity it does not, in the interests of jus- tice and society. Therefore, I must sentence the country to maintain you. You will be each imprisoned and kept to bard labour for 18 calendar months. The prisoners were removed below.
THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
MAKTNO A START WITH POULTRY.

Every Spriniand Autumn we have a number of in- quiries as to thete,st way in which tocommence poultry keeping, for it is at one or other of these seasons that most persons make their.first start in this pursuit. We always feel, therefore, that at these times we should provide some hints as fe, guide to those who have not hitherto been in the ranks of poultry keepers, and those whp do not come under the designation of novices, will, we are sure feel that the space given is well utilised in this way. They, themselves, have known the difficul- ties, the doubts, the troubles of novitiate, and can sym- pathise with such as are in a like condition now. It is to the interest of every poultry breeder to encourage others to follow in their footsteps, and itis one of the best traits of poultry fanciers—both exhibitors and non- exhibitors—that they are ever ready to give the fruits of their experience to those who are new in the pursuit. But for this the path of the amateur would be very much,harder than it need now be. If he will ask for, he can have the mature advice and wise counsel of others, who will thus help him very materially. Of the two great seasons for starting with poultry, namely, the spring and the autumn, weprefer the latter. Our reasons are these :—ln the spring it is true that by purchasing eggs and hatching the required fowls from them, the first cost will be small, but then there is the long summer, the autumn, and perhaps the winter to wait, ere the birds begin to be productive. Whereas, on the other hand, pullets can be bought at reasonable prices in the autumn, for breeders are very desirous to gat rid of their surplus stocks. And these if bought rightly—that is, young pullets hatched in March or April—will begin to lay probably at once, continuing more or less all through the winter. Thus there will come an immediate repayment for the outlay, and the fact of getting some new-laid eggs will entirely make up for the annoyances and troubles which ever come to the amateur at first. It is surprising what a state of ex- citement there is when the first egg is laid, especially if it is soon after the birds are first introduced. General joy is felt„ and the enthusiasm for the new venture is universal in all that household. But if by some mistake r the hens do not commence laying, the daily journey to the nests may be regarded as a duty, but it soon loses its pleasure. "Efope deferred maketh the heart sick" is as true of poultry keeping as anything else. The zest of the business speedily assumes an evanescent charac- ter, and gradually vanishes away. In this manner many a budding poultry fancier has been chilled at the outset, and this frost of disappointment is deadly in- deed. Nothing can ever bring back the first glow of enthusiasm, as nothing can make to bloom again the withered leaf. E'er these reasons, therefore, we suggest the present as the best time to commence poultry-keep- .

I am, Sir, yours truly. William Brent.
Mr. A. J. White.

Now, it is useless buying fowls without there is a place to put them. And the first consideration is, how are they to be housed? On a farm there is seldom. much difficulty. in this way. Usually; there are sheds or outlying, buildings which, without much expense,. can be devoted to the birds. But with suburban or town residents and cottagers the case is altogether dif- ferent, and they must needs adapt some existing build- ing, or, what is more often the case, put up some eree• tion for thepurpose. If the former has to be done, the. great thing, is to seeethat it is dry, well ventilated, but not draughty, and, not too, cold.. If a stone or brick erection, it should be carefully pointed and the root examined, and if theinsicle:of the walls are very rough,. the creviceslad better be filled up with mortar, and, then well whitewashed over with thick limewash, in which some carbolic acid has been mixed, three or four times. The. object is to prevent, as far as possible, any harbourage•being give to vermin. Nothing gives better shelterto these pests than an uneven surface on the walls of a. poultry-house. They, capnot be seen in the. day-time, but at night they come mit on their predatory errand, to the utter misery of the luckless fowls. . Generally when a house has to be erected wood is the material chosen, arul if of a proper thickness, well put together, and tarred or painted, it is just as warm as brick or stone. It will not last so long, but it is much cheaper-to, begin with, so that all things considered the two are about equal. If the house isto be a small one, say not more than five or six feet square, it is best to. build it entire, as. then it can be readily moved. But if larger than that, the sides should be made each separate;. the roof also, and put together with bolts, so that it can. be taken,to pieces and removed at any time. We re- cently were in the yard of a once large exhibitor, who, had at a great expense put up large permanent houses.. He has given up keeping fowls on an extensive scale), but the houses are unsaleable simply because they can- not be removed. If they had been made in sections they could have been sold at good prices half a dozen times over. /n a matter of this kind to prepare for what may happen, though improbable at the moment, is always the wiser course. Wooden houses remain tenant's property, and provision should, therefore, be made in case a removal is necessary, or, if the property is occupied by the owner, and he decides to put up a brick erection, which it may be well worth his while to do, it will be a good plan to pla,ceit in such a position, and build it in such a manner,that if for any reason . the fowls are afterwards dispensed with, it can be 'adapted to some other purpose, We have often seen money wasted for want of a little simple forethought. SEASONABLE HINTS.

We have often been asked whai..ii--the best soft food for poultry and have recommended barley, wheat, and buckwheat meals. If millers would take the trouble to grind it properly they would soon find plenty of custom for it. But prejudice dies hard. The oats must be stout and dry, and the stones newly dressed.
