div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The House met a 4-15. THE FRANCHISE. Lord GRANVILLE rose in an attentive House to make a proposal on the part of the Government with the view of solving the difficulty in connection with the Reform ques- tion. Having observed that the action to be taken by their lordships' Heuse this week would be of great importance in its geneial bearings, and having briefly stated the points of difference between the majority of their lordships and the Ministry, he said he was authorised by her Majesty's Government to state that they thought it pessible to meet the objections raised to their mode of procedure by some of the members el their lordships' House. Without semi- 'ficing their object, the Government could not come to any understanding unless they received an assurance that the Franchise Bill should pass at an early date, that was this autumn ; but, if they received that assurance, they would be prepared to make the main provisions of a Redistribu- tion Bill, or even a draft of a bill drawn in accordance with the plan sketched by Mr. Gladstone on the 7th inst., the -subject of friendly communication. They would under- take to more in the House of Commons the second reading of the Redistribution Bill simultaneously with the Fran- chise Bill going into Committee, or reaching any further stage in their lordships House; and they would further undertake to proceed with the Redistribution Bill at all I possible speed so that it might pass through the House of Commons at an early period of next year.—Lord SALTS- Huss, without at the moment expressing any opinion on the proposal itself, asked whether the passing of the Fran-, chise Bill before Christmas was to be a condition precedent and whether an agreement between the Government and the Opposition on the principles of redistribution was to be a condition precedent.--Lord GRANVILLE answered the fret question in the affirmative, and the second in the neg- ative.—The LORD CHANCELLOR added that an agree- ment to pass the Franchise Bill must precede everything. If there were to be communications between the Govern- ment and the Opposition, time must be allowed for them ; but, on an assurance that the Franchise Bill would be pas- sed without delay, the Government would be prepared to at once produce their Redistribution Bill. THE BERLIN TREATY.—Tbe Duke of ARGYLL, having made some observations to justify his inquiry, asked whether the Secretary for Foreign Affairs had any recent information as to the fulfilment by the Turkish Government of the Treaty of Berlin, and as to the alleged outrages by. the Turkish authorities in Macedonia.—Lord GRANVILLE stated that Her Majesty's Government had succeeded in pro- curing the fulflment by Turkey of some of the provisions of the treaty. As to others they had been unsuccessful. Our own Consuls had not confirmed the accounts of the atrocities in Macedonia, and the Turkish Ambassador denied the veracity of those accounts. Their lordships rose at 5.50. HOUSE OF COMMONS—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. NEW Wnors were ordered for Greenock and county Down. Mr. O'DONNELL gave notice of his intention to question the ruling of the Speaker in suspending him. THE REFORM BILLS.—GOVERNMENT STATE- MENT. Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with cheers, said a great deal had been said in regard to the present circum- stances—about an interchange of views between the dif- ferent parties, and about the question whether the Govern- ment ought to introduce a Bill relating to the redistribution of seats before the Franchise Bill passed the other House. 3 here was no very conclusive objection to-such communica- tions. He continued: With respect to the Bill recently before us, and with respect to the settlemer,t of the question of the representation of the people, the object of the Go- vernment is to secure the passing of the Franchise Bill with- I out delay. (Ministerial cheers.) We could not, consistently, with our-sense of duty, enter into any understanding, and we could not take any step as to the immediate introduction of a bill relating to the redistribution of seats, or relating to any particular connection therewith, unless the understanding were each as to afford us an adequate assurance that we should thereby secure the attainment of our purpose—viz, the passing of the Franchise Bill without delay—that is to say, during the present autumnal sitting. (Cheers.) The House is aware that if that object was attained, the Franchise BM would then come into operation, and take effect on the let of January, 1886. (Hear, hear.) Now, if we are ade- quately assured of the attainment of that object, I am not aware of any demand likely to be made in relation to pro- ceeding upon the other measure to which we should not be able to accede. (Hear, hear.) I specify the three follow- ing points :—Tri the first place, we should be ready either to make the main provisions of our bill, or tbe draft bill itself, the subject of friendly communication at once, and before its introduction, and to make every reasonable effort for accommodation in regard to its particulars, or we should be ready, apart from what I have just said, to presents bill to the House at once in the spirit of that sketch which I may best describe by saying that it•was noticed very much by the right hon. member for Ripon, and which, as we thought, was favourably received by the right hon. baronet the member for North Devon, on Friday, the 7th November. The second point is that we should be ready to prosecute the measure with all possible speed, even to the point of moving the second reading simultaneously with the passing of the Franchise Bill into Committee of the House of Lords, or, if procedure there rendered that im- practicable, then simultaneously with any subsequent stage. Ido not refer to any proceeding simultaneous with the second reading in the House of Lords, because the time is too short to introduce that practically into the question, and, secondly, because we have understood that the second reading of the bill is not to be a contested stage upon the present occasion. Thirdly, we are quite willing to make the passing of our bill for the redistribution of seats a vital question for ourselves, and also to use our best efforts to bring it to an issue in the House of Commons early innhe coming year. (Hear, hear.) That is the subject of the communication I have to make, and which I have been authorised by my colleagues in a matter of such deep in- terest to convey to the House. (Cheers.) Sir S. NORTHCOTE reserved his opinion on the statement, and subsequently, in answer to Mr. S. Morley and Sir W. Lawson, Mr. GLADSTONE said that his pledge to make the Redistribution Bill a vital question referred to both Houses, and that the Government might be trusted to see that the security which they took was adequate. THE LETTER FROM GENERAL GOWDON.—CoI. STANLEY asked the Secretary of State for War whether he was able to give the House any further information respecting the letter from General Gordon, or whether there were any fur- ther details that he could communicate without detriment to the public service.—The Marquis of HARTING- TON : We have received an abstract of the letter from General Gordon, which was received by Major Kitchener, dated 4th November. The contents of that letter have been stated with accuracy in the news- papers, so far at least as it is expedient to make them public at present. I may state that General Gordon himself says, "The Mandi knows everything, so care must be taken of what is published." There are two items which I am not quite certain have appeared in the newspapers. One is that General Gordon states that the Greek and Austrian Consuls are all right, and he wishes the newspapers to say that be has received letters from Sir Samuel Baker, his sister, and ' Stanley on the Congo, but he does not want any more pH. vete letters sent, as the risk is too great. q may add that news has been received from another source that a friendly tribe have captured a convoy of 3,000 camels on their way to join the enemy. WOMEN'S 617FFRAGE.—Mr. WOODALL intimated that he did not Mid himself in a position to move the second read- ing of the bill for extending the Parliamentary franchise to women.

THE WAR EXPENDITURE.—ADDITION TO THE INCOME TAX. The House having gone into Committee of Supply, The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER explained his financial proposals for meeting the supplementary estimates for the Nile and Bechuanaland expeditions. At the outset he reminded the House that by the Budget estimate of last session he had provided for a revenue of £85,533,000 and an expenditure of £85,427,000, leaving a surplus of £lOO,OOO. The expenditure had gone on much as was anticipated, and there had been a slight increase in the receipts. The usual supplementary estimates of the year would be provided for by savings on other votes. But the supplementary estimates in connection with Egypt and South Africa‘ in- cluding the vote of credit of £300,000 of last session, amounted to £2,34.9,000, which, if not provided for by ad- ditional taxation, would leave a deficit at the end of the financial year of about £2,C00,000. Raving carefully con- sidered the various modes ,by which this mightbe met, and giving due weight to the consideration that an increasee indirect taxation at this period of the year would cause great disturbance of trade, he announced that he would pro- pose to raise the income tax from 5d to 6d. The total sum: thus to be obtained he calculated at £1,020,000, of which 0n1v,1,200,000 would be received in the current financial, year, leaving £720,000 to be collected after March next.l The balances, he added, would be sufficient to make good' the differences until they were ,recouped by the incoming of the arrears. Lord C.I.EORGE lIAMILTRN condemned the enormous ex- penditure of the Government, who bad spent £29;006,000 more during their first five years of office than the late ,Government in their last five years. The present expendi- .turo was the largest ever known, and he trusted the extra imposition 'would bring home to everyone the cost and price .of perpetual vacillation and ineptitude. Mr. PETER RYLANDS was not surprised at the proposals of ,the Government and the dismal statement of the Chancellor .of the Exchm-ter, seeing how much the Government had gone in the footsteps of their predecessors. Extravagance had gone on in the dockyards and la other departments, and he almost abandoned hope of seeing economy practised. Mr. Gorst, Mr. H. IL Fowler, and Mr. W. IL Smith con- tinued the debate. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tunsriax. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15, ard a quarter of an holm later, when public business began, there was a large attendance of peers on both sides. A number of peeresses were seated in the side galleries, and the CommOnS and strangers' galleries were crowded. Amongst these who stood on the steps of the Throne were Sir S. Northcote, Sir Charles Dilke, Sir R. Cross, Lord John Manners, Mr. Low- ther, Mr. W. H. Smith, and Mr. IL C. Raikes. THE FRANCHISE BILL READ A SECOND TIME. The Earl of lirutimmcv, in moving the second reading of the Representation of the People Bill, said as there was, he believed, now a very general agreement in favour of the principles of the Bill, it was quite unnecessary for him to trouble the Hoisee rrith Any advocacy of those principles.

he measure was precisely the same as that which was be- fore the House last session. As to the question how and when the Bill should pass into law, and the question of the Redistribution Bill, width had engaged so much atten- tion in the ether House, he had nothing to add or take from the declaration mode by Earl Granville on the pre- vous night. kThe noble Earl's remarks occupied three minutes only.) The Marquis of SALISBURY entirely concterred with the noble Earl that there was no need to enter into a prolonged discussion on the principles of the bill. With respect to the matter of the speech, he was at first not so well satisfied. He drew from the language of the noble Earl the inference that before any consultation or communication could take place with regard to the Redisttibution Bill for the purpose of corning to an arrangement, it was an indispensible con- dition—precedent in the eyes of the Government—that the Opposition should undertake that the Franchise Bill should pass into law before the close of the year. There were ob- jections to that, for they -would, if they entered into such an undertaking, have been parting with their liberty with- out obtaining anything in return. Some of his friends did not understand the Prime Minister's statement to have been of that character, and, in answer to a communication from Mr. Balfour asking whether the entire surrender of their liberty with regard to the Franchise Bill was to be a condi- tion of the agreement, Lord Hartington intimated that the Government woald receive a request for -consultation in a spirit of trust, and assuming that the intention was to come to an agreement, would not ask for an adequate assurance beforehand. The importance of that statement it was impossible to exaggerate, for according to it, it was now possible for the Opposition to enter into communication with respect to the details of the Bedistribution Bill, and if they did not enter into an agreement which would enable the Franchise Bill to be passed, they would stand precisely in their present position. Mr. Gladstone would receive any proposal or communication in a spirit of trust, and the feeling was entirely reciprocal on the part of the Opposi- tion. (Cheers.) He should propose on Thursday that the committee stage of the bill should be adjourned for a fort- night to enable communication to be entered inte. If their lordshiptecarried their minds back to the controversy last Jaly, they would remember that the objection to the course taken by the Government was that the Opposition feared there might be no Redistribution, or that there might not be a good Redistribution scheme to accempany the Franchise Bill. The Government gave an assurance that they intended legislation on the subject, bet then there came the question as to their power to carry a Redistribu- tion scheme into law. The security the Government now proposed to give was substantial, and he anti his friends thoeght it ample. If they understood it rightly, the Go- vernment would press the measure forward with all possible speed, and the important point was that they would regard ,it as vital to their Government. He understood that to mean that they would regard as vital not merely the second reading,'out all the provisions upon which both partierfagreed. Mr. Gladstone had been understood to say that the question of-vitality applied to the passage of the bill through the House of Lords as well through the Commons, but the right hon. gentleman bad since said that he desired to re- consider that statement. The alteration was important, and I induced him to press upon the leader of that House to in- clude in his definition of the failures which should be vital to the Government the failure to pass the Redistribution Eill in 1885. He welcomed with great -satisfaction the dis- position the Government had shown to meet that House in a oonciliatory manner, and the position they had taken up fully satisfied the requirements the Cpposition had laid down. (Cheers.) Earl GreeNvILLE fully acknowledged the conciliatory spirit of the noble marquis's remarks, and was glad to find that the willingness of Mr. Gladstone to put a favourable construction upon what occurred on the previous evening was more than justified by the willingness of the leader of the Opposition and his friends to enter into communi- cation with the Government on the -subject of redistribu- tion. As to the passing of the bills:Rely next year, he did not think he could add anything- to the pledge of the Government to use every effort to mush it through at an early period. With regard to their power so to do there could not be the slightest doubt if the efforts of the Govern- ment were seconded, as after what had fallen from the , noble marquis he was sure they would be by the Conserva- tive party. (Hear, hear.) He was authorised by Mr. Gladstone to say that the answer given by him on the pre- vious night was intended to widen the assurance that had been given to their lordsbipe' House. After what had passed he felt satisfied -that this great question was about to be brought to a final and satisfactory settle- ment. The Marquis of SALISBURY asked whether the making of the bill a vital question referred to details as well as prin- ciple ? Earl GRANVILLE did not like answering questions upon his own responsibility, but speaking for himself he had not the slightest doubt that it was meant to make a vital ques- tion of the passing of the bill with all its general principles and characteristics. Their lordstriee would not, of course, expect the Government to pledge themselves not to admit amendments agreed upon by both Houses. The Marquis of SALISBURY wiehed to understand whether it was to be made a vital question that the bill should be passed next year? Earl GRANVILLE thought the Government ought not to be expected to give a more precise answer than they had done on that point. They had made a solemn declaration involving their personal honour to do everything in their power to pass the bill next year. The bill was then read a second time, and on the com- mittee stage being formally fixed for Thursday, the Marquis of SALISBURY gave notice that on- that day he should move the postponement of the committee for a fortnight. Their lordships rose at 5-15. Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Lord G. Hamilton,vindicated his Midlothian comparisons of Conservative and Liberal finances, and insisted that the whole war expenditure of the present Government was due to the acts of their predeces- sors, and especially to the engagement to support the Khe- dive in conjunction with France and the ill-omened and dis- honourable annexation of the Transvaal. It was true that there had been banded over to them a set of questions such as, were never left to any Goverment. Had it always been. the case that every outgoing Administration had left to its successors a legacy of difficulties such as now seemed to be the case? In 1874, when the late Government came into office, it had not been in office a week or a fortnight before be who held the seals of the Fereign Office declared that in every portion of the world the relations of this country were thoroughly satisfactory. (Ministerial cheers.) In conclu- sion, the right hon. gentleman replied to Mr. Rylands, and 3aid he was convinced the nation wculd be just to the Go- ment, to the difficulties they had had to contend against, and to the efforts they had made to meet them. (Ministerial cheers.) Sir S. NORTHCOTE ridiculed as an insult to common sense the Prime Minister's contention that his Government was not responsible for the expenditure which the House was now providing. After some further debate the resolution granting the in- 'crease of the income tax was agreed tc, and the House ad- . ;earned at 8-25 until Wednesday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter to one, there being no quorum before that hour. NEW WRIT.—On the motion of Lord R Grosvenor, a new writ was ordered to issue for the election of a member of Parliament for Scarborough in room of Mr. Caine, who has accepted the office of Civil Lord of the Admiralty. -PEERS AND THE CIVIL SERVICE„—Mr. A. Arnold gave notice to ask whether, in view of the recent Treasury minute declaring Civil Service appointments to be inconsis- tent with candidature for Parliamentary seats, an address would be submitted to the Queen praying that the writ of summons for the House of Lords, in the case of any peer accepting office in the Civil Service, should be cancelled. • COMPENSATION FOR IMPROVEMENT (IRLLAND) BILL.— Colonel Notes moved the second reading of this Bill, the object of which he explained to be to give the tenant a right to compensation for improvements in small towns and eillages.—Mr. CAmpBELL-BANNERMAS said the Govern- ment could not accept any proposal of this sort on the ground that it was a simple extension of the Land Act. That Act had been passed on principles that did not apply to this.onestion at all.—Mr. J. McCARTny said he thought the Bill would be good for large towns, and for England and Scotland.—Mr. A. ARNOLD supported the Bill on its being distinctly provided that the compensation should be limited to the improvement of the letting value.—The Bill was supported by Colonel Colthurst, Mr. McCoan, and Mr. O'Sullivan.—The House divided—For the second reading, 32_Ld against, 40—§. WOMAN BUFFRAGE.—Mr. WOODALL moved for leave to bring in a bill for extending the Parliamentary franchise to women.—The SPEAKER put the question, and his deci- sion that the" Ayes" had it was challenged by Mr. War- ton. The Speaker then asked the hon. member who would " tell " with him, when Mt. Kenny volunteered to do so, amid loud cries of" Oh " from the Liberal benches. The House then divided, when there appeared--Tor the motion, :29; against, 8---21. The Bill was brought in and read a first time. The House adjourned at ten minutes post two o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THCRE.DeIf. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. Lord Howard of Glossop took his seat and signed the roll of peers. SCATE OF THE NAVY, &C.—The Earl of NORTHBROOK announced that his statement as to the condition of the navy wou:d not be made until Monday week. Whilst in posses- sion.cf the House, the noble earl took occasion to complain of the multitudinous rumours which had been circulated regarding his report to the Government upon Egyptian finance, and which were mostly without foundation. The telegrams from Egypt, he added, were notoriously fall of inaccuracies. InisnPoolt-LAw GUARDIANS.—The Irish Poor-law Guar- dians Bill was briefly discussed as a Government measure, read asecond time, and referred to a Eelect Committee. THE FRANCHISE Bree.—On the order for going into com- mittee on the Franchise Bill a (short discussion ensued.— Earl GRANVILLE said it was not pronoced that the House should sit next week except on Monday or Tuesday.— Lord SALISBURY said they would be ready to proceed with the bill on Monday week, and if contentious matter should arise they could taite a further adjournment.---It was then agreed to postpone the committee until the let prox. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty-five minutes after five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THrESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS—Mr JACOB BRIGHT questioned the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs about the instructions which had been given to the British representative at the Congo

Conference in regard to the claims of Portugal.—Lord E. FITIMAITRICE said he must decline to give any information on the subject, but, as he had already stated, the discussion lof territorial claims did not come within the purview of the Conference. The same noble Lord informed Mr. Bartlett that Her Majesty's Government had been in communication with the French and Chinese Governments with reference to the suspension of the hostilities between the two coun- tries, but as Yet without any practical result. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL.— Mr. LABOUCHERE asked whether the House would be put in possession of the redistribution scheme as settled by Her Majesty's Government, and of the alterations thereof agreed to at the instance of Lord Salisbury, and whether the Government would regard as vital the passing of the Redis- tribution Bill by the House of Lords.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the communications between the Government and the repre- sentatives of the Opposition would be confidential. He thought hecould say that an understanding prevailed as tt) what wan just and equitable in the matter. The Govern- ment would regard the passing of their bill in the House of 'Commons as a vital question. As to the House of Lords, It was impossible to answer absolutely for the action of the majority there, but what was justly to be expected of the Government in the House of Lords was that they should use every effort to pass the Bill in 1885. In answer to further questions, Mr. Gladstone said the report as to the appokatment of a joint committee on the Redistribution Bill was, so far as he was aware, without any foundation. It was not possible for communications to be held on the subject with the several sections of the House combined, but he would be glad to give his attention to any communications ow the subject. It could hardly be supposed that Her Majesty's Government would have pro- ceeded down to this point without holding communication with the senicr member for Birmingham (Mr. Bright). EGYPTIAN FINANCE, &c.—ln reference to Egyptian finance, the PREMIER said that the Government had given their beat attention to the recommendations of Lord North- brook, and were now engaged in framing proposals which they intended to bring under the consideration of the Powers.—Mr. GORST afterwards criticised Sir C. Warren's instructions, and received from Mr. CHAMBERLAIN assur- ances which Mr. Forster and Sir M. Hicks-Beach thought satisfactory. The House ad4.curned at six o'clock.
FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N. LETTERS FROM GENERAL GORDON.—TRIBAL CONFLICT NEAR bUAKINI. DONGOTA, SATURDAY.—Lord Wolseley received last night a letter from General Gordon. The General deeply regrets the wreck of the steamer which he despatched to Dongola with Colonel Stewart, Mr. Power, M. Herbin, and thirty others on board, and the massacre of those gentlemen. He is much delighted to hear of the advance of the British troops, and hopes to be able to hold out until their arrival. He continues with his steamers to harass the Mandi's force, which is attempting to approach Khartoum. The Mandi himself is at a day's journey from Khartoum. The letter, which is dated November 4th, is the first which Lord Wol- Beteg has received from General Gordon. The same mes- senger was sent by Major Kitchener two months ago with despatches to General Gordon, and took the caravan route between Debbeh and Khartoum. WADY HAIFA, SATURDAY:A squadron of the 10th Hus- sars arrived here to-day, and one company of the Royal Engineers started far the front. The advanced party of the Staffordshire Regiment has reached Tangur. Over 400 whale boats have now passed the second cataract, and 200 of them have proceeded on their journey up the Nile. WADY EIALFA., SUNDAY.—The passage of the advanced ' detachment of the Ist South Staffordshire Regiment up the Ambigol Cataract was not effected without mishap. Col. Eyre's whale boat struck en a rock while it was being towed up the rapid and sank, all the stores and kits being lost. Only two Canadian boatmen were on board at the time of the accident, and they were rescued. Two other whale boats were damaged near the same place, and a sergeant was drowned. WADY HALFA, MONDAY.—Lord Wolseley returned here last night in order to discuss matters with General Sir Redvers Buller, being unable to do so by telegraph. He will return to Dongola to-night. CAIRO, SUNDAY.—The friendly Beni Amers have inflicted a severe defeat on the Hadendowas, near Suakim, capturing a convoy of provisions and corn destined for Osman Digna, together with 3,000 camele. Cam, MONDAY,—The Mudir of Dongola has sent a tele- gram saying that he has received a message from General Gordon conferring upon him the high rank of Mushir, and also promoting several of his officials and etnployAs a step I in rank. The General likewise states that several sums of money are to be expended on objects which he specifies. The messenger is to receive half the reward agreed upon for the safe delivery of the message from the Mudir, General Gordon having paid him the other half before he set out on his perilous journey. The Mudir telegraphs that the rest of the message is not important, the General saying only that he is well, and is expectiug the British troops. Re ex- horts the Mudir to hold out to the last, as he intends to do himself. The hearing of the case between the Government and the Caisse is deferred until the 25th inst. DONGOLA, TUESDAY—lntelligence has been received here that about twenty days ago the rebels returned in force to Omderrean. General Gordon sent two steamers to shell them, but the rebels replied with Krupp Ltins, disabling the paddle of one steamer and compelling both to return to Khartoum. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—The military authorities have under consideration the eventuality of deferring the return of the Nile expedition until the next rising of the river. DONGOLO, WEDNESDAY.—Eight mild cases ef small-pox have occurred among the troops here. Every precaution against the spread of the disease has been taken, and the camping grounds where it appeared have beerechanged. The Nile is falling rapidly, thus rendering large nuggars useless at the cataracts. FRANCE AND CHINA.—TRE OCCUPATION OF TAM-

PRISONERS BEHEADED. PARIS, SA.TIIRDLY.—The following has been received from Shanghai:—" Some European firms have received a tele- gram from Amoy stating that it was reported there that Tamsui had been taken." SHANGHAI, SATURDAY.—From a European source, dated Haiphong, 30th ult, we learn that "the Annamite Auxili- aries decapitated 500 Ch'nese prisoners at Kep. Bac44 is unoccupied by the French. who have feztified Ken, Dong- lieu, and Kwangyen, on the northern edge of the Delta. Large reinforcements are required to recommence cpera- lions. Several hundred sick left in a transport yesterday*" Other information gives the recent losses at 500 men.—

SHANGRAT, MONDAY.—The Chinese Government has arranged for English and American blockade-runners to Formosa from various points of the coast. Thirteen Ger- mans engaged for war service by the Chinese Government arrived at Tientsin on the 7th met, and 42 more are daily expected. Twenty to thirty thousand Chinese soldiers rossed the Yang-the southward last month near Poynam Lake. Operations blocking Woosung Bar are actively pro- ceeding. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—The France of this evening states that a telegram has been received from Admiral Courbet announcing the appearance of a few Chinese blockade run- ners off Formosa, thus compelling the Admiral to extend the line of position of his squadron and to remain on the defensive until the arrival of reinforcements. FRANCE.

MONITEATI-LES-MINES, SATDRDAY.—Five other arrests I have been made here in connection with the recent attempt to blow up the house of a foreman with dynamite, making a total of 18 arreste up to the present. Pears, MONDAY.—In the,Chamber of Deputies to-day M. Leroy read the report of the Tonquin Committee in favour of the despatch of further reinforcements, adding that the Government had declared that the sum of 40,800,000 f would be required for the maintenance of the troops during the first half of 1885. PARIS, TUESDAY.—The Tariff Committee of the Chamber of Deputies to-day approved, by six against five votes, the principle of the increase in import duties on corn and flour. It was resolved to confer with the Government on the amount of the increase. THE CHOLERA IN PARIS. PARIS, TUESDAY EVENING.—The cholera deaths in this city for the last four days have been :—Sunday 44, Monday 36, and up to 6 p.m. to-day 30. Two deaths have been reported from Nantes, and four occurred on the French ironclad Admiral Duperre. Four deaths are reported from Oran. Peale. WEDNESDAY —There were 41 deaths here yester- day from cholera, 16 of which occurred in the city and 25 in the hospitals. This morning there have been only four deaths. Forty cholera patients were yesterday admitted to the hospitals.

SOUTH AFRICA. CaPrrowN (rod PLymorrru), Ocr. 29m.—The text of General Joubert's letter conveying his resignation to the Volksraad has beea transmitted here from Pretoria. He denies that his resignation was due to any difference with President Kruger, and describes it solely to his entire dis- approval of the breach of the Convention by the proclama- tion in Bechuanaland of a Protectorate. Umquikela has recovered from illness, and has expressed his willingness to co-operate with the Government in putting down border dis- turbances. On Sunday last desperate fighting occurred between the rondos and the Xesibes in the Xesibe country., and the Pondos were driven back with loss. More fighting is expected between the parties. ROBBERY AND MURDER IN GREECE. ATHENS, SATERDAY.—The cashier and sub-cashier of the French Lauriurn Mining Company, while driving to the mines front Laurium with 100,000 in money to pay the workmen' were fired upon by a party of men who were in ambush, and were both killed. Their coachman was also dangerously wounded. The Assassins escaped. ATHENS, MONDAY—TWO of the assassins of the cashier and sub-cashier of the French Mining Company at Lan- rium have been arrested at Liborici, in Northern Greece, and a sum of 41,000 f. in bank notes was found in their pos- session.

THE MARQUIS OF RIPON. DEVITT, SATURDLY.—Upwards of a thousand addresses .'rom all parts of India have been presented to Lord Ripon. In replying to some of. these his Lordship ex- pressed the belief that India was never more loyal than at the present time. Lord Ripon referred in eulogistic terms to the successful working of the local self-government scheme in India. UNITED STATES.—THE PRESIDENTIAL ELECT/ON.

NEW YORE, SATIIRDAY.—An accident has occurred on the Houston and Texas Central Railroad through a train running off the metals and being. precipitated down the embankment. Ten persons were killed and fifteen others injured. PHILADELPHIA MONDAY.—The New York city official count was completed on Saturday. Some slight errors were found and were corrected. Mr. Cleveland has 1,105 majority over Mr. Blaine in New York State. The aggre- gate vote of the State is :—Cleveland, 463,103 ; Blaine, 461,998; Butler, 16,918; St. John, 25,115. Tbis result, which makes Cleveland President, giving him 219 electors to 182 for Blaine, is universally accepted. The Democrats already show a disposition to claim the Federal offices when Cleveland is inaugurated, but there are strong indications that he will observe the Civil Service reform docrrine, which largely brought him the support of the independent Republicans. BECHUANALAND DIFFICULTIES. CAPETOWN, SATIIRDAY.—Mr. Upiegisan, the Premier and, Mr. Gordon, Treasurer-General of the Cape Ministry, have arrived in Bechuanaland with the object of effecting a peaceable settlement of existing difficulties. They have had' an interview with Mankoroane, at which the latter said both he and Montsioa had been duped, and that he placed no confidence in anybody but Sir Charles Warren. Accord- ing to reports received here, the Goschem and Stellaland Boers have broken off their alliance with the Transvaal, stating that they will fight on their own account in order to retain their farms. THE WEST AFRICAN CONFERENCE. BERLIN, SATIIRDAY.—The Sittings of the West African Conference were formally opened by Prince Bismark, at two o'clock this afternoon, in the dining-hall of the Imperial Chancellor's residence, the same room as was occupied by the Conference of 1878. After presenting their full powers and eo_sidering certain preliminary merely formal details, the delegates were addressed by Prince Bismark in a short speech, which created general satisfaction by its moderate and pacific character. The details of the Conference were not touched upon by the Imperial Chancellor. The proceed. ings terminated to. day about four o'clock. The Times states that to the opening address of Prince Bismark Sir Edward Malet replied by reading a short paper, in which, while echoing the Chancellor's philanthropic sen- timents and accepting the three points enumerated as the basis of discussion, his Excellency made this reservation with respect to the Niger :—Hi a Government, he said, was

Played on the ground of the latter. The game was evenly contested in the first half. When they changed ends neither side had scored, and when time was called the result was a victory for the Albion by one goal and one disputed
to nil. RuNcoRN REcREA.Ttox 2ND (LATE WANDERERS) V. RUN-

CiORN TAM O'SHANTERS.—This match was played last Saturday on the Recreation ground, the result being as fol- lows :—Tam O'Shanters, 3 tries; Recreation, 1 try. This was acknowledged by all to be the most satisfactory. The play of Davies at half-back for the Recreation is worthy of mention, while the forwards all worked well together. WARRINGTON ERCELSIOR V. SIMII'S CROSS AMATEURS (Widnes).—The return match between the above clubs was played on the ground of the former at Warrington on Sat- urday. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors, it was de- cided to play twenty minutes each way. Warburton kick- ed off for Warrington, and after some sharp play Allford obtained possession of the ball, and after a good run punted over the line, when nether rushed up and secured a try. Warburton failed to score. After the change of ends, Wid- nes tried hard to score, but could not owing to the good play of the Excelsior forwards, and Speakman and Mather half-backs. At the call of time Warrington were left vic- torious by 1 try 4 minor points to 1 minor point. RUNCORN RECREATION V. WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES. —On Saturday afternoon last th 3 Recreation paid a visit to Warrington to play off their fixture with the above club. The Warrington captain won the toss and elected to play with the wind, the Recreation captain kicking off. For some time play was kept up in neutral ground, until W. Riley ran in and obtained the first try for the Recreation, no goal resulting. After a series of touchdowns in self-defence by ' the Blues, Lunt obtained the second try'for Runcorn. After half-time play was kept up in the home 25 for a time, when W. Riley obtained another try. After a touchdown time was called, leaving the Recreation after a very noisy and rough game, victors by three tries, five minor points to one minor point. PEASLEY CROSS Y.M.C.A. T. ST. HELENS AMATEURS. —The newly-formed club of the Y.M.C.A., at Peasley Cress, played their first match on Saturday last, on their own ground, against the St. Helens Amateurs. The Y.M.C.A. won their first match by two goals and one dis- puted to one. Teanes—Peasley Cross Y.M.C.A. : Goal, R. Litherland ; backs, E. Rogers and A. Baldwin ; half- backs, J. H. Garner and R. Guest ; left wing, %V. Mil- ler and T. Davies; right wing, J. R. Turner and J. W. Crooks; centres, J. Johnson and T. Grundy. St. Helens Amateurs: Goal, J. Wright; backs, F. Sutton and J. Gibbon; half-backs, J. Holt and M. Sexton ; right wing, R. Scott and T. Howard; left wing, W. Lowe and J. Hill; centres, S. Etheridge and J. Makin. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. ST. HELENS (Sr. TEIOMAS'). —On Saturday afternoon one of the best games in which , the newly-formed Warrington Association Club has taken ' part came off in the field off Knutsford-road. The result was a victory for the Warrington team by one goal to nil. At the commencement of play the St. Helens team were one man short, and it was then that the Warrington men most severely pressed them. The visitors, however, pluckily de- fended their ground, but the Warringtonians were not to be denied, and the first and only goal was soon recorded in their favour. Soon after the ball had been again set going the St. Helens team were recruited by their missing com- panion, and during the whole of the remainder of the time the game was evenly contested, and neither side was able to score. Play was continued till darkness set in and the latter part of the game was little better than a scrim- mage in the dark. WARRINGTON T. ALTRINCFIA3I (SECOND TEAMS).— Played on the Warrington ground on Saturday in the pre- sence of a fair number of spectators, and resulting in favour I of the home team by one disputed try and three miners to two minors. The forwards on both sides commenced play in a vigorous manner, the Warrington team securing the first minor by rushing and dribbling the ball in an effective manner. The home team half backs, by passing in an un- selfish manner, gave the three-quarter backs opportunities to cross the visitors lines, but they were unsuccessful. On a throw-out from near the visitors" lines one of the Altrincham forwards threw the ball ever his head in an endeavour to pass it to his backs, but Russell intercepted it and grounded it over the lines, when one of the visitors seized Russell and drew him in play. The home team claimed the try, but the visitors would not accept it. The kick at goal was a failure. The Warrington team was as follows :—Hewitt, back; J. Boardman, J. Ashurst, and 11. Boardman, three- quarter backs ; T. Lightfoot and J. Whittle (captain), half backs; Jones, Russell, Balshaw, Brimelow, Parry, Little. wood, Holbrook, Savage, and Lisbman, forwards. HAYDOCK TEMPERANCE V. TRANMERE.—RaIIying from the defeat of Saturday, November Bth, the Haydock Tem- perance team appeared in the field in good form against Tranmere firsts at Haydock, on Saturday. The Visitors kicked off, but before ball had travelled far the home team succeeded in getting the ball, and here the onslaught began, the home forwards beginning to play a splendid passing game, with the result that the teetotallers notched their first point in about seven minutes from the start. The visitors again set the sphere rolling, but the teetotallers were not long before they .managed to get hold of it, and the for- wards again exhibited some beautiful passing, which had , the effect of puzzling the Tranmere backs. But their goal- keeper was equal to the occasion, stopping some fine shots. I The home team were, however, not to be denied, for in a very short time they scored their second goal. Play being resumed, the home team took the leather in Tranmere's quarters, the ball being fouled by one of Tranmere's backs, in mouth of .goal, with the result that a third goal was registered. This, however, was objected to by the visitors,. the free kick having to be repeated, when a beautiful scrim- age in the mouth of the noel ensued, the leather being shnffleci through amid cheers. Shortly afterwards half time was called, and on play being resumed the visitors tried hard to pull themselves together, but to no purpose, for toe home team again commenced their redoubtable passing, scoring four more points, making the result seven goals for Haydock Temperance to Tranmere nil. All the Temperance men played well, the most prominent of the visitors being Myers (captain), who played a splendid game at full back. WARRINGTON V. ALTRINCRAM —These clubs met to try conclusions for the first time this season on Saturday, at Altrincham. Losing the spin, H. Kenyon was deputed to put the leather in motion, Barnes punting ieto touch at centre. The home forwards momentarily looked dangerous, when Warren stopped a strong rush, and a scrimmage en- suing, Speakman passed to Warren, who cleared his line, but Cowsill tackled him finely. The visitors then pressed their opponents, and Ashton played the ball into the open, and when E. Smith interfered Povey received the oval, and evading opposition crossed the line. Barnes was successful at goal. An appeal was raised, the place kick being taken under protest. Play re-started where informality occurred, and Warrington compelled them to save. After the drop out quick play on the part of the visitors threatened, Bar- nes making an ineffectual drop, but Hayes followed up and secured a try, the place failing. Half-time was then called. Turner resumed, but the return was feeble, Some neat exchanges enabled Massey to cross the line after a good run. This point was also disputed. After a long alterca- tion the visiting captain waived his claim. The respective captains then decided to abandon the match owing to dark- ness. There was only twenty minutes' play during the first half and five in the second. Had the usual time of thirty- five minutes each way been practicable, the result would have been a very severe defeat for Altrincham. Score : Warrington one try and two minor points to one minor point. Teams: Warrington—Frank Turner, back ; J. T. Massey, T. Barnes, and J. E, Warren, threequarters ; W. Speakman and E. Gilbert, half-backs; H. Ashton (cap- tain), W. Povey, T. Davies, J. Jolley, J. R Calvert, L. Humphries, J. Robinson, Fairfield Turner, and W. Hayes, forwards. Altrincham—E. Rustage, back; E. Smith, T. Cowell, and R. B. Smith (captain), tbreequarters ; A, Bab-

BRUTAL MURDER OF A LADY. A very brutal crime was perpetrated near Torquay on Saturday morning. A lady named Miss Keyse, 63 years of age, was found murdered in her dining-room. She had re- ceived terrible wounds, and an attempt had been made to destroy the house by fire in order to remove all traces of the crisis. Her butler, John Lee, has been arrested on suspic- ion.—At the inquest, on Monday, Mr. George Whitehead, of Fdinburgh, said the deceased was his step-sister. She kept a quantity of plate in the house, but no more money than was necessary to meet her household expenses. On arriving at her residence on Sunday from London he saw that the house had been set on fire in three places, and that Miss Keyse's bed had not been slept in,although she had un- dressed herself. Paraffin had been thrown on the stairs and overthe furniture in the dining-room, and there were traces ef blood on the side-posts of the dining-room door and in the passage. No one-could have entered the house from outside unless admitted by someone inside.—Elizabeth Harris said she woke up and discovered that the house was on fire between three and four o'clock on Saturday morning. Lee was the first person she saw when she came out of her room, and he was partially 'dressed. The room in which Miss Keyes was lying was all on fire. She noticed after- wards that Lee's arm was bleeding, and he told her that he had,cut'his arm in breaking the window -to let the smoke out, as he could not otherwise open it. Lee assisted Mr. Gasking, who came to the house when the alarm was raised, in carrying the body out of the room.—Jane Neck, parlour- maid to the deceased, said about a week ago a gallon of AleEandra oil was purchased, and she was eurprised on Sun- day morning to find that it was all gone. There had been no altercation between Keyse and the servants. The deceased was a little cross with Lee-sometimes when he had not come in at the proper hour. She wanted him to emigrate, as she could not afford to keep him. Witness heard Lee say that Miss Keyse was the greatest friend he had. A short time ago he seemed displeased because his wages had not been increased, but he did notuse any threats:—Witness's night- dress was here produced, and was found to be blood-stained. Lotted to account for this, she said Lee must have touched her when he accompanied her through the smoke in the colonnade to the staircase.—Mr. Chilcote, surgeon, proved that besides a wound in the thrut the deceased's skull was fractured in two places, all the main arteries and vessels of the throat were severed to the very vertebrm, and even the bone was notched. It was impossible for the deceased to have inflicted such wounds noon herself. While examining the body he noticed on the flannel around it a very strong smell of paraffin. Lee came to him to have his arm dressed, and the wounds were -such as might decidedly have been caused by broken glass.—After this witness's evidence the inquiry, which had already lasted the greater part of the day, was adjourned until next day. On Tuesday the inquest was resumed at Torquay.—Mr. .Gasking, landlord of the Cary Arms`Kotel, said he helped to move the body from the drawing-room. The room smelt strongly of paraffin. A portion of the burnt clothing of de- Teased was produced, and also smelt of paraffin, as did the trousers of the prisoner John Lee. The latter said he had cat his arm in breaking the window, but witness saw no blood on Lee's arm when they were moving the body.—A. footman named Richards deposed that the prisoner Lee about two months ago complained to him that he only re- ceived half-a-crown a week from Miss Keyse, and that (as •she said she could not afford to keep him) if she did not get him a good situation soon he would "put an end to -someone."—The inquiry was.adjourned until Friday. On Wednesday, the Torquay magistrates were engaged several hours in investigating theocharge against John Lee of having murdered his mistress. The evidence given at the inquest was repeated, and some portions of it which ap- peared to implicate the prisoner were cleared up in his favour. The police have constructed an ingenious theory as to the way in which the murder was committed, but up to the present it has not been supported by any evidence. The funeral of Miss Keyse tookipiace on Thursday, in the presence of a vast concourse of people. The Treasury has instructed Mr. Isidore Carter to proescute the accused, John Lee. A diamond ring is missing, and search is being made 'for it. The betake and knife with which it is supposed the deed was committed have been sent to an analyst for ex- amination. The prisoner maintains his careless de- meanour.

The Archbishop of Dublin's health improves, but it is an- nounced that he will resign his see at the Diocesan Synod, on the 28th. The Dean of Westminster has expressed his willingness to find A suitable.site in Westminster Abbey for a memorial of Mr. Fawcett. _ . .

Professor Lushington. formerly Greek Professor, was on -Saturday duly erected Lord Rector of Glasgow University, there being no other nomination. TROOPS FROM INDIA.—On Tuesday, her Hajesty's Indian troopship Malabar arrived at Portsmouth with drafts, time I expired men, and invalids, numbering d 235 men altogether. I,C:one of the crew died on the voyage. ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—Port of a Great Nor. 'them goods train left the rails at Etneall, near Derby, on Tuesday morning, awing to the breaking of an axle-tree. 'Tbe guard's van was precipitated down an embankment, and the guard seriously injured. The permanent way was much damaged and traffic delayed. IRISH NATIONALISTS AND EARL SPENCER.—On Tuesday, at a meeting in Dublin of members of the National League, a letter was received from the Lord Lieutenant, declining to grant an inquiry iota the justice of the sentence passed on the men who in 1882 were convicted in connection with the Armagh murderconspiracy. Mr. Mayne, M.P., said of all the outrageous acts Earl Spencer had committed since he came to Irelang—to curse it with his presence—none would reflect more on his character than thie. (Applause.)—Mr. Harrington, M.P., said Earl Spencer was undoubtedly morally guilty of the blood of that innocent man. Myles Joyce. He hoped the Irish party would do all they could to wrest power from the present guilty Government. BRITISH SHERBRO AND SIERRA. LEONE.—On Monday, a deputation of merchants of Manchester and Liverpool inter- ested in British Sherbro and Sierra Leone had an interview with Lord Derby at the Colonial Office. Amongst those I present were Lord Claud Hamilton, M.P., and Mr. J. F. Hutton. President of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce. —Mr. Slagg, Ml'., introduced the subject, and stated that for several years past there had been distarbances which very seriously affected trade, especially the trade of Man- chester, and produced a disastrous result on the settlement I of Sierra Leone. Lord Derby, after asking a number of questions as to the district affected by these dietnrbances, replied that he would take the suggestion into his serious consideration, and have an early interview with Sir Samuel Rowe to see whether the request of the deputatien could be carried out.—The deputation retired expressing their satis- faction at the anticipations held out for.speedy settlement of their difficulties. HACKNEY ELECTION.—LIBERAL ,VICTORY.—Tho polling to fill the vacancy in the represeatation of Hackney took place on Wednesday. The candidatec were professor Stuart, of Cambridge University (L), and Mr. M'Alister, a local Conservative. Great exertions were made by both parties, but the poll was not so heavy as at the general election. when Mr. Fawcett and Mr. Holrns had majorities of SAO and 6,000 respectively over their solitary Conservative op- ponent. The result was declared on Thursday morning as follows : Stuart (Liberal) Mac Alister (Conservatlwe) 8,534

Majority At the general election in 1880 the polling resulted as fol- lows :—H. Fawcett (L), 18,366 ; J. Holms (L), 16,997 ; G. T. C. Bartley (C), 10,322. After the declaration of the poll, Professor Stuart briefly congratulated his friends from the steps of the Town Hall. Mr. Mac Alister did not speak. It is stated that, allowing for deaths, removals, (Sit., the actual number who have polled is a little over 40,000. Dissatisfaction is expressed at the length of the time occu- piedin counting the votes, it being greater than en the last occasion. Professor Stuart, M.P., in addressing the crowd early on Thursday morning, congratulated them t.pon the noble vindication of Liberal principles which the election had afforded. The magnificent majority was a triumph for right and justice. By this election Hackney had rendered a good service to the country, and had laid the miss- able phantom of Fair Trade. A protest has been lodged against the validity el the election. Nearly 1,000 ballot papers are missing, and a scrutiny is demanded.

In the London Cup competition, on Saturday, Clapham Rovers beai. Bartholomew's Hospital; Upton Park (holders) beat Casuals. and Old Etoni ins beat Unity ; in the Walsall Cup competition, Walsall Town beat Aston Shakspere, and Birmingham Excelsior defeated Sutton Coldfield ; in the Birmingham Cup competition, Aston Villa beat Burton Strollers ; Lockwood Bros., in the Sheffield Cup competi- tion, heat Barnsley; in the fourth round of the Scotch As- sociation Cup, Battlefield beat Pollockshields Athletic, Hibernians beat Ayr, Renton beat St. Mirrens' Vale of Levee beat Arthurlie, and Arbroath beat Glasgow Rangers; in the Welsh Cup competition, the Druids beat Wrexham Olympic; at Kennington Oval, Oxford University beat Royal Engineers ; at Cambridge, the University eleven beat Sussex ; at Nottingham, Sheffield Wednesday beat Notts Forest; at Port Glasgow, Queen.s Park beat Port Glasgow Athletic, Dumbarton beat Clyde, Glasgow Pilgrims beat Heart of Midlothian; at Nottingham, Notts Club defeated Brentwood; at Bolton Great Lever beat Ilalliwell; 3rd • L.R.V. Glasgow beat Hamilton Academicals. The Warrington Association team, on Saturday, played a ' good all-round game with the St. Thomas's team, St. Helens, which resulted in a victory for the Warringtonians. Warrington met Altrinckam at the latter place, where some good play was witnessed, bat the match was abandoned owing to the darkness. Had it been possible to play the full time, the result would no doubt have been a severe de- feat for Altrincharn. The junior teams of the same clubs met on the ground at Wilderspool, when the game ended in favour of Warrington by one disputed try and three minor points to two minor points.

SERMON ON TEMP EltiN OE, AT WARRINGTON. In Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday, the Rev. J. Yonge preached an eloquent and powerful sermon to a large congregation on "Temperance." The reverend gentle- man took for his text Romans xiv., part of the 15th verse, "Destroy not him with thy meat." These words of the apostle, he said, embodied a great principle in the form of an urgent practical precept. That principle was to regulate the conduct of men who are strong in relation to men who , are weak. And, further, it recognised not only that it was the duty of the strong to help the weak, but also that the strong have no right because they are strong to act in a way that should hinder or injure the weak. Haying explained that the chapter from which the text was taken was meant by Paul to settle some rather delicate and difficult questions which had arisen at Rome between Jewish and Gentile con- verts, air. Yonge said he proposed to follow the line of Paul in what he had to say that night upon the question of Tem- perance. He wanted to reason quietly and calmly with Christian young men, and, for the matter of that, with Christians male and female, old and young, as to what Christian duty was in the matter of total abstinence. He would say, then, to Christian people that the cross of Jesus Christ was the supreme argument for Christians in favour of total abstinence from the use of intoxicating drinks. Of course there were various other arguments, all of them more or less powerful, and all of them having a bearing upon the Christian conscience. There were the physical argument, the economical argument, and the social argument, all of which the preacher briefly dealt with. But he was not concerned so much that night with those arguments. He referred to them simply by way of remembrance, and that having them in their mini the distinctive and supreme Christian argument might strike them with the greater force. Remembering then the vast evils produced con- tinually throughout the land by the use of alcoholic drink —drink which, as Mr. John Bright pithily puts it, are "so seldom useful and so often pernicious "—let them, as Chris- tians stand at the foot of the Cross of Christ and learn their duty. They might assume if they liked, although it was a dangerous and even arrogant assumption, that none of them were ever likely to come to personal harm through ttle use of these drinks. Those of them who used them used them in unquestioned moderation, and they were strong enough in principle, strong enough in power of self-control, strong enough in their regard for personal character and respect for personal influence, to stand firm against any possible temp- tation to over [indulgence. No one had ever been able to impeach their conduct; no one ever would. They would, he said, aseerne that, dangerous and conceited though the assumption be. What then ? Did that personal safety and unimpeachableness cover all the ground of their respon- sibility ? Could they stand at the foot of Christ's Cross and say that their supreme concern was to save themselves? He asked this question; whether as Christian people they had not before Christ a responsibility concerning their fellows as well as that concerning themselves in this matter of drink ? Paul answers the question with a decided" Yes; " and adds in language of earnest and even impassioned entreaty and command "Destroy not him with thy drink for whose Christ died." The strong disposition was, as he knew only too well, to avoid consideration of this matter as one not touching their personal responsibility. They were disposed to say, and to act upon the idea, "men should take care of themselves; if they can't use these things without abusing them, surely their abuse cannot be charged against us." That was a notion which would do very well if the Creator had made them other creatures than they were. But "they were members of one another." They were bound closely together, and they could not escape the relationship. There were hosts of men who couldn't take care of themselves; hosts of men who couldn't safely touch alcohol. And if they Saw them touch it they were putting a fatal example before them. They would do as they did, and being unable to stop where they stopped would go to ruin before their very eyes. That was a fact, and it ought to influence their conduct as soon as ever they realised it. At the conclusion of his discourse, Mr. Tonga said it would be an unspeak- able gratification to him if any one in that audience would come forward after the servic. and aien the pledge. The Royal Commission ha toe exhibition of Colonial and Indian products in London in ISBG is gagetted. The Prince of Wales is president, and several Indian princes and chiefs are included. MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SElClDE.—lntelligence from Monaghan reports a shocking murder and attempted snicide. It appears that a small farmer ritmed Bell, living at Drums. coon, after sending his son out of the house, cut the throat of his daughter, aged two years, and then attempted to end his own life in the same manner. Bell had lived unhappily with his second wife, who lett him and went to America. His family troubles preyed on his mind, and his conduct latterly has been strange. The child's head WAS almost severed from the body. The father may recover.
GENERAL NEWS;
"Jack," the Newcastle-on:Tyne police dog, is dead. His
ohiet characteristic was swallowing coins. The repair of the exterior of Westtninster Abbey, es!ima- .
ted to cost £55,000, has been commenced in earne;t: Lord Coleridge made some remarks on Saturday at War- . ... . . .

wick Assizes on the practice of "turning libels into crimes." His Lordship said that "it had became too fashionable nowadays if a man's character was slandered, which was a civil matter, to convert it into a criminal case." CATTLE POISONED BY ACORNS.—A considerable loss of cattle has been susta.incd by a farmer at Brinasla le. Wits Eleven heifers and seers were turned in Savernake Forest. Marlborough, and seven of them were afterwards found
dead, having, it is supposed, been poisoned through over- feeding on acorns. It was feared that the others_ would
also die. Several ag-ric-uitu;s--in. the neighbourhood of Ramsey have lately hadserions losses through cattle eating acorns.

BRACE OF TILE NEW MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS Acr.—A.t Sheffield, on Monday. was heard the first case under the Municipal Elections Act, 1884. Mr. Ingham, a well-known local printer, and his, manager, were summoned for issuing _

a placard at brightside Ward 'contest without an imprici, contrary to the Ace The hill was really issued by the United Kingdom Alliance against the drink traffic, and the prosecutor was Mr. Ellis, a licensed victualler. The defen- dant was fined £2 and costs. DISGRACEFUL EVICTION PROCEEDINGS.—To prevent a farm house in Tipperary from which the tenant, who owes nearly £4OO rent, was evicted, being taken possess:en of by the landlord, Colonel White, a body of men have t .rn away the doors, windows, and grates, and carried off *he gates. The partitions of the rooms were also brokea dee e. Six armed caretakers have been hurriedly pat in, and tey have barricaded the place against attacks. A PE.termous MILLIONAIRE.—The funeral of Mr. Jamie Parry, a well-known character in Chester, took place on Monday. Statements were afloat that the deceased, whose parsimony in life was very great, died worth over a mill ien of money. Next to the Duke of Westminster, he was the largest pmperty owner in Chester. Many anecdotes char- acteristic of Parry are told. On one occasion be is said to have instructed a tenant paying over £2 to bring the rent in two instalments, in order to avoid a stamped receipt, thns rendering himself liable to a heavy penalty. ANOTHER SUPPOSED ;MURDER OF A LADY.— The Ash- bridge magistrates have remanded John Frost Orney Day, a highly respectable young farmer of Lympsham, near Wes- ton-super-Mare, and Emily Stallard, governess to his chil- dren, charged with the wilful murder of Matilda Hicks, aged 77 years. Deceased was a person of independent means, and resided with Day, who had married her niece. She died suddenly after partaking of some oatmeal pre- pared by Miss Stallard, the remainder of the gruel after- wards being thrown away by order of Day. The supposition

is that deceased was poi-soned. A LARGE SURPLIJS.—The report of the meeting held ea Monday, in Barnsley, recalls the disastrous explosion at the Oaks Colliery 18 years ago, wher.by 365 persons were killed. A national fund was raised fer the relief of the 678 widows, children, and others dependent upon the miners who lost their lives, and £48,700 was contributed. The number of beneficiaries is now very small, and in addition to a surplus capital of £28,000, there has accumulated nearly £3,000 as interest upon the fund. The committee decided to hold the capital sum intact, but distributed the interest in varying amounts amongst certain medical and charitable institutions in Yorkshire. THE LYING SPIRIT—Mr. Herbert Gladstone, replying to a Liberal elector at Rhyl relative to a statement in a pam- phlet recently published in that town under the title of "The Liberal Ministry judged by its Actions," says "Dear sir,—l return the precious effusion to which yon were good enough to draw my attention. It is crammed with lies, of which that relating to myself—namely, that as a Lord of Treasury I have received a salary of £l,OOO per annum is the most unimportast. No wonder the author is afraid to publish his name.—l am, dear sir, yours very

faithfully, HERBERT GLADSTONE." THE FUTURE OF THE IRISH PARTY.—Mr. JlHtin McCarthy, M.P., and Mr. Justin H. McCarthy, M.P.' de- livered addresses on Sunday at the National Irish Club at Birmingham. Mr. J. H. McCarthy delivered his inaugural address as President of the institution. He said the party to which he belonged was not exactly conspicuous by its' I silence, and kept Parliament pretty well occupied, and would continue to do so until they had a Parliament at College Green, which he prophesied would not be longer than five years from the present time. Mr. Justin McCarthy said three of the most influential members of the Cabinet had already declared in favour of the principle of Home Rule, and he believed that in five years the question would be affirmed by an English Parliament. THE ESCAPE OF A LUNATIC —The Rev. Mr. Bruce, of New York, who escaped from Brookwood Lunatic Asylum, and saw the American Minister, is believed by the authori- ties to be a harmless lunatic, subject to extraordinary de- lusions. Bruce WRS handed over to the asylum from the Southwark Workhouse, he having been sent there from a Lambeth school, where he acted as schoolmaster, and where his eccentricities were most conspicuous. Bruce has often made applications for release, but the authorities evidently did not consider his case one of wrongful detention. He has written essays, while in the asylum, on the causes of in- sanity and its cure, which he forwarded to the doctors in attendance. There is no doubt that Bruce. though eccentric,

is perfectly harmless; and if any friends claimed hint he would be epeedily released. He has only been visited once, a lady of colour being the visitor. THE ASTON DEMONSTEATION.—ATTEMPTED FORGERY. A "young gentleman" named Walter Kirton was charged at West Bromwich,on Saturday, with "inciting "a printer at Gloucester to forge tickets of admission to the now cele- brated Conservative meeting at the Aston Lower Grounds. The defendant enclosed one of the genuine tickets to a rela- tive of his at Gloucester, and asked if he could print some like them. As a matter of fact none were printed, but the Conservative Association bearing of the " attempt " insti- tuted a prosecution. The allegation was that if the atterrpt had been successful the tickets would have been given away to persons who might otherwise heve paid for ad- 'mission to the grounds. On the day of the riot it was arranged that persons who had not tickets should be called upon to pay Eld each, and in this way about £l5 was taken. The defence was that the defendant had only been guilty of a boyish freak, but the magistrates committed him for trial. INSURANCE COMPANIES, CO-OPER:I.I'ITE STORES, AND THE INCOME Tex.—The Court of Appeal had to decide on Satur- day an important point relating to the assessment of insu- rance companies to the income tax. A surveyor of taxes had claimed to assess not only the portion of the surplus profit which was divided among the shareholders, but also the portion which was paid to the holders of "participat- ing "life policies. It was held in the Queen's Bench that such additions to the "life fund" were not sebject to the income tax as profits, and the Crown appealed. The At- torney-General suggested that if the Company's contention was good law all that a life insurance company would have to do to avoid paying income tax altogether was to become a policy holder and divide the profits as bonus, and that, moreover, co-operative stores might claim exemption on the same ground. The Court of Appeal decided in favour of the Company, holding that the money thus paid to policy holders was not liable to be assessed. In the language of the Master of the Rolls, such money was "no more than so many words to the shareholders," and Lord Justice Cotton was equally clear in his declaration that it was paid with a view to increasing the Company's business and was part of their expenses. COLLISION IN THE ENGLISH CHANNEL—Snip SUNK AND SEVEN MEN DROWNED.-1 portion of the crew of the steamship Magdeburg arrived at Salcombe on Friday, after their vessel having sunk through collision with a barque about two o'clock on Friday morning, between Portland and Start Point. The Magdeburg, which belongs to West Hartle- pool, sailed from Liverpool on Tuesday with a cargo of coals for Constantinople and a crew of 17. All went well until Friday morning, when the look-out man say a light, and in about a minute the Magdeburg was struck on the port bow and swept from stem to stern. The Magdeburg at once began to sink, and the only boat that could be get at was the punt. Into these the ten survivors jumped. 'They were only just clear of the wreck when it went down. carrying seven of the crew. The survivors of the Magde- burg then pulled about, and, not seeing the barque, were under the impression that she, too, had foundered. They were eventually picked up by a Cardiff vessel, and brought Into Salcornbe late on Friday evening. The American ship I Henry Villard, last from Queenstown, with a cargo of flour for London, put into Plymouth on Friday, with bows stove and catwater and stern considerably damaged. This was evidently the vessel which had been in collision with the Magdeburg. THE CROFTERS' AGITATION IN THE ISLE OF SKYE —A. meeting of the crofters in the disaffected districts of Skye was held at Dig. on Saturday afternoon. Only about 200 attended, about half coming from Glendale, about thirty miles distant. It was resolved—" That this meeting of tip crofters at KilatuEr, held at Uig, to-day, resolve to ap- point a deputation of their number to wait upon Sheriff Ivory, to give him assurance that any of them charged with an offence are willing te deliver themselves at Portree for justice, and to thereby save the unnecessary propoeed police expedition to Uig, which, in the opinion of this meeting, would only serve to irritate the people of the dis- trict." The police from Inverness arrived at Strome Ferry at 1 pm, and embarked on the steamer Lochiel. They were accompanied by Sheriff Ivory, Mr. James Anderson, Procurator Fiscal, and Chief-Constable Mcilardv. About twenty warrants will it is believed, be issued. Sheriff ivory received the deputation on board the steamer Lochiel at Portree, and returned a courteous reply. A Uig correspon- dent says :—The police landed from Lochiel about nine o'clock on Tuesday morning, together with 300 Marine and Bluejackets. and the whole marched through the ham.. let. The crofters made a display of flags evincing their loyalty, but none of the people were about. The police and Marines marched to Staffin and Valtos districts, which are the chief centres of the agitation, andwhere a body of police is to be stationetl. H.M.S. Banterer, which had been lying in Portree all night, left on Tuesday morning for Uig to join the other vessels of the expedition, and arrived there about noon. Everythine is quiet at Portree. The troopship As- sistance, gunboat Forester, and steamer Lochi -1 arrived in Uig bay at noon On Monday, but the place was quiet, with no sign ef a gathering of tbe crofters. It is expected that arrests will be made in connection with the expulsion of the police on the 30th ult., but no resistance is anticipated. The Commission of the Free Church of Scotland met on Wednesday in Edinburgh, and adopted for presentation to the Government a memerial OD the subject of agrarian dis- turbances in Skye.
