"It's a far cry to Loch Awe," but fur- ther still is that which comes from the Crof- ters of Skye. Their cry has at last been heard, and some heed is being taken of it. The circumstances of these poor cottars in the Highlands and islands of Scotland are in many respects analagous to those of the Irish peasantry for whom leaislation has of late years done so much ; but in some re- spects they are even worse. It was common to both to find that the more valuable they made the land they tilled—land redeemed in many cases from the sterile hillside—and the higher rose their rents, so that they be- came hopeless of receiving the legitimate re- ward of their toil. What the Crofters so just- ly complain of is that the land which their families have held for generations—since the time in fact when the right to its use was common to the clan—is being gradually and ruthlessly taken from them. It is not that, as in our Lancashire valleys, the land is , wanted for building sites; but just the re- verse. It is being converted in many in- stances into deer forests; or set aside in other ways for purely sporting purposes. It is another illustration of the ancient fable of the boys and the frogs. What, in this in- stance, is sport to the "landed gentry "is death to the Crofters. It does not auger well for the future of this country when the producers are being turned off the land in order that the non-producers may use it as breeding ground for deer and grouse. 11l fares the land to hastening ills a prey, When 4‘ game" accumulates- and men decay. But it will be asked—Cannot these landow- ners do what they like with their own? And the answer is—first, that many of them are, strictly speaking, holders rather than owners of the land; and, secondly, that land is a commodity of such a peculiar kind, as the basis of all other commodities, that the owner ought not to be permitted to do with it absolutely as he likes. To take the first point: it is notorious that up to compara- tively recent times land in the Highlands was regarded as belonging to the clan. The chief was the nominal owner; but it would have been as much as his life was worth to dispute the title of the clansmen to pasture their cat- tle in the valleys and upon the hills. Changes of time have, unhappily for the cot- tars, brought change of custom, and z;us- tom has so hardened into law that the land- grabber can have police and soldiers and sailors at his back to protect him in what, in too many cases, is a shameless usurpation. There are, it is true, landlords in Scotland as elsewhere who have a high sense of duty, and who, not unmindful of the traditions of their fathers, deal fairly and considerately by the Crofters in maintaining privileges which have: been so long enjoyed. But there are. others possessed of the evil spirit of greel, who, holding by their titles in law, have, regard- less of equity, " improved " the original til- lers off the soil. They have despoiled farms occupied by their fellow-men to make farms for sheep; and finally, as was admitted by the HOXE SECRETARY in Parliament, con- verted these Sheep walks into deer forests. It is not that the original farming didn't pay; it paid well in that it kept the Crofters in comfort, and left a steadily increasing rent for the landlord. But game rents, it would se•ern, pay better. The rapid accumulation of wealth in this country during the present generation has caused a great demand for wide tracts of land for sporting purposes. There are not a few men who commenced life in "iron clogs," and, as a result of their industry, foresight, and skilful trading,
imiliAL

have had gold showered upon them. All honour to them for what they have achieved But a time comes when they want to "take ; things easy ;" " shooting " is fashionable, -and it is withal "recommended by the faculty" as healthy exercise. If they cannot do much more themselves than hit a keeper occasionally, they can invite "born gentle- ,' -men " who are good sportsmen, and thus get themselves "into society." It is in this way that enormous rents have come to be paid yearly for shooting in the Highlands; and it is in this way that the Crofters have been robbed of their rights of 'pasturage. Can we wonder that, when they see and feel these things they should proclaim their griev- ances from the house-tops, and that, when they find matters are getting from bad to worse, they should show signs of rebellion ? The wonder is rather I that they have suffered so long and so pa- tiently. But they are a hardy, industrious, God-fearing people, who do not cry out until they have been hurt much and hurt often. It is a discredit---qt is a disgrace—to the landowners of the North that the aid of Parliament should be needed to redress these grievances. They, at any rate, have not been hard put to it. Year by year they have grown richer, whilst the poor on their lands have been 'brought to the verge of starvation. It would have been an easy thing—it would yet be an easy thing—for these lords of the human kind" to set apart certain acres of land solely for the use of the Crofters, as compensation for the rights-in-common of which they have been so long deprived. The landlords can well afford to do it, for we have it on the tes- timony of Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT that "where an estate was worth hundreds, the landlord now finds it to be worth thousands." But if they will not yield to reason they must be compelled to surrender to force. If the law does not apply, it can be made to apply— in Scotland as well as Ireland, and, for that matter, in Wales as well as England. If they are wise they will move ere they are made to move. We are not far distant in any case from an upheaval in our landed system. Democracy, when it once feels its strength, will no longer tolerate land laws which are to-day amongst the most barbarous in Europe. It will not permit of millions of acres being appropriated to game, while men willing to work are denied access to the soil; it will recognise that land was created for the people—not the people for the land; and strive, arid not in vain, to ensure that there shall be less in the future of "man's inhu- manity to man," which, as Scotland's poet so truly and so pathetically says. " makes count- less thousands mourn."

THE PRIME MINISTER is about to succeed in that upon which he has set his heart—the passing of the Franchise Bill and a Seats Bill during the remainder of the life of the pre- sent Parliament. His patience, perseverance, and unrivalled skill as a tactician are about to bear fruit. The Opposition, instead of set- ting everybody at defiance, as they did little more than a week ago, when Lord JOHN MANNERS flouted the proposals of the Govern- ment, have been brought to their senses ; the Lords have passed the second reading of the Franchise Bill ; and Lord SALISBURY is actually in conference with Mr. GLADSTONE as to the bases of the Redistribution Bill ! There has been what is called a compromise; that is to say, the Lords have walked over the slender bridge that has been all along open to them, and for a time at any rate they have staved off the storm which threatens their de- voted heads. For our part we must confess to feeling somewhat disappointed that they have not had the courage to "die game" ; it would have been such a satisfaction to do a little in the way of paying off old scores against them. Still, the reckoning day will come, but for the present it must be put off. Looking at the proposed bases of settlement of the Reform Controversy, it is gratifying to observe that the Government have everything to gain and nothing to lose by the course they are taking. If the worst should come to the worst—if the Lords should again allow their constitutional stupidity to get the better of them, and refuse, at the last moment, to pass the Franchise Bill, the deadlock will present no more terrible features than have alreadybeen disclosed. "The resources of the constitution " will still remain unexhausted, and it will be for the PRIME MINISTER, backed as he will be by an outraged nation, to bring them into active play. The object of Lord SALISBURY has been to force a disso- lution upon the present register of voters ; it was with that end in View that he induced the majority in the House of Lords to reject the Franchise Bill; and it is that at which he and his abettors have been aiming in seeking to compel the Government to produce their Redistribution Bill in the Commons whilst the Franchise Bill was yet under the considera- tion of the Lords. With two strings to their bow, they made cock sure of being able to bring the PRIME MINISTER down; but the fly has seen what they have been about, and Would not step into the parlour of these very hungry spiders. As matters stand, the Op- position , are to be permitted to have a share in the moulding of the Redistribution Bill; but the Bill itself will not be laid before Parliament until "adequate assur- ance" has been given that the Lords will pass the Franchise Bill. Mr. GLADSTONE thus gets his way; he has always insisted that the Franchise Bill must be out of harm's reach be- fore the Seats Bill could be laid on the table of the House of Commons. But more than this; he has always urged that Redistribution should not be dealt with as a party matter; he has again and again invited the Opposi- tion to make known what they want. He will now obtain their views in the negotiations that are proceeding, and, as these will be taken into account in framing or re-framing the Bill, the Opposition will, it may be anti- cipated, find themselves disarmed. There is therefore every likelihood that, without sur- rendering anything, "the Grand Old Man" will achieve the crowning glory of his life by placing on the Statute Book, during the pre- sent Parliament, a measure of Reform which in its scope and magnitude will be unparal- leled in the history of England.

The Police Authorities of St. Helens have been making a raid upon lottery and betting houses whic has been most successful. Four cases were heard on Monday, with the result that fines were inflicted varying from £ o and costs to £3O and costs, and it is understood that another batch of offenders is to be , brought before the magistrates. It was sta- ted that the practices of betting, and of selling racing lottery tickets, have been going on for some time in public houses, and shops, and the Bench made it clear that so determined were they to put an end, if they could, to these illegalities that, if they were con- tinued, they would subject those who were found guilty of them to the punishment of imprisonment without the option of a fine.

So far as betting is concerned, it is satis- factory to reflect that the police have been pretty consistent in their efforts to sup- press it; but with regard to the other offence that of "keeping, open a lot- tery "—the attempts to put it down have been of a most irregular and spasmodic character, and, worse than that, they have been allied to the odious habit of "making fish of one and flesh of another." In making this observation, we do not re- fer to the authorities of St. Helens in particular ; the remark is of general appli- cation. " Lotteries " and " raffles " are, of course, contrary to the law, a fact which was no doubt within the knowledge of the shopkeeper and pork-butcher who were so heavily fined on Monday; but these people will, nevertheless, feel that they have been harshly dealt with in being singled out for punishment. It will be pertinent for them to ask why they are fined for "keeping a lottery," whilst churchwardens and chapel deacons who are alike guilty of infractions of the law (when a Bazaar, or Christmas Tree, is being held). are allowed to go scot-free. And no answer, or, at any rate, no satisfactory answer can be given them. If the goose is to be spitted, the gander should also be put to the fire We do not doubt that racing lotteries are more mischievous in their operation than the lot- teries which are so often regarded as " indis- pensible "at Bazaars—as if it could possibly be defensible—not to say indispensable, in such a case, for "law-abiding citizens" to break the law ! The matter beyond dispute is:that " lotteries" are illegal, no matter whether they are held at Bazaars or Butchers' Shops; and this having been settled, the question is—why should a distinction be made between one and the other? Why should the small shopkeeper who sells a ticket along with an ounce of tobacco be pounced upon, while the merchant who puts down his guinea for the raffling of a screen is treated as it he had done a meritorious thing? So long as lotteries in connection with our churches and chapels are carried on with impunity, so long will it be open for people to say that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor. It has a bad effect on a community when such an impres- sion prevails ; for the law, which should b,t no respector of persons, ceases to be re- spected. The times and the manners have changed since Shakespere's day, and yet not so much but that it might even now with propriety be said—
Plate sin with gold, And the strong lance of justice hurtles breaks; Arm it in rags—a pigmy's straw doth pierce it. We need a reform in this matter; it is time to begin and "reform it altogether."

OAKLAND-STREET GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.—An ordinary meeting of this mission was held in Oakland-street Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. Mr. Charles Jones presided. An enter- tainment of songs, recitations, ere., was given by the chil- dren, and addresses on temperance topics were delivered by the chairman and others. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL RUNCORN.—Special sermons were preached in this place of worship on Sunday, by the Rev. John Jones, of Aberystwith, on the occasion of the anniversary of the Sunday school. In the afternoon a service of song entitled " Heaven" was rendered by the choir and scholars. Om Monday evening Mr. Jones again preached. There were large congregations at each service, and the collections amounted to £l7 SALFORD AND THE SHIF CANAL RA.TE.—A memorial to the Horne Secretary is in course of signature in Salford against the resolution of the Borough Council passed at a meeting on the 12th lost, namely, that a sum not ex- needing 2d in the pound upon the rateable value of the borough should be contributed out of the borough fund towards the cost of promoting the Ship Canal Bill. Mr. Woodcock, solicitor, 8, St. James's-square, has charge of the memorial. THE EXTRAORDINARY BIGAMY CASK—At Crewe, on Thursday, John Joseph Hardman, glass-cutter, of Cadis- head, was charged with contracting bigamous marriages at Preston and Crewe. Witnesses were called to show that at Warrington, in 1876, the prisoner married Hannah San- key. Three years later he married Elizabeth Slater at Preston, and last month he married Sarah Wood at Crewe. The wives appeared in court. Prisoner, who admitted the offences, was committed to the assizes. JUVENILE TEMPLARY IN WIDNES.—At Malins Temper- ance Hall, on Saturday evening, a recitation contest, ar- ranged by the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple, took place. Mr. John Duxbury, of Halebank, presided. The competition was divided into two sections, a prize being awatded to the best reciter amongst the males, and the best reciter amongst the females. Mr. Thomas Reay and the chairman acted as judges, and the prizes, consisting of two handsomely bound bibles, were awarded to Jessie Hughes and Walter Dixon. There were 19 competitors. DISGRACEUL Row IN A CHESHIRE CHURCIL—ti sum- mons, in which considerable interest is taken, has been issued returnable at Eddisbury (Cheshire) Petty Sessions. According to the statement which Mr/David Jones has laid before Dr. Stubbs, Bishop of Chester, he entered Banbury Church a little late, and took his place on a vacant seat near the door. He had no sooner done so than the clerk came up and ordered him to move. He refused to do so, and the clerk then seized him while the service was proceeding. He vigorously resisted, and a struge le ensued in the presence of the whole congregation, the service being stopped while the disgraceful fray lasted. Ultimately Jones was ejected on to another seat. The Bishop of Chester has written to the Rev. W. Lowe, vicar of Bunbury, saying his impression is that the clerk used unnecessary violence, and Le hopes that the vicar will take care for the future to prevent anything of the sort occurring. A NEW LOCAL BAILWAY.—NotiCes have been issued by several railway companies of proposed additional works in connection with their respective undertakings, but the most important affecting this district appears to be an application for Parliamentary powers to incorporate a company to enable them to make a new line between St. Helens and the Wigan Junction Railways. Daring the last few years there have been many complaints from the inhabitants of St. Helens, Elaydock, Ashton, and neighbouring villages of the great want of better railway accommodation in the populous districts named, and meetings have been held at which it was decided ta solicit the Midland Railway Company to in- clude St. Helens and its neighbourhood in its system, if such a plan was feasible. The agitation is at last beginning to bear fruit, and the proposals to establish a new railway connection between St. Helens and the districts in question have created a very favourable impression. The new line, it is proposed, shall commence at a station to be placed near the top of Hardshaw-street, St. Helens, passing through Parr, Haydock, Ashton-in-Makerfield, Golborne, and Lowton, where it will form a junction with the line of the Wigan Junction Railway Company. This is evidently the outcome of the various meetings which have been held, including the action taken by a number of enterprising tradesmen in the town some few years ago, when an enthusiastic meeting was held at the Fleece Hotel, and numerously-signed requisitions were prepared and after- wards presented to the directors of the Manchester, Shef- field, and Lincolnshire Railway Company by a deputation who were most cordially received. At the time the requisi- tionists pleaded for a loop line from Sankey to St. Helens, but it was evident that the directors had no sympathy with anything but a scheme which would give them direct through communication. The proposed line, if constructed, would connect St. Helens with the Cheshire Lines Railway, and open a new route to the Midlands and also the principal Lancashire towns. The new company seek powers for the compulsory purchase of land, power to take part of property, to provide homes for labouring classes displaced by the new Act, to levy and take tolls and charges. to make working arrangements with the Wigan Junction Railway Company, the Cheshire Lines Committee, the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, or the Midland Com- pany; to obtain powers over part of the Wigan Junction Railways, and to get permission to pay dividend out of capital during the construction of the works. The notice is signed by Messrs uppenheim and Malkin, solicitors, St. Helens, and by Messrs Darlington and Sons, solicitors, Wigan. If the proposals are carried out St. Helens will thereby be placed in a more direct connection with South- East Lancashire and other parts of the country than is at present afforded by the circuitous route through St. Helens Junction.

div.p: nu EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1884

DISASTER TO A RUNCORN VESSEL.—WhiIe riding with two ancuors down and the masthead-light burning in St. John's, Newfoundland, on the 22nd ult., the vessel Brodrick Castle, of Runcorn, Captain P. Smidt, managing owner, was driven down upon by the barque Elbe, Greenock. The latter vessel had only one anchor down, and was without a light. The Brodricic :.:astle sustained serious damage to spars, bulwarks, and planking. She is now repaired and at Fogo, loading fish. THE OBSTRUCTION OF WEST BANK-STREET, WIDNES. To a meeting of the Highway Committee of the Widnes Local Board, Messrs. Bolton and Son, of the Mersey Cop- per Works, Widnes, have intimated their intention of ap- pealing in the Court of Quarter Sessions against the refusal of the Local Board to allow them to block West Bank- street by extending their works. The firm argue that the street is a private one, while the Board contend that it has been need as a public thoroughfare for upwards of twenty years. DEATH OF AN OLD RESIDENT AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Thomas Turner, who has for 27 years been employed as col- lector to the Runcorn Gas Company, died, on Wednesday. in his 79th year. In June last, Mr. Turner was advised by Dr. Robinson to relinquish all labour, and he ceased to per. form his duties, his constitution gradually giving way until death occurred. He was greatly esteemed by the firm as a faithful and conscientious servant, and was much respected by the public for his courtesy and kindness. The body will be interred this (Saturday) afternoon. LACROSSE —St. Helems v. Widnes: In this game, played at Denton's Green, St. Helens, on Saturday last, Widnes were victorious by one goal to nil. Playing down hill dar- ing the first half, the game was much in their favour, and from a pass from behind the posts Robinson scored a lucky point about fifteen minutes after starting. Soon afterwards W. Gossage claimed a goal from a good shot, but the direc- tion of the ball being somewhat doubtful, the umpire declined to decide, and the claim was waived. During the second half the game was more evenly contested, and the Widnes custodian had some little work given him to do by the home attacks, but still St. Helens were unable to make matters even, victory resting with the visitors as above stated. E. F. Gossage played well at point, as did also W. W. Gossage on the attack. The game was characterised by a little rough play on both sides, and one dispute arose therefrom, which is much to be regretted, but fortunately it did not interfere with the general harmony and good feeling which prevails between the two clubs. Team—St. Helens: H. Varley, M. J. Hammill, G. H. Bramwell, W. H. Robert- thaw, A. M. Booth, J. J. Hartley. IL S. Wilson, E. Foreman, W. A. Booth, J. Cotton, C. A. Fowler, and S. Robinson. Widnes W, W. Gossage, E. F. Gossage, R. W. Robinson, G. Helsel!, L. Kilcross, F. W. White, J. R. Wylde, J. Wylde, J. Turner, G. E. Sayce, J. H. Hedley, and J. H. Lyon. THE DEATH OF A CENTENARIAN AT RUNCORN.—The Globe says:—The number of epecifices for insuring long- evity being without end, we feel no scruple in adding another to the lengthy list. Whether infallible or not, it has, at all events, the merit of being quite out of the com- mon run. To begin with, you must discover some town where chemical works abound. Having found this para- dise, the next thing is to take up residence as near as pos- sible to the largest concern. That is all ; you may then look forward confidently to attain the years of the Hebrew patriarch whose centenary has just been celebrated. There is one proviso, however; you must rarely, if ever, go be- yond the area whose atmosphere is affected by the fumes from the works. We derive these simple rules for the guidance of would-be centenarians from provincial corn- ments on the recent death of an old lady at Runcorn. She was in her hundredth year, had enjoyed excellent health up to the last, and retained her mental faculties unimpaired. Can it be doubted that these results were mainly owing to her having lived for the last 60 years" under the shadow of a chemical works chimney?" At all events, even if the direct connection between cause and effect cannot be traced, it is a warrantable theory that chemical fumes suited her constitution. When people who are exposed to their influ- ence die at an early age, it is assumed that the pollution of the atmosphere cut short their lives, and, on the principal of common fairness, this case must be accepted as evidence of the contrary hypothesis. FUNERAL OF MRS. MIDDLEBROOK AT RUNCORN. The funeral of this aged lady took place at the Parish Church, on Tuesday morning. Although the weather was very cold a large number of spectators had gathered in the vicinity of the Parish Church to see the last of the oldest resident in the town, while the tradesmen in Church-street had par- tially darkened their shop windows, and there were signs of •mourning in many parts of the town. The hearse, which was supplied by Mr. S. Yarwood, left High-street shortly after eleven o'clock. It was preceded by the Revs. E. J. Robinson, R Edwards, T. Hackett, E. Williams, J. Jones, and S. Mees ; Dr. Robinson; Messrs. J. W. Woodlands S. Coventry, Herren, R. Norman, S. Hampden, S. Ravenscroft, J. Unsworth, J. Fox, and C. Littler. The pall bearers were Messrs. John Simpson, J. 0. Jackson, W. B. Gibson, R. Lea, T. Shnister, J. R. Fritb, H. Randle, and P. Speakman. Fol- lowing the hearse were Messrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, Neil Matbieson, Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, J.P., Arthur Bran- drit, T. Middlebrook (nephew, Birstall), A. Middlebrook (Birstall), C. B. Hemingway, and the Rev. J. Hind (Keighley.) The corpse was borne from the hearse to the church by Messrs. James Lunt, John Haddock, John Leathwood, Wm Brown, Samuel Taylor, William Horton, Thomas Molyneux, and James Dutton. At the entrance to the church the cortege was met by the Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. John Brundrit, J.P. Cr. L. Wigg, W. Whittaker. The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. R. Edwards. Wreaths were sent by Mrs. John Hazlehurst. Mrs. Thomas Hazlehurst, and a beautiful wreath was placed on the coffin by Mr. G S. rtazlehurst. The arrangements for the funeral were carried out by Mr. H. Handles, and the coffin, polished oak with black furniture, was supplied by Mr. Jas. Dutton. •, CONCERT AT RIINCORN.—BeIbeeda schoolroom was filled to its utmost capacity on Tuesday evening by an audience assembled to hear a vocal and instrumental concert in aid of the widows and orphans of deceased members of the Run- corn Lifeboat Crew Division of the Order of Sons of Tem- perance. Mr. F. J. Norman presided. The concert opened with the prize glee, "Forest Queen," by the Mill-brow Brass Band, who performed the piece with great credit under the conductorship of Mr. Ainsworth. The duet, "Minute gun at sea," was tastefully sung by Messrs R. Morris and C. Pownall; while later, the solo and quartette, "Come where my love lies dreaming," was given in good style by Miss Horton Messrs R. Morris, C. Pownall, and J. Birkett. Miss N. Handley sang "Fairly caught" with great refinement of vocalisation and expression, and she was enthusiastically applauded. She was also highly succesful in her rendering of "The Quaker's daughter." Mr. F. Fairhurst favoured the audience with a capital interpretation of the song," An- chored." and Mr. R. Morris sang with much taste and power "The Newfoundland dog." Miss Horton sang, in a manner which evinced a high degree of culture, "The gates of the west." For his admirable rendering of Randegger's song," A freshening breeze," Mr. J. H. Harrison was en- cored and then gave 'Three jolly sailor boys." Mr. C. Pownall gave the pretty song, "Sweet violets," With good effect. The comic element was supplied by Mr. T. Davies, of Widnes, who was twice encored, his songs being "Measure your wants by your means," and "The boy can say papa." Pianoforte solos were creditably performed by Miss B. Wright and Miss F. Handley, the latter of whom ably officiated as acconipanist. Tennyson's fine poem, "The revenge," was recited by Mr. C. Nickson, who displayed much elocutionary ability and dramatic power. Mr. S. Coventry read "A perilous adventure." A very enjoyable concert was brought to a close by the band playing the " Hallelujah chorus." ZION METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES. The an- nual sermons connected with this church were preached on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev. J. W. Chis- holme, of Liverpool. There was a good congregation in the morning, and in the evening the edifice was crowded. The choir, conducted by Mr. John Betney, rendered music spe- cially selected for the occasion. Collections were made on behalf of the trust fund. On Monday evening a tea meet- ing was' held ender the auspices of the Band of Hops, and there was a good attendance. The following ladies presi- ded at the tables :—Miss E. Betney, Miss F. Cawsey, Miss Rimmer, Miss Harrison, Miss Robinson, Mrs. Turton, Mrs. Scriven, and Miss Harvey. An entertainment was subse- quently held, presided over by Mr. S. Lamb, and a large audience assembled. The following programme was gone through in a creditable manner by the members of the Band of Hope : Recitations "Only a boy," Joseph Bushell ; "Up lads, and at him," Timothy Wilcock; "Love for water," Lilian Wright ; "Making believe," Moses Gough ; "Dead and alone," Mary Wilcock -, 'My pledge," Jessie Betney ; "The young teetotaller," Henry Wilcock ; "Jane and her father," Jessie Hughes; "The bunch of grapes," Ellen Ferber ; song, "Don't marry a man if he drinks," Miss A. Betney ; and a song and recitation, " Right over wrong," by Mrs. Betney and John Ferber ; song, "I wonder why he comes not home," Miss Betney. A humorous dialogue entitled " Professor Parker's Models," taken part in by several adult members, created much mer- riment. Several melodies were sung by the choir under the leadership of Mr. Jos. Betney. Mr. A. Ogden presided at the harmonium. Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. WESLEYAN MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES.—The annual meeting in aid of the Wesleyan Homo and Foreign Missions was held in Victoria-road chapel on Tuesday even- ing. There was only a moderate attendance. Mr. B. Brown presided, and be was supported by the Revs. E. J. Robinson, of Runcorn, R. Harper, J. flothersall, and T. Jones. In a short address, the Chairman referred to the fact that while the Missionary Society did not receive those handsome donations it did in the early part of its career, the income was very much larger at present than it formerly was, and explained that this was owing to wealth having become more distributed amongst the working classes. The country was passing now through a long period of trade depression, but notwithstanding this the income of the country was as great as ever it was and the capital was largely increasing, and in any increase of prosperity he did not think the Methodist people would profit the least. He therefore made an appeal on behalf of the society for aid in the great work it had yet to accom- plish.—The Rev. J. Hothersall read the report, from which It appeared that the Widnes Branch of the Zenana Mission, of which Mrs. Robinson ( Moerside) is secretary, Mrs Duxbury treasurer, and Mrs. Joseph Robinson, Miss Proctor, Miss Edith Taylor, and Miss Harper, collectors, had contributed during the twelve months ending October last the stun of £l5 4s 9d, a decrease of lie 5d on the previous year. To the Home and Foreign Missions the Widnes circuit Int year paid £ll3 20 3d, an increase on the previous year of -L3l 16s 2d. (Applause.)—The Rev. T. Jones advocated the claims of missionary enterprise, and the RAN. E. J. Robinson described his labours as a missionary in the island of Ceylon in a highly interesting manner. A collection and the usual votes of thanks Concluded the meeting.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE—The fortnightly meeting was held In Regent-street School-room on Thursday evening, Mr. J. Midwood in the chair. There was a good attendance. A capital programme of glees (sung by the choir, conducted by Mr. James Stubbs), songs, and recitations was gone through. A burlesque entitled" King Alcohol " was creditably performed. ACCIDENT TO THE LONDON EXPRESS AT RUNC3RN.— °lrina to a failure in the action of the vacuum brake con- nected with the engine of the exprees which left Liverpool at 45 p.m. for London on Wednesday, the train was delayed for upwards of an hour. eerentually the train was des- patched to Crewe by the local shunting esigine. The traffic was much delayed in consequence of the accident. DISCOVERY OF AN OLD ROMAN ROAD.—A few days ago while excavating on some land at the easterly end of tbe ' Big Pool at Runcorn, Mr. Thomas Astmoor came across a portion of an old roadway paved for a width of several yards. The read appeared to extend underneath the pool, and it is supposed to be part of an old highway between Runcorn and Weston, which was diverted when the Bridge- water Canal was constructed more than a century ago. TEMPERANCE SERMONS AND MEETING AT FRODSHAM.— On Sunday special sermons were preached in Frodsham Parish Church by the Rev. G. Burwell, M.A.. Rector of All Saint's, West Gorton, in aid of the funds of the Church Temperance Society; and on Tuesday evening a temperance meeting was held in the Girls' School, Frodsham, when the room was crowded. The Vicar presided, and a children's concert was given by the infants from school, under the management of Miss Barker, the successful efforts of the young performers being loudly applauded. The meeting was afterwards addressed by the Rev. A P. Reynolds, formerly senior curate at Frodsham. CONCERT AT Sr. MARY'S SCHOOLS, WIDNES —Au enter- tainment in aid of the day school attached to St. Mary's Catholic Church was given on Monday evening in the school-room, the Rev. Father Clarke presiding. The Chair- man. alluding to overpressure, said the mental capacities of children were being too severely taxed by the system at pre- sent sanctioned by the Government. A capital programme was gone through in good style by the Rev. J ,ho oldhim, and Messrs. Forster, Gustave, B. Sheridan, Callaghen, and Faulkner ; and Misses Middleton, Cawley, and Hewitt. Miss Hewitt was the accompanist. Tha band of the Total Abstinence League performed several selections of muaic. THE BuNCoRN GAS COMPANT.— This company purpose applying for Parliamentary powers to erect new works upon a site known as Culvert Meadow, which they have pur- chased in Halton-road. The preeent site occupied by the company will not permit of any further exeension, and the Purchase of land elsewhere has proved absolutely necessary. Upon the new site, which is fully described in our adver- tising columns, they purpose to erect large Storage works, to which the gee will be conveyed by pipes from the pre- sent manufactory. Eventually, it is intended to put down plant on the site, and to commence the manufacture of gas, which will enable the company to meet all requirements for the future. THE CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES TELEGRAPH MES- SENGER.—Robart Arthur Gusto (19), messenger, was char- ged at the Liverpeol Assizes with having, on the 27th of August, wilfully and unlawfully detained and delayed a number of past letters, at Widnes. In August last, the pri- soner, who was a telegraphic messenger, was temporarily employed to deliver letters in Widnes. On the 25th Oc- tober, a labourer, going through a railway tunnel in that town, saw over one hundred letters in a recess. They were taken to the Post Office, and some of them were recognized as having been given to the prisoner for delivery. Tne pri- soner was found guilty, and was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment with hard labour. EIALTON tRADESMEN AND THEIR SCALES.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Leach, coal dealer, Hal- ton, was summoned to answer a charge of being in posses- sion of unjust scales. On the 11th instant Superintendent Leah visited the defendant's place of business, and found on the scales which were used for weighing coal two pieces of iron which could be removed at will.' When this iron was removed the scales were Subs, against the purchaser.—The defendant, who said he was not aware that it was necessary to fix the iron, was fined 103. and costs.--Samuel Hum- phreys, greengrocer, Halton, was summoned under a simi- lar charge.—Superintendent Leah found a small weighing machine an ounce and a half eat of balance in favour of the purchaser. If, however, the defendant was purchasing by his own scales it would be in his' favour.—The magistrates considered the defendant had acted in ignorance, and fined him 2s. and costs 10s. 6d. THE BITER BITTEN AT RIINCORN.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Mr. W. Bankes, at Runcorn Petty Ses- sions. on Monday, Edward Paul, a tramp, was charged with obtaining relief from Inspector Roche, assistant relieving officer for the Runcorn district of the Union, by means of false pretences. About nine o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner applied at the police office for a ticket for a night's lodgings. He stated he had no money, and Police-clerk Wallace was directed by Inspector Roche to search him. Not a coin was found, upon him, and he was accordingly supplied with a ticket. P.C. Wallace took the prisoner to Mrs. Higgins' lodging-house in Mersey-street, and from his manner suspected that he had not made a truthful state- ment. The officer allowed the prisoner to remain in the lodging-house about a quarter of an hour, and then he took him into custody and brought him to the police station, where a second search revealed that the prisoner had Is in his pocket.—The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A WIDNES LANDLADY.—Before Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Susannah Wallis, a married woman living in Cholmondeley- street, was charged with stealing £9 17a, the property of John Gallighan, a labourer. Mr. W. T. Husband defended. Gallighan lodged with the prisoner, and on the Bth inst. he went to his work leaving the money mentioned in his trousers pocket, The trousers were banging behind the bedroom door. On returning in the afternoon the prisoner informed him that she had heard somebody in the bedroom, but she had searched the house and could not find anyone. Gallig• han then discovered that his money had been taken, and information was given to P.S. Clarkson. It was ascertained that during the week following the robbery, the prisoner had paid bills to the amount of £3 us, although her hue' band, who ie employed at Messrs Gossage and Sons works, only receives Ll per week. She was taken into custody, and was now committed. to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial, bail being allowed. ACTION AGAINST THE WIDNES ALKALI Co:enema—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Smith, the Case of Banner v. the Widnes Alkali Company was heard. In this case Mr. Banner, the trustee of the estate of Messrs. Tobias and Co., formerly chemical manufacturers, of Hackinsehey, Liverpool, sued the detendant company for breach of contract. Mr. Collins, QC., and Mr. Mullholland - were for the plaintiff; and Mr. Gully, Q C., and Mr. French represented the company.—The case for the plaintiff was that on the failure of Messrs. Tobias the defendants repu- diated certain extensive contracts which they had entered into for the supply of bleaching powder in regard to which the market was against them, whilst claiming the right to deliver under other contracts in regard to which the market was in their favour.—A legal discussion took place on the terms of the contract; and his lordship, without calling upon Mr. Gully, held that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover. A counter claim was struck out without prejudice to the rights of the company under the bank- ruptcy. RUNCORN STARR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY Anna°. PRIATIONS.—an appropriation Of the first society took place in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom on Thursday evening, and there was a fair attendacce of members. Mr. Peter Riley presided, and Messrs Cunnah and Hough acted as scrutineers. The ballot resulted in number 150 being drawn, and the chairman announced that Mr. James Pritchard, a workman at Messrs Vickers chemical works, Widnes, was entitled to £lOO free of interest for 121 years. The first appropriation in connection with the second society which was announced about seven weeks ago, and in which up to the present 111 members have been enrolled, took place in Bethesda schoolroom on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. R. Frith occupied the chair, and Messrs Bellamy and Hawkins acted as scrutineers. A boy named Robert Birkett Mus- grove, was the ballot drawer. Numbers were twice drawn, which were in excess of the number of members, and a third ballot was taken resulting in 9 being brought to light. After the usual formalities, the secretary was declared en- titled to an advance of £2OO. Mr. Hanley announeed that he should defer claiming the appropriation for twelve months, and consequently another appropriation will short- ly be held. CHARGE AGAINST A. WESTON LANDLADY.—Phoebe Bar- row, landlady of the Royal Oak Inn, Weston, was sum- moned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday to answer a charge of having on Sunday the 9th inst., opened her premises for the sale of intoxicating liquors during prohi- bited hours. Mr. A. E. Fletcher of Northwich defended. P.C. Cooper gave evidence to the effect that on Sanday morning, the 9th inst., he and constable Finney visited the public-houses in the neighbourhood of Weston. They were dressed in plain clothes. At a quarter to ten they went to the back door of the Royal Oak Inn. The door was bolted, and after they had knocked several times, Mrs. Barrow came to a small side window. Half a minute later she opened the door, and Cooper asked her if there was anybody in the house beside lodgers. She replied "No, but you can come in and lock for yourself." The constables then walked into the kitchen. Sitting besides a small round table was a man named Murphy, who lives in ,the village, and at another table Samuel Jones, a lodger, was sitting. As the officers were entering the room they saw the defendant's son, who is about 14 years of age, in the act of putting something under the table, near which Murphy was sitting. Cooper found uader the table a pint cup half filled with freshly drawn beer. Jones claimed the beer as his, and Cooper asked him if it was is why TM it concealed close to Murphy.—The land- lady said Murphy had only just eOrtie to see if Burns lodged there, but he did not —Mr. Fletcher, in addressing the Bench for the defence, remarked upon the fair and impar- tial manner in which the officera had given their evidence, and argued that to constitute the offence of keeping open for the sale of intoxicating liquors, the door of the house must to open, or ajar, or some person mnst be ready to open it at some signal from a eustomer.—He called the de- fendant, who stated all the doors were locked on the morn- ing in question. She explained that Murphy was in the habit of doing work about the place. On Sunday morning he stillaged the beer, and was afterwards sitting in the kitchen inquiring about his friend Burns. He was not sup- plied with any beer, but showould have given him a pint If the officers had not come. The beer found by the officers was supplied to Jones, and her boy was so frightened when the officers appeared that he concealed the beer under the table.—,Samuel Jones, plumber at a Widnes chemical works and Thomas Murphy gave corroborative evidence,—'tee Bench dismissed the case.
ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES.-OPENING CEREMONY.

The new church of St. Paul's, Widnes, was opened for divine service on Tuesday afternoon by Bishop Ryle, Lord Bishop of Liverpool. With the completion of this church the scheme of church extension for Widnes, to which the manufacturers of the town have so liberally subscribed, comes to an end, and the lack of church accommodation is to some extent satisfied. When the proposal to elect the edifice was first brought before the pirishioners in a prac- tical form it was only intended to erect the nave, as the £3,000 guaranteed by the Building Committee would not defray the cost of a more pretentious plan. Through the energy and earnestnees of the vicar, the Rey. J. Wright William., and the generosity of the congregation of St. Mary's Church, the financial difficulty was, however, over- come, and it was decided to build the nave, chancel, and transepts, leaving the erection of a tower to a future period. The plans of Mr. H. Shelmerdine, architect, of Liverpool, were accepted, and the contract was given to Messrs. Morrison and Sons, of Wavertree. The work has progressed rapidly, and there has now arisen a handsome structure which will be a welcome addition to the architec- ture of a town lamentably deficient in public buildings of any description. The church, which is built on an acre of land given by Mrs. Leigh, is situate at Anderson's Corner, and faces Widnes-road. It is cruciform in shape, is built in the early English style of architecture, and is estimated to seat 750 worshippers. The walls are built of picked gray bricks relieved by red brick bands, and the roof is composed of red tiles. There are two entrances. At the south-west corner there is an open porch of handsome design, the in- terior being embellished with terracotta panels, in which a cross ar.cl emblems of Gee evangelists are placed. The church in the interior is 120 feet long, 70 feet broad across the transepts, and measures 50 feet across the nave, and is divided into north and south aisles and nave. There are two vestries—the choir vestry, 15 feet by 11, and the clergy vestry, 11 feet by 12. Light is obtained by "lead lights." The beauty of the interior is greatly enhanced by the design of the nave columns, which are composed of led Wootton stone, with alternate octagon piers and moulded capital and bases. The arches are composed of moulded bricks,, with terra colta bands, and above them rise a row of elevated lights with terracotta Beings. The roof is composed of stained and varnished boards, free access for the air being gained by ornamental loopholes. The floor is of wood block paving in geometrical pattern, while the aisles are tiled. The seats, which are all free and unappropriated, are made of pitch pine, varnished. The heating apparatus; which is on the hot water principle, is situated in a fireproof basement. The edifice is surrounded by a boundary wall erected by Mr. Beach, of Widnes, at a cost of between tsoo. and £6OO, which has been borne by Mr. T. Sutton Timmis. The fol- lowing interior appointments have been presented:—The lecteru, by Mrs. Marshall. of Allerton; the communion table, the chairs, the cover, for the table, and the footstools, by Mr. John Brock, J.P. rails for the communion, by Mr. T. Sutton 'rimmis; the baptismal font, by Mr. George Pilking- ton, J.P.; a set of silver plate for the communion service, by Mr. F. Neil, one, of the churchwardens. Mr. J. B. liaison has promised to give the illuminated tablets for the commandments and the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge have forwarded 300 books of common payer, and Messrs. , Kilowatt and F. 'Neil have forwarded hymn books. There was a crowded congregation at the opening ceremony and in addition to the Bishop the following clergy were present :—The Revs. Canon Diggle, J. Wright-Williams, Vicar of Widnes.; W. Preston, Vicar of Holy rinity, Run- corn ; T. Chambers, Rector of Halewood; George Bond, Vicar of Farnworth ; A. P. Stewart, Vicar of Hale; S. A. Spooner, of St. Ambrose Church; and C Ittuntit and A. P. H. Wilson, both of St. Mary's, 11 idnee. rue choir, which numbered about forty voices; was led by Mr. Cie.% ford, sod Mr. Imison presided at the harmonium. His Lordship took for Lis text Corinthians is, xv., 3 and 4—" For I delivered unto you, first of all, that which I also received; how that Christ died for our sins, accordine to the Scriptures; and that He was buried;, and that He rose again the third day, according to the Scriptures." He remarked that he had taken the text because of the re- markable occasion which called them together—viz, for the solemn setting apart of a new house ef God for worship according to the Church of England. He hoped that when there was a pulpit in that church there would always go from it the faithful sound of the Gospel ef Jleeus Christ. When, in the providence of God, he came, four years ago, to be the bishop of the dieces.., one of the first places he visited was the town of Widnes. He remembered when many years before he passed through it and the spot pre- sented such a different appearance. He was astonished on seeing the teeming population, and when he heard that there was but one little church for all that rich, wealthy, and in- telligent congregation his heart was deeply touched. He well remembered going up and down the place, and coming to the decision that, with God's help and blessing, he would never rest until he had seen another church built there He thanked God for having stirred up the spirit of their worthy vicar, strengthened his hands, and given him the encouragement which had caused him to persevere by rais- ing up a band of ready labourers among the rich, and also among the poor, whose united endeavours had brought that church to the condition in which he then saw it. He trusted that the time was not far distant when he should come there again for the purpose of consecrating it, and solemnly setting it apart for the service of Almighty God. Might God cause men to come forward and liberally contribute, so that everything might be done which the law required be- fore the building could be consecrated, and thus set apart to he one more fortress for the Church of England. It had been a cause of sorrow that they bad so many populations gathered together in the great county of Lancaster' where the Church bail not made adequate provision for the spiritual wants of the masses of the people. He thanked God for the way in which he beard the working classes of Widnes had taken up the project of building that church. They had shown, as he bad always said the members of that class would show when they had a really faithful clergyman amongst them, how ready they were to give most substan- tial proof of how deeply interested they were in such a mevement. He was one of those who was never afraid of the working classes forsaking the Church of England so long as that Church did not forsake her own principles, and tkas true te those grand verities for which her founders suf- fered so much three hundred years ago. In the evening the Very Rev. Archdeacon Bardsley preached to a crowded congregation. The collections at both services amounted to £BO 10s 10d.
WIDNES COUNCIL OF __EDUCATION : DISTRIBU-

TION OF PRIZES. The annual meeting of the Widnes Council of Education for the distribution of prizes, was held in the Volunteer Hall, on Wednesday evening. The building was crowded with an audience composed of parents and scholars, while in a large gallery behind the platform, was a chorus of about SOO children from the various schools in the town. During the evening these children under the conductorship of Mr. J. C. Crawford, sang a number of songs in a very pleasing manner. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Sut- ton Timmi., president of the council, and he was supported on the platform by Mrs. Timmis, Mrs. A. McLennan ; the Revs. J. Wright Williams, George Bond, S. A. Spooner;, Dr. O'Keeffe ; Messrs J. Brock, J.P., H. W. Deacon, S. K. Muspratt, Allen Deacon, R. Bradshaw, B. Brown, R. H. Davies A. McLennan, H. Brun- ner, T. Swipe, and d. H. Danby. Amongst the audience were Rev. A. P. H. Wilson ; Messrs Joseph Morrison, Dr. McLennan, P. Glover, James White, F. Lawrinson, F. Cane, W. Crabtree, dm. Mr. C. Bushell, of Liverpool, had been invited to deliver an address, but be was unable to be present, and he forwarded a long let- ter in which he referred to the work of the Widnes Council in highly congratulatory terros. He said it was highly satisfactory to observe that of a total number of 2,703 pu- pile upon the rolls of the three Board schools, no less than 651, or more than 24 per cent had gained rewards for the very high standard of regular and punctual attendance at which the council so wisely aimed. It was not lees gratify- ing that a large number of prizes bad also been gained by the pupils in the voluntary schools, although the offering to each of them had been more recently made than in the case of the Board schools. Mr. Bushell mentioned that the aver- age attendance in England and Wales of the number of children upon the rolls was, as shown by a recent blue book, 732 per cent., while in the Widnes schools they bad already attained an average of 84, which per centap they had every reason to hope would continue to in- crease. The letter concluded with a reference to the gen- erosity of the governors of Farnworth Grammar School in. instituting three free ezhAarships, adding that the cam. petition and examination for these tended to raise the. general standard of instruction throughout the whole public: elementary school system. The Chairenan, who had a cordial reception, explained that for two years the prizes had been confined to the chil- dren of the Board schools, but they were so appreciated, and bad such a marked effect on the good attendance that the managers of the Denominational schoolsin Widnes wore anxious that the system of prizes should be extended to their schools. The donors of the original prizes were only too glad to fall in with this idea, and in consequence the 4 Council of Education was formed. Aninceme was assured for three 'years, and he was glad to say that a scheme was drawn up which embraced all the elementary schools in Widnes whether Board scheols.or denominational schools. It was found impossible to continue the prizes on the same scale„ but it was highly satisfactory that although the amount of the prizes had been reduced, the attendance had not fallen off. It was very deeirabla that all the de- nominational schools should join in the council for all who ; had anything to do with elementary education were aware that denominations carried on their work under great dieser vantages compared with the Board schools. The Boaad sahoole. if the school pence and the Government grant failed to pay the expenses had the public purse to fall back upon, but if the denominational schools were short they had to appeal for private subscriptions, and it was unfair that they should tae handicapped further by a system of prizes ex- tended to Board schools only. (Applause.) Although the Board schools were doing a good work, there was a time when all the education in the town was given by the de-. nominational schools, and to them a great debt of gratitude was due. (Hear, bear.) The main object of the council that night was to ask the approval of the inhabitants of Widnes in what they had done, and resolutions would be submitted by gentlemen of all shades of thought. (Ap- plause.)—Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from the Revs. Father Clarke and Father Finegan, and. Mr. Watte, the headmaster of Farnworth Grammar School—Mr. H. W. Deacon delivered an address, in which he stated that the first prise of 45 and a certificate bad keen gained by 317

children; the second prize of 2s and a certificate by 403 children; and the third prize, a certificate, by 414 children. The total number of children who had gained certificates was 1,134, and as the average number on the rolls was 5,454, they would see that one child out of every five had ob- tained the reward. (Applause.) That was a very large proportion for the first year, and the figures were quite trustworthy. The average attendance at the Board schools for 1883 was 82i per cent., in 1884 it was 82.1 per cent., an increase of a half per cent. In the voluntary schools in 1883 the average attendance was only 701 per cent., in 1884, ' the past year they had participated in the prizes, the aver- age had risen to 764 per cent. ',Applause.) He hoped they appreciated those figures. He pointed out that Mr. Bushell in estimating the average attendance of children at school ia Widnes at 81 per cent, had made a mistake. The average for last year was 791- per cent., but still that was a conrider- able increase on the average for England and Wales. He appealed to those present not to be satisfied with the present attendance, and referred to the great effect home influences had upon attendance.—Mrs. A. McLennan then distributed the prizes. It had been deci- ded to make the presentations to the individual prize win. ners at the various schools, and the prizes were now received from the hands of Mrs. McLennan by representatives from those schools.—The Rev. J. Wright-Williams moved "That this meeting cordially approves of the action of the Council of Education, and strongly urges on the inhabitants of Widnes its claims for .support." After alluding to Mr. Tim- iris and Mr. Deacon in highly eulogistic terms, the vicar pointed out that of the income of the Council 2100 Was given by two gentlemen well known in the town, and the other £lOO was subscribed by about thirty gentlemen. In an earnest speech he appealed for more aid, and depicted the advantages which would accrue to the rising genaration from the ezcellent education offered thein.—Or. O'Keeffe seconded the motion. All the inhabitants of Widnes, and all lovers of education owed a great debt to the Council, and oughtto aid it in its career by subscribing—The motion was supported by the Rev. G. Bond, Mr. R. Brown, Mr. R. H. Davies, and Mr. T. Snape;and was carried unanimously. —Mr. J. Brock, J.P., moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. MC- Lennan for distributing the prizes.—Mr. H. Brunner seconded the proposition, which W4B heartily carried.—Mr. A. McLennan responded on behalf of his wife in suitable terms.—A vote of thanks W4B accorded the chairman on the proposition of Mr. S. K. Muspratt, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING Ar RUNCORN.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING Ar RUNCORN.

A public meeting in support of the movement for closing public-houses on Sunday was held in Runcarn Public Hall on Monday evening. -There was a large attendance. Mr. Jas. Handley, Le., presided, and was supported on the plat- form by the Rev& Canon McNeile, M.A. (deputation), W. Preston, M.A., Norman E McNeiele, M.A. (Vicar of Braffer- tno),J.Haskett, and J. Fick well ; Messrs. S. C. Beckett, J. R. Frith, J. N. Lello, J. D. Jones. and J. Faulkner. The Revs. Canon Barclay and J. D. Thomas; Messrs. W. Whittaker, J. Buckley, Geo. Summerfiuld, H. White, M. Barker, B. Dutton, and F. Beck occupied seats among the

audience. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman said it was al- ways a pleasure to himeand be might say a duty to takee part in any m wement having for its aim and object the well-being or The community, and he thought it wonld be Impossible to find any measure of which the adoption would sooner tell for the advantage of the entire people than the curtailment of the liquor traffic. He was a total abstainer, and be was glad to say he was not aingulac in that respect, for he thought there were many on that platform, and in that meeting, who could lay claim to a similar honour, and ihey therefore would be prepared to go much further then the association in whose interests they were gathered together. Sunday closing was only part of a much larger subject, and whilst there were many who world not go in for the total stoppage of the common sale of intoxicating liquors, they felt confident that the large majority of the Englieb peope are with them as far as Sunday Closing was concerned. They believed the Sunday liquor traffic to be produceive of a large amount of drunkenness, domestic misery, pauperism, crime, ignorance and all sorts of evils, and in asking those present to advocate and agitate for its legal suppression, they were not introducing any new principle in the legislature. It was already the law for Public-houses to be closed on Sun- day in Scotland, in Ireland, and in Wales and the gradual adoption of Sunday closing in these three counties had furnished unmisttkeable proofs that the more the facilities for obtaining drink were lessened there would proportiona- tely be less drunkenness. Let them look for a moment at Scotland, where Sunday closing was first brought into opera- tion, and at the improvement they found there after 30 years experience. In 1853 in the city of Edinburgh the avesage annual number charged with being drunk and incapable was 6,279. In 1883 the number was 2,738. (Applause.) Sun- day cases alone had fallen from 702 to 219; Monday cases from 772 to 337 ; Saturday cases from 1,351 to. 847. But the best effect of all resulting from the Act in that city was shown by the cases of drunk and incapable persons from be- tween eight o'clock on Sunday morning and the same hour on Monday morning, which had fallen from 383 to 40. (Ap- plause.) Similar results had followed in the other large centres of population in Scotland. The Irish Sunday Clos- ing Act came into operation five years ago,. and what had been the result ? Five million sterling reduced consum- ption of intoxicating liquors in those five years, and as a consequence of this a very great decrease in the arrests for general drunkenness. So satisfied were the members of the government with the operation of the Act that they were anxioue to make the Act perpetual and to apply it to the five cities at, present exempted from its provisions. The same beneficial effects had followed the adcption of Sunday closing in Wales, and with this mass of evidence in their favour they had the fullest confidence in appealing to the sympathy of the people on behalf of this movement. They were anxious that the blessings I:ljoved by the Scotch, Irish, and Welsh should be shared in by the English, and they would not relax their efforts until that was accom- plished. He referred to the great preponderance of opinion in favour of Sunday closing, and said that Mr. G. IL Sims attributed much of the great mass of misery which he found in London to the excessive consumption of intoxicating drink. He was forced to that conclusion after very search- ing inquiry and visitation of the lower quarters of the city which he himself undertook. In conclusion the Chairman reminded the audience that they were only asking for peblic-houses to be closed on one day out of seven, and he asked them to consider what would be the effect on the home manufactures of our beloved land if they could di- vest into that channel one-seventh (about seven millions sterling) of the amount annually spent in intoxicating liquors. Did not they think the bitter cry of which they at present heard so much would soon- be silenced'? They firmly believed it would, and it was because they were per- suaded that reduced facilities'for obtaining drink would he of immense benefit to this country, materially,. morally, and, above all, spiritually, that they confidentlee asxed for their support on behalf of the resolutions which would be submitted to the meeting. (Applause.) Mr. J. N. Lello moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting considers that the sale of intoxicating liquor on the Lord's Day is unfair and injurious and ought not to be sanctioned by the laws of this country." (Applause.) The Rev. Canon McNeile seconded the resolution, and observed that the Sunday closing of public-houses was no qeestion of party politics, or even of teetotalism or modera- tion. It was a question of the prosperity of the country. It was a question of the lives and the happiness of thousands and tens f thousands of their fellow-countrymen--a ques- tion-of the honour of God and the sanctity of His holy day. (aepplause.) He pointed out that the only real oppo- sition to the movement came from "the trade." itself, but that opposition was sympathised in to some extent by per- oons who thought that what they were pleased to call "class- legislation" was unfair and injurious. There was a great deal ii the minds of Englishmen that responded to an ape peal of that kind, and they heard a great deal about i•ob., bing the poor man of his beer, as -if it were a very hard and unkind thing to do. One of the most obvioas replies to that opposition was that it was the very man they were going to deprive of his beer who was asking them to de it. There were. a larger number of petitions presented to Parliament, and a larger number of signatures in favour of the total closingeof public-houses on Sundays than there were presentedifor every other object petitioned for throughout the country. (Applause.) He bad yet to learn that the Franchise Biee,. about which there was no much agitietion, bad bean ask-ed for in the way that Sunday closing had. There had- been no ,petition with half a million signatures as there hadheen. in favour of Sunday closing. Mr. Gladstone no doubt had had enormous audiences when he had spoken about the Fein- - obise Bill—(applause)--but if Mr. Gladstone would only spoken for Sunday closing, he promised them that he would have had larger audiences. still—(applause)—andi- ienoes of Liberals and Conservatives who world have ap- plauded him-to the echo. (Applause.) Yet they were kept waiting for this booo,which the country had been demand- ing for years, becavoee. for some reason or otbcr the Govern- ment did not feel it to be so important as these other party and political questions, Surely social questions were in- ' finitely more important. If t ea> millions of their fellow- men weee to be enfranchised it was of infinite iemortance that they should be sober men and know how to use the. power given to them. Therefore the very, streagth of the agitation now. going on in reference to thia 'great political question strengthened their cause .te asking tint tee legielature would hoar west had been addressed. to. them from every part of the,countree, from both partioe and ale classes--an eeriest, strenuous, persevering, and consistent req=st that they would treat the trade in intoxicating liquors on the /owl's Day the same as other trades. (Applause) The seeaker *en reeerred to the beneficial resultsof Sonday closing in IrelandeScotland, and Wales, and referring to the depressed 'state of trade throughout the kingdam, expressed theopiniolt that the evil had beans aggravated by the drinking habits a the people. (Applause.) The resolution was unanimously canoed. The Rev. W. Preston, M.A.„ moved " That the chairntan be requested to sign on behalf of this. meeting n memorial in favour of Suaday closing, end to forward tho same to the Prime Minister, the Home Secretaey, and the men:there of Parliament for Mid-Cheshire." The speakee- arguecl that pure morality bad its basis upon pure religion, but pare re- ligion demanded the Sabbath for its development, and on these grounds he earnestly advocated the entire stoppage of the liquor traffic on the Sabbath. (Applause.) The Rev. Norman RMcNeile seconded the resolution. The Chairman read a note from the Rev, Canon Barclay, who stated that he hoped to be able to attend the meeting that night, though he would be unable to take any part in the proceedings. He trusted their efforts would be success- ful. (Loud applause.) Mr. J. D. Jones then read a zopy of the memorial to be forwarded, and the resolutive was passed unanimously, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDOII, THUBSDAI.

This time last week the two great political parties were standing sword in hand and foot to foot preparing for a fina struggle round tile Franchise Bill. To-day, the Franchise Bill having been read a second time in the House of Lords without a division, arraegements are being made for a Con- ference of the leaders, at which the broad principle of the Redistribution Bill shall be determined upon. Politics are always full of surprises. But the progress of the Franchise Bill towards the Statute Book has been more strongly marked by surprises than anything that has gone before. A fortnight ago, whilst the air was full of warlike sounds, suddenly came Sir R. Cross with his pacific epeech, and settlement seemed certain. On the next day came the South Warwickshire election, and on the following Monday Mr. James Lowther breathing fire and fury,a new departure of the Opposition, confirmed by Lord John Manners's speech, of the following night. Last Monday Mr. Gladstone in the House of Commons, and Earl Granville in the Lords, once more waved the flag of truce, and on Tuesday night Lord Salisbury publicly took off his armour, laid down his spear., and entered into peaceful counsels. This sudden determination of the Premier to make a statement in the House of Commons on Monday night is only one indication of the consummate skill with which he has conducted the campaign. To the people Mr. Gladstone is known as a great statesman and a great orator. lo his- colieagues and to those who watch him closely in the House of Commons he is known as a remarkable tactician, and, when occasion arises, a profound strategist. This re— newed proffer of peace on the very eve of the meeting of the Conservative party at the Carlton Club, was meant less for Lord Salisbury's consideration than for hie coercion. It was well knowe that there were scores of peers who would only too gladly find an excuse for withdrawing from the path along which Lord salisbury would lead them. To have waited another day would have been too late. Had Lord Salisbury at the meeting at the Carlton succeeded in inducing the Cons:rvative party to continue on the war path, it would have been tenfold more difficult thereafter to turn them aside. Whilst there was yet time, Mr. Gladstone spoke, and with marvellous effect. The statement was designed, one of the ministers told me, in vigorous imagery "to put fire under the stomach of Lord Salisbury." It certainly moved him, and having once been compelled to abandon his stubborn position, he seems honestly and honourably inclined to desist from further mischief.
The preliminary agreement arrived at between the two parties naturally finds querulous critics in es.treme sections
Of either side. With the Conservatives, men like Mr. James
Lowther grind their teeth in impotent rage. With the Liberals, Mr. Labouchere growls and shakes his head, aid. talks about surrender. At the outset, even so shrewd and
clear-headed a man as Mr. John Morley was led away by

appearances, aad viewed with some distrust the amicable turn affairs had taken. On the Conservative side there is, apart from Mr. Lowther and his mates, a large- class who do not quite understand the affair, and are inclined to regard it with distrust. What excites their suspicion is the pleased manner in which Mr. Chamberlain, for example, looks- upon it. But they are accustomed to follow their leaders, and they dolt now marvelling but not murmuring. On the Liberal side, the more things are discussed and the more clearly they are understood, the deeper is the satisfaction. Lord.Salisbury,on Tuesday night, made a great deal of what

he called the withdrawal of the demand forailequate assurance& t go forward with the Franchise Bill to be given by the Conservatives before the Redistribution Bill is introduced. This led away men like Mr. Labouchere, who immediately

, began to cry out about a surrender. It turns out, after all, that there is no surrender. The position of the Government is exactly what it always has been—that before the Redis- tribution Bill is laid on the table of the House of Commons the Rouse of Lords must be in Committee en the Franchise Bill.

But supposing concessions of this charactsr bad been made to the Conservatives, and it cannot be too strongly stated that they have not, what would that weigh against the enormous advantages gained for Liberalism by the ar- rangement just brought about? in the first place two millions of our fellow citizens will forthwith be enfran- chised. Net, a Redistribution scheme would be set in operation with the consent of both parties. Supposingthat such a scheme fall short of the desires cf the Liberals; that

would be regretable. But it would be a drawback not com- parable for a moment with the gain. The Franchise Bill will be for all time. The Redistribution Bill might be remedied at. any time its defaults became strikingly ap- parent. But it happens that the Redistribution scheme that will come out of the crucible over which Liberal and.
Conservative leaders are even now working will be of a
much more Radical character than that tOe Government

were prepared to submit. Mr. Gladstonee influence in this. quarter had, as neual, been overmastering. He who has dis- establishedm church and enfranehised the land of a nation is now, above all things, for moderation. "The practical question," he is accustomed to say, "Is not what you want, but how much can you get." Thus the Redistribution scheme of the Government was based upon a spirit of com- promise. But it turns out, as yet an unempleined marvel that the Conservatives, led in this instance by Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, are prepared with a thoroughly Radical scheme of Redistribution. This being proffered to him, Mr. Gladstone will not refuse it, whilst men like Mr. Cham- berlain and Sir Charles Dilke jump at itt It is a long time since English politics afforded such a striking personal episode as that of yesterday, when Lord Salisbury calleclem Mr. Gladstone to talk-over tbe arrange- ments for the approaching conference. It. is many years since these two sat together and talked. In English Doliti- cal life controversy closes at the deer of Parliament, and men who have been hurling hot words at each other-across the floor of the House of Commons, erequently walk off arm. in-arm, to dine. I may mention as a striking illustration of this happy condition of affairs that I made the personal acquaintance of Lord Randolph ehurchill at the dinner table of Mr. Chamberlain. But Mr. Gladstone,„soaring high, above the common eight, has always moved apart; and has. known nothing socially of his political adverairies, more es- pecially those who are personally arrayed against him. Of course he and Mr. Disraeli acknowledged each other's pre-- Bence when they accidentally met. But they maintained no social intercourse, and the same statement applies to Lord Salisbury. It must have been a curious meeting that-of yes- terday, these two gladiators, fresh from a great bout of - Homeric warfare on the platform end in the forum, sitting quietly together to arrange a friendly gathering. There is, just now current:- a charm;ng story about the younger son of a well-known house. He war-travelling with a companion down to Sevenoaks the other day when the train happened to be crowded. The two aorepamions Sound a firsteclass carriage in which there was ona seat empty and another which had upon ite, travelling bag,pre-. samably the property of a crusty looking old gentleman sitting in the corner seat opposite. " May I move your bag ?" said the young gentleman emletely. "No," said the Itrusty old gentlemen, "that seat's engaged:- " 04, very well," said the young gentleman, 'we're not going fir." So I. he panted-himself on the elbow of the seat occupied by his-. friend. When the train Pulled upe at London Beedge, he looked anaiously out of the window as if expecarg some- one. Bat no one arrived. The train sped on, and still he. sat on the elbow of the seat, tha travelling bag,. having a, whole cashioned seat to itself and the crasty, old, gentleman diligently reading his 11fornin ,rest. As soon as the train, now oa full speed, passed New Cross, the young gentleman opened the window, took up the travellirrg bag, and dropped it out. "What are you doing ?" screamed the crusty oldgentleman. " Year friend's missed thr trainee said the younger one, comfortably e.eopping into the now empty seat. Lord Dudley. still finds it necessary to continue his mile freer. public Ble. He woe at one time a pretty frequent at, tendant upon the House of Lords. nut the place, and others whither he was want ta.resort, Limy him no more. Some. times, on great occasions, a beautiful lady dressed in black with a tiara el diamonds flashing in her blaek hair is seeu. sitting am.Arg the peeresses in the gallery of the }louse of Lords, andeael eyes ereturned in pity and admiration upon the Coustess of Hadley. lent these appearances are very' , rare, the young wiee in the prime of he life and beauty* having devoted eerself abeelutely to the care set her hus- band. With hire, she livea in close seclusion. Bet if nothing happens between, now suet, then the old. Dudlee hospitality is noaemonth. to be revived with meeptional splendour. Wieley Condon Worcestershire, is to have its long closed gates re-opened, for the Rrincoand Princess of Wales are to ha the guests- of Lord ald Lady Dudley. Miss Buddon makas bitter complaint that though her- aovels—noialaly "Laly Aucliey's Secret,"" Aurora Floyd," and " liselrY Dumber "—have been drametised, ancl have brought large sums of money into some-. body'a pocketas not a shilling has ever found its way into eters. Mr. Hugh Conway, wiser in his geneeation, has taken means to secure for himself the full prOut,whatever it may be, of a dramatised version of his last book, "Dark Days." One quiet night, when it was supposed the Prince's Theatre was closed, a dramatised ver- sion of "Dark Days," which he has prepared in collaberae tion with Mr. Cornyns Carr, was placed moon the stage, and played throughout before reputable witnesses. This estab- lishes copyright for him, and it would now be impossible for freebooters to forestall him, at least in England.

At the Heywood Police Cow,t, on WednesCay, George Townend, formerly the principal rate collector in the ern- povment of the Heywood Corporation, was committed for six months for embezzling money belonging to the Cor- poration. The investigatirm of his books is not yet con- cluded, but the amount already ascertained to be missing is over MOO.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Mr. John Fairclough. The defendant, it ap- peared, had been amusing himself by exploding a small cannon on the night of the day in question in Sandy-lane. He put a heavy screw nail into the cannon, and on explod- ing the nail flew through the window and venetian blind of Mrs. Hutchinson's house, and struck and broke the mirror which was standing on the mantelskelf. Mr. Brook, who is the landlord of the house, claimed for the window and blind, and Mrs. Hutchinson for the mirror.—The Benet, after severely censuring the defendant, said they would be as lenient as they could with him, and would order him to pay the costs, 343, and to replace the damage done.
