div.head: FARMERS AND HIGH RENTS.
div.p: FARMERS AND HIGH RENTS.

The farmers in the fee of Makerfield commenced an agi- tation a few months ago for obtaining a reduction in their rents and in connection therewith meetings have been held at Ashton, Newton-le-Willows, ,a.c. On Monday evening another meeting was held at the Stork Inn, Billinge, for the purpose of discussing the present depressed state of agri- culture and to receive reports as to petitions to be addressed to the landlords asking for a reduction of 25 per cent. in the rents. Mr. T. atone, Leigh, presided, and there were about 60 tenant farmers present from all parts of the fee of Makerfield. The Pemberton representative said he had conferred with his colleague, and it had been decided to hold the matter in abeyance. They intended to have a meeting to consider the question, and to get the farmers to sign the petition. Some had al- ready signed, but there was room for more.—The Windle representative said his application for signatures to the pe- tition had been highly satisfactory.—The Billinge-Chapel- End representative said all the farmers in his district bad signed with the exception of one.—The Chairman said he thought on the whole that things were very encouraging. What they bad to consider was the rents as they existed at the present time, and to endeavour to get them reduced. No doubt other questions could be taken up afterwards, and if they were tackled in the same spirit they had tackled the question of rent, he confidently believed that success would attend every effort made. He had heard from a tenant of the Earl of Crawford and Balcarres that his lord- ship had received the petition favourably, and doubtless other landlords would !eel constrained to do the same. He knew two instances where rents had been reduced, in one case 60 per cent, and in the other 30, and that of itself was a hopeful sign. The tenant farmer was suffering at every turn, and he required sympathy and help from all classes, and especially the landlords. They called on the landowner to share in the general anxiety and suffering there was at the present time. In other parts of the country landlords were reducing their rents without any pressure being brought to bear upon them. Theirs was a humble petition, and they almost went down on their knees. If the landlords would only consider the manner in which they bad approached them, he thought they would grant their request —The Billinge representative said it was not that they had anything against their landlords that they were raising the present agitation. The depression in farming was very great, and there was little hope Of improvement The local rates pressed very heavily upon them, whereas formerly it was not so bad. He had seen depression, and he had seen fairly good times, but he never knew in all his experience farming in such a depressed state as it was in now, nor when wages were so high and the price of produce so low. It wonld be well for the landlords to look to their tenants before their capital was exhausted.—The Blackrod representative observed that the landlords could not say they had been in a hurry about this matter. They were not asking for mercy, they were asking for justice. The land was not as valuable now as it was formerly, and why should they pay the same rent for it ? They wanted to have land at a price at which they could make an honest living. The farmers of Scotland were appealing for a reduction rents, the farmers of Ireland had got a reduction, and why should not the English farmers follow suit? He was glad to say that already in his district some of the farmers' rents had been reduced 25 per cent., and if the whole of them would persevere they would all get it.—The Westboughton representative said the farmers of this district had been liv- ing for some time past not upon profit but upon hope. They had struggled on, trusting that each succeeding year would prove better than its predecessors, but instead of that they found that year by year their position was gradually and continuously becoming worse, and in looking round as a man of the world he could see no earthly reason to hope for any substantial improvement. The causes which had led to a reduction in the price of agricultural produce were permanent ones. If the landlords would not consent to take some portion of the rent off the farmers would have to make the best hf it. The course being pursued by the Farmers' Association was a respectful course, they were asking in a respectful manner, and ins manner to which he was sure exception could not be taken. He trusted and hoped that the landlords would see their way to looking at the matter in a favourable light and grant their request.—The Pemberton representative said be began farming in the first year of the depression, via, 1879, and since then they had gone from bad to worse. Instead of things mending there were signs of still greater depression, and to combat that depression they must have a reduction in their rents.—Several other representatives Id- dressed the meeting, and it was resolved that the associa- tion should not present their petition for a reduction of rents until after the meeting at Pemberton. The usual votes of thanks brought the proceedings to a close. Another meeting of an association which has been formed at Westhoughton to secure a reduction of rents and the abolition of tithes, was held on Wednesday night. It was reported that nearly all the farmers in the district had signed petitions, and the chairman observed that their movement was spreading all over Lancashire. An associa- tion would next be formed at Hindley. The speaker held that foreign wheat was so cheap that, with the present rents, they could not compete.

_ fn interviews with several farmers occupying land in Sankey and the neighbourhood, a representative of this journal learns that although a decrease of rent would to them be a very desirable thing, they have not yet as a body taken any active part in the agitation at present being car- ried on to attain that result. They do not complain as a rule in such strong terms of the high rents as do farmers in some other districts, but declare that what with rents, tithes, and taxes combined to pay, they are utterly unable to make any appreciable prod': out of the land they culti- vate, and are, in fact, toiling for mere bread and cheese, and in some instances working to a loss.
It is said to be virtually certain that we shall have single member constituencies all over the country, in boroughs and counties alike.

NATIONAL RADICAL FEDERATION.—At the second annual conference, in London, on Monday, Mr. William Trent in the chair, resolutions were passed demanding a thorough reform of the land laws, the abolitiob of the House of Lords, and desiring a redistribution of seats on the basis of equal electoral districts according to population. The Rev. S. Headlam, Mr. Henry George, and Dr. Hankhurst were among the speakers. LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, George Bowden, 20 years of age, was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment with hard labour for having broken into a house. In the case of William Marsh, in- dicted for bigamy, the prisoner was released on his own recognisances. John M'Quade, vete was found guilty on Tuesday of the manslaughter of a sailor named Keogh, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. GREAT GLOVE FlGHT.—lntelligence has been received in Birmingham of the result of the great glove fight in New York on Monday night between J. L. Sullivan, the American champion pugilist, and Alf. Greenfield, of Bir- mingham, whose champion belt was stolen the other day during his absence in America. Two desperate rounds are said to have been fought in Greenfield's favour, when the police stepped into the ring and stopped the fieht. ANOTHER ELECTION AT SCARBOROIIGH.—The Conserva- tives have resolved to contest the seat vacated at Scar- borough by Mr. Caine's appointment as Civil Lord of the Admiralty. Sir George Sitwell, who was so recently de- feated by Lieutenant Colonel Stable, will be the Conserva- tive candidate, and has issued his address. Mr. Caine ar- rived in the borough to conduct his canvass on Wednesday, when the writ was issued. The writ for filling the vacancy In county Down has reached the High Sheriff, who has fixed the nomination for Monday and the polling for Thurs- day in next week. The nomination is fixed for Monday, and the polling for Wednesday next. WIFE MURDER IN MANCHESTER—Arthur Shaw, a tailor, aged 31, was indicted at the Liverpool Assizes on Thursday fer the murder Of his wife, Ellen Shaw, by strangling her, at their house in Dalton-street, In Manches- ter, on the 3rd inst. It is alleged that the prisoner quar- relled with his wife OR the evening of that day, and that when she became exhausted with struegling he seized her by the throat and strangled her. He afterwards called in several neighbours, who found the deceased on a chair quite dead. There were marks of pressure having been applied to her throat, and the medical geßtlemen who examined the body had apparently no hesitation in attributing death Ito strangulation. Some of the appearances produced by strangulation were, however, absent. He was found guilty of the capital crime and Sentenced to death, the Judge ex- pressing his entire co.ncurrence in the verdict. The jury recommended the convict to mercy, and the Judge said he , i would at once state the fact n the proper quarter. I M 0 EIS

div.head: 'RUNICENNESS.
div.p: 'RUNICENNESS.
THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22. 1884

THE FRANCHISE AND REDISTRIBU- TION AGITATION. ACCEPTANCE OF THE GOVERNMENT TERMS OF COMPROMISE. As will be seen from our Parliamentary report, the com- promise offered by the Government has been accepted by the chief of the Opposition. The Daily lrews offered the following explanation of a statement made on Monday night:—" The Prime Minister'e reply to Sir Wilfrid Law- son, indicating that an appeal to the country would follow upon the Lords rejecting the Redistribution Bill, caused ' much consternation in Liberal circles. We are in a position to state that the answer was given under a misapprehen- sion. What Mr. Gladstone intended to state was what Lord Granville made clear in the House of Lords, that, in order to meet the objection raised in Conservative circles that should the Franchise Bill be paseed the Opposition in the Commons might throw out the Redistribution Bill, the Go- vernment pledged themselves either to carry the bill through the Commons or at once resign." The Pall Mall Gazette's version of the compromise was as follows :-1. The Standard story that the Government in writing waived their demand for adequate assurance is incorrect. 2. The Government, before bringing the nego- tiations to a satisfactory conclusion, had received assur- ances which they regarded as adequate. 3. A meeting will shortly take place between Lord Salisbury and Mr. Glad- stone to arrange the details of the Redistribution Bill. 4. That the Bill will be b ised upon the following principles, which are practically identical in outline with those fore- shadowed by Lord Randolph Churchill. 5. These prin- ciples, so far as they are known at present, are supposed to be as follows :—(a) Representation to be adjusted on the basis of population ; (b) separation of urban and rural voters •, (c)boroughs under 10,000 to be merged in the coun- ties; (d) boroughs between 10,030 and 25,000 to be grouped with the neighbouring urban populations ; (e) no borough with less than 25,000 population to have distinct represen- tation ; (f) large towns, entitled to mere than two mem- bers, to be split up into single member wards. 6. The Franchise Bill to be passed by the House of Lords before Christmas. MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY. The Press Association states that the special interest taken in Tuesday's private meeting of Conservatives was in- dicated not only by the very large attendance of members of the Opposition from both Houses, but also by the unusual crowd of onlookers who gathered in Pall Mall opposite the Club to watch their arrival. Previous to the general meet- ing several of the leaders met in private for a preliminary consultation at the residence of the Marquis of Salisbury, Arlington-street, when it was decided to recommend their followers to accept the latest proposals of the Government, subject to the conditions which had been further explained in writing since the Ministerial statements were made on Monday night by Earl Granville and Mr. Gladstone. At the subsequent meeting in the large,upper room of the Carl- ton Club Lord Salisbury, who presided, was supported by Sir Stafford Northcote, the Duke of Northumberland, the Duke of Richmond, Earl Carnarvon, Lord Randolph Churchill, and other leading members of the party from the two branches of the Legislature, as well as by so nu- merous a muster of the rank and file that the sitting accomo- dation of the hall was insufficient, and many had to be content with standing room. The attendance numbered fully 300. The Marquis of Salisbury, as chairman, was the first speaker, and he referred with satisfaction to the material concessions announced on the'part of the Government, which he regarded as practically vindicating the course taken last session by the House of Lords His Lordship remarked that the peers would now have some means of assuring themselves that the promised Redistribution Bill would be of a moderate and equitable character, that its rapid ad- vancement would be guaranteed, and that its main provi- sions would be made known to them before they passed the measure for the extension of the franchise. Under these circumstances it had been agreed to advise that the second reading of the Franchise Bill should not be opposed, and that its subsequent stages should also be aereed to upon the introduction, in the meantime, in the House of Commons, of such a reasonable Redistribution Bill as might be based upon the mutual conference between the representatives of the Government and the Opposition. Sir Stafford North- cote's speech was in the same sense, and Earl Cairns also ex- pressed concurrence. In the course of a brief discussion which followed, Earl Jersey and other speakers expressed , themselves satisfied with the soktien of the difficulty. Among the other speakers were Lord Oranniere, eed Drewne, Mr. Chaplin, Sir W. Hart Dyke, and Sir Walter Barttelot. It was agreed that Lord Salisbury, in consenting to the second reading of the Franchise Bill, should endeavour to obtain a more precise and explicit statement than had yet been given by the Government upon certain doubtful points regarding which questions were asked. No resolu- tions were proposed, nor was any division taken, the re- commendations of the leaders of the party being agreed to with unanimity. The proceedings lasted little more than an hour.

If Mr. Sutton wished for an as- sietant clerk the proper and legitimate course was for him to send in a written application to the Board, and the Board would then probably, according to custom, appoint a com- mittee to consider the application.—The CLERK said he was not aware of any such duty. He (the clerk) also pointed out that Mr. Harrison bad been at the previous meeting when the matter was discussed, and that he had mentioned it so far back as April last.—Some more discussion having taken place, Mr. HARRISON said he should like to have the minute he had asked for read.—Mr. JEANS said that it was only the salary of Mr. Sutton as clerk to the Board of Guar- dians that had not been increased since he was appointed. That was £3OO, but there was £145 from the Assessment Committee, and £5O from the School Attendance Commit- tee. The latter committee had been formed since Mr. Sut- ton was appointed, and he wished to know what Mr. Ged- des, Mr. Sutton's predecessor, got from the Assessment Com- mittee.—The CLERK: In 1862 Mr. Geddes had £l4o.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said he was surprised that Mr. Harrison should have raised the objection he did. He (Mr. Darby- shire must say that when he was appointed to the commit- tee, he understood that tht assistant clerkship was the main point the committee were appointed to consider.—Dr. MACKIE asked Mr. Harrison to waive his objection.—Mr. HARRISON said the only reason why he took the objection was to prevent similar irregularities in the future. He would withdraw his technical objection in order that Mr. Darbyshire might put them in order by moving a resoln- tion.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE then moved that Mr. S. Sutton be appointed deputy clerk as recommended by the committee - Mr. BROWN seconded the motion.-Mr.HARRISON rose to move an amendment. He regarded that motion, he said, as one to increase the clerk's salary by £l2O. When they consi- dered that proposal they ought to consider seriously the present stagnation of trade, and the way in which people were crippled in order to pay the legitimate rates they were called upon to pay. It was their duty as guardians of the poor and as representatives of the ratepayers, at the same time to watch with jealousy the expenditure of public money. He was not animated in the least by hostility to the clerk. He considered him a very valuable clerk, but he felt that under the present circum- stances he must contest against the course which had been adopted,although he had waived his technical objection which he still contended was a valid one, and which really dispossessed them of the power of dealing with that question. He did not object to the appointment of an assistant clerk, but he did object to the fact that they should pay him £ll5 a year. He would be willing to appoint an assistant clerk at a nominal salary and let the clerk do the rest. This was because he was deeply impressed with the fact that the clerk was very handsomely paid. He made it out that the emoluments paid to the clerk or incidental to the office of clerk to that Board could not possibly be less than £9OO ("No, no.") In the first place, the clerk had £3OO a year, and Mr. Geddes had not £3OO a year, as had been stated, and he (Mr. Harrison) thought the clerk had forgot that he had had his salary increased within the last five months.— The CLERK said that he had had a special allowance of £45 from the Assessment Committee for wprk in connection with railway assessments.—Mr. HARRISON, continuing, said that beside this £3OO a year, there were £14.5 from the As- sessment Committee, £l6O from the Rural Sanitary Au- thority, and £5O from the School Attendance Committee, which made £595. Then there was the post of superin- tendent registrar, which was incidental to the office, and which he (Mr. Harrison) estimated to bring in £3OO a year. That was a total of £895, or call it ha round numbers £9OO a year. The clerk, he was sure, would not pay more than £250 a year for clerks' salaries.—The CHAIRMAN thought the matter had nothing to do with the question.-The CLERK also mentioned at this point that the minute book had ar- rived, and that the minute appointing the committee spe- cially referred to the assistant clerkship. He (the clerk) also added that Mr. Harrison was about £2OO a year wrong with regard to the superintendent registrarship, and what he did get was paid by the Government, not by the Union. —Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that Mr. Harrison was doing guess work and was hundreds and hundreds wrong.--Mr. HARRISON said he was not exaggerating. The clerk's salary would then be £695 -The CLERK: £595, that is another hundred. (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. HARRISON: The clerk has to pay two clerks. The CLERK : Three clerks. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Martinson then went on to say that at the very least the clerk would have £4OO a year. He would frankly confess if that were so that he did not think Mr. Sutton was over well paid, but he thought he was fairly paid. He would consequently conclude with a different motion from what he had intended, and move that the assistant clerk be appointed at a salary of £5O a year.—Mr. APPLETON seconded this motion.—Mr. RYLANDS thought that no one could charge him with any desire not to be economical. (Hear, hear.) Representing, as be did, a concern which was heavily rated at over £5,000 a year, he should not be likely to propose anything that was extrava- gant. He had listened to what Mr. Harrison had said, and it had only strengthened his opinion that the proposed increase of salary was sadly too little. He knew the kind of talent Mr. Sutton happened to possess, and he knew its worth in the market, and he could only say that if Mr. Sutton were in his employment and exercised the talent that he showed at that Board, it would not be a question of a hundred er of two hundreds. The state of trade had been referred to, but that only made it the more necessary that they should have such a man as Mr. Sutton. He knew from his own experi- ence at the Assessment Committee that a very little mis- management might load to a very great loss, and if Mr. Sutton preferred to have his son appointed assistant clerk he (Mr. Rylands) saw no objection to that.—The proposal was also supported by Mr. Jolley, Mr. Cover, Dr. Mackie, and Mr. Long, the latter gentleman asking Mr. Harrison to withdraw his amendment.—Mr. HARRISON said he would withdraw it on the assumption that the Clerk was not mis- taken in stating that the emoluments arising from the office of superintendent registrarship for the whole Union did not exceed £lOO —Mr. PIERPOINT thought the amendment ought to be withdrawn without any conditions of that kind. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN having spoken in favour of the increase, and Mr. DARBYSHIRE having reminded the Board that Mr. Sutton had lost £54 a year by the abolition of annual elections, a division was taken on the amendment, for which only Mr. Harrison, Mr. Appleton, and Mr. Grange voted. All the others voted for the appointment of assist- ant clerk, as proposed by the committee, which was accordingly adopted.—The other increases recommended by the committee were unanimously adopted.—The CLERK then thanked the Guardians for their confidence in him and in his son. He added that he highly appreciated the kindness of the ex-officio Guardians in having attended to support the proposals of the committee. The county magistrates had all through his official life been excellent friends to him, and it was a county magistrate, who still lived, who a quarter of a century back, after an interview with Mr. Peter Rylands, waited upon him (the clerk) to say that if taking steps to be admitted to the law was a question of money, the money would be provided for him. He knew also that that was a subject that the late Mr. Benjamin Pierpoint was very anxious for, and the letters then before him if perused would show the kind feelings entertained towards him by the magistrates generally.—This was all the business.

div.head: TERMS AND PROGRESS OF THE NEGOTIATIONS.
div.p: TERMS AND PROGRESS OF THE NEGOTIATIONS.

The .9f. James's Gazette, of Wednesday, says—We have received the following communication from Mr. Gladstone's secretary:—" In view of certain misapprehensions as to the effect of the recent negotiations between the party leaders, the Government require to receive the adequa'e assurance as regards the Franchise Bill before you can produce or pre- sent their Redistribution Bill. This requirement, however. does not preclude the holding of friendly and confidential communication between the leaders of both sides before the assurance is given. The leaders of the Opposition have asked for such communication."
In answer to a request despatched by the editor of the .

Western Daily .21ferAry to Mr. Chamberlain, to the effect that he would explain whether the Government had really surrendered, the right hon. gentleman teleeraphed back to say that the first article in Wednesday's Times accurately explains the situation. The Times points out that the terms offered by the Go- vernment and now definitely accepted by the Opposition are as follows : .

1. The draft of the Redistribution Bill shall be submitted in private to the Conservative leaders in order that, by suggesting the alterations they think necessary, they may convince themselves of the equity and fairness of the mea- sure.

2. It is agreed that when a Redistribution Bill satisfactory to both parties has been framed, the Opposition will give to the Government adequate assurance that the Franchise Bill shall pass the House of Lords.

3. It is agreed that on receiving such an assurance the Government will lay the Redistribution Bill on the table of the House of Commons, and will carry it to the second reading. 4. The Opposition undertake that simultaneously with the affirmation of the principles of that Bill by the House of Commons they will redeem their pledge by passing the Franchise Bill into law.

5. The Government pledge themselves to take up the Re- distribution Bill as early as possible in the new year, to push it on through its remaining stages with all possible expedition, and, relying upon the loyal support of the Op- position being given to the joint scheme, to stake not only their credit but their existence upon the passing of the Bill into law in the session of 1885. These are the bases of the agreement in their logical order.
The Standard understands that the Redistribution Bil

.. —... will be ready for introduction on Tuesday or Thursday of next week. In the event of the Redistribution Bill being read a second time in the House of Commons, there will be an adjournment, and not a prorogation. It is rumoured that further questions will be addressed to the Government as to the meaning of the words "vital to their existence," and that in particular they will be asked whether the failure of the Redistribution Bill in the Lords would involve the resignation of the Ministry or a dissolution of Parlia- ment.
The Daily News .understands that the Government are in

full possessron of the views of the Conservative leaders in the matter of Redistribution. They are certainly not lack- ing in Radical qualities, and the majority of the House of Commons will, it is believed, find no difficulty, in accepting them. With reference to the mach-disputed matter relating to " adequate assurances." it is authorised to state that no change whatever has taken place in the action or intention of the Government with respect to "adequate assurance." The Seats Bill will not be presented till after this has been received from the Conservative Peers. Meanwhile confi- dential communications are going forward. If they result in agreement the assurances to pass the Franchise Bill will be given by Lerd Salisbury, and the Bill would thereupon, but not till then, be produced in the House of Commons by Mr. Gladstone. Should the consultation fail to reach the point of agreement, the Government will occupy precisely the same position they filled before the consultation was entered upon.
On Wednesday Lord Salisbury met the Prime Minister, and settled with him the arrangements for a meeting of Leaders on both sides in friendly consultation upon the Redistribution Bill.
The first meeting of the party leaders to consider the Seats Bill will be held forthwith. It will consist of about a dozen gentlemen, half from either side, and will include members of both Houses.

div.head: _MEMBERS ON THE COMPROMISE.
div.p: _MEMBERS ON THE COMPROMISE.

Mr. John Bright was the chief gues"t";Ft-h;—Eighty Club, on Tuesday night, at their dinner held at the West- minster Palace Hotel. Responding to the toast of his health, he briefly reviewed the rapid progress made in public opinion during the last 20 years on the question of reform. The right hon. gentleman discussed the question of redis- tribution, and expressed himself in favour of disfranchising boroughs up to 20 000 instead of 10,000, holding that no harm would Joe done by largely increasing county consti- tuencies. He condemned the grouping of boroughs, which would increase the power of the landlord class, a power already too great, and exercised invariably for selfish class interests. He objected to special consineration being given to landed proprietors. He also condemned minority repre- sentation, either by means of t'.,ree-cornered constituencies or the cumulative vote, and he was unable to understand what some men sought to support by proportional repre- sentation. He expressed great confidence in the present Government and the Premier, but if he was a member of the Government, he would not subserve Liberal interests or purchase Conservative c)nsent. A redistribution scheme must be just and reasonable, and consult not party but the permanent interests of the nation.

Sir Wilfrid Lawson, addressing a most enthusiastic meet- ing at Shoreditch, on Tuesday night, in support of the candidature of Professor Stuart for Hackney, said that Mr. Gladstone from first to last, in regard to the Franchise Bill, had been fair, square, honest, and earnest; and such was his confidence in their grand leader, that be would be much sufprised if, when the whole thing was settled, it was not found that the Prime Minister had got much the better of the Lords in the controversy. But when the Franchise and Redistribution Bills were passed they would have to deal with the Lords themselves and tho Peers must not lay the flattering unction to their sluts that they would escape because they had allowed those two measures to pass. He would do his best to promote an organisation to secure the abolition of the hereditary chamber. , Mr. Mundella opened the Elswick Library and Political I Club, Newcastle, on Wednesday afternoon, in the evening a public meeting was held, at which, the right hon. gentle- man, referring to the recent negotiations, denied there had been any surrender on the part of the Government. They were no.e in a much better position than before. Mr. Brand, M.P., speaking at a public meeting at Hit. chin, on Wednesday night, said that after a campaign peo- ple counted up their losses and gains. As Liberals, he did not think they had lost much, while their gains had been many and important. They had gained for the Franchise Bill the unanimous approval of the country, and they had gained the public withdrawal by Lord Salisbury of the claim of the House of Lords to dictate the time of dis- solution.

Sir J. Whittaker Ellis, M.P., speaking at the Licensed Victuallers' Protection Society dinner in London, on Wed- nesday evening, said that Lord Salisbury had been success- ful in the recent crisis, and the House of Lords had main- tained their equilibrium.

div.head: LORD SALISECRY'S VIEWS.
div.p: LORD SALISECRY'S VIEWS.

The Marquis t-iil;lZUrTy'ra; waited U.pon in the course of Wednesday afternoon by a deputation of Essex Conser- vatives, who desired to express their satisfaction with his action in the negotiations on the subject of Parliamentary reform. His lordship said the crisis, or the so-called crisis, was passing away. The Government had, he thought, con- ceded as much in the way of arrangement as might be anti- cipated if the crisis was to be settled by concession and ar- rangement. He denied that the Conservative peers had been trying to force a dissolution, though they would have been glad of an appeal to the constituencies. The House of Lords had a right, and it was its duty, to refuse its consent to whatever it considered to be inexpedient until the opinion of the people could be obtained, but it was not the duty of the House of Lords to refuse its consent to arrangements which it con- sidered judicious merely for the purpose of bringing about a diss,lutieh. Dealing with the objection that they bad only the pledged word of their opponents in the ar- rangement which bad been made, the noble Marquis said they were dealing with English gentlemen, and he was quite sure that any pattering with their pledged word would be as repugnant to the natural instincts of their opponents as it would be fatal to their position. He had no doubt that both parties would do their best to secure that the coming measure of redistribution, if they could agree upon it, should do justice to all interests. He did not regret the past action of the House of Lords, which had, he tbought. forced the country to give its mind to this great question, and to treat it with the deliberation which alone would secure that the sound common sense of Englishmen should prevent any evil which might arise from the mistaken ardour of partisans.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. INCREASE OF SALARIES. _
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. INCREASE OF SALARIES. _

An adjourned meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wedeesday, for the purpose of considering the report of a committee in which the following increases of salary were recommended, viz. :—Miss Mackie, Work- house schoolmistress, £5; Mr. Caldwell, inquiry officer, Newton district, £5; Mr. Basil Shearer, collector, Warring- ton district, £lO. The committee recommended the ap- pointment of Mr. Samuel Sutton to the office of assistant clerk to the Guardians with an annual salary of £ll5. There were present—Messrs. Greening (chairman), Blackhuret, Mackie, Hunt, Jeans, Cooper, Jolley, Brown, Bonnet], Owen, Appleton, Harrison, Worthington. Foreter, Gibson, Balharry, Grange, Greenall, William Houghton, Derbyshire, John Houghton, Humphreys, Kilshall, Sid- dellay, Swinton; the ex-officio Guardians present were Messrs. John Rylands, W. Long, R. Pierpoint, and T. J. Gillespie; Mr. J: C. Sutton (clerk).—Prior to a commencement being made with the business of the meet- ing, Mr. Harearsote expressed his pleasure at again seeing the Chairman looking so well after his journey to America, and, on behalf of the Board, congratulated him upon his safe return. Ths Chairman briefly and appro- priately replied.—A question then arose as to whether reporters should be allowed to report the proceediegs whilst the Board was in committee.—Dr. MACKIE thought it would be wiser for the Board to leave the matter to the discretion of the reporters. (Hear, hear.) He thought that as a rule they only reported that which was reportable, and that they were not likely to say anything which was either offensive OT painful. If the Board went into a sort of secret conclave over a matter of that kind he was afraid they would put themselves into an awkward position. He believed that every man's vote and speech at that meeting 'would be looked to with considerable interest, and he had not the slightest objection to anything he might say, although it might be mistaken, being reported and going before his con- stituents. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RYLANDS thought it would be better to allow the reporters to take notes, and if there was anything that it was desired'hhould be left out they would, he was sure, do so.—Mr. APPLETON was also in favour of the proceedings being reported. The people of Earlestown, he said, took a greater interest in that matter than he bad before thought. They seemed to feel that they had not been properly acquainted with the duties the Board was met there to perform, and they protested against anything being done without the knowledge of the ratepayers generally. —The CHAIRMAN said it was customary for reporters not to attend committee meetings, but he did not think there would be any objection to their remaining.—The CLERK remarked that he had no objection personally, but some- times information was obtained from officars of other Unions which they did not care about being made public -It was ag- reed that the reporters should remain.—The CLERK then read letters of apology for non-attendance from Col. McCor- quedale, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, and Mr. Broadbent. Mr. Roberts said that after he had learned more accurately the facts of the case he was in favour of the proposals of the committee and should have supported them had he been present ; while Mr. Broad- bent said he would gladly support any increase of the Clerk's salary that the Board thought well to make, but that his experience of the appointments of deputies was that , they tended towards the partial lees of the principal. Sub- I sequently another letter from Mr. Ziba Armitage, in which he expressed approval of the proposals of the committee was placed before the Board.—A memorial was also read, signed by 49 Barlestown ratepayers, protesting against the creating of a new office under the Board at an increased expenditure of £ll5 a year at a time when trade was bad and thousands starving. They considered the Clerk fully paid, especially as he had an increase to his salary of £45 per annum within the last eighteen months. The memorialists saw no harm in making an appointment of a deputy clerk provided the Clerk paid hissalary •, and they also expressed the wish that the Board would look at the matter from a ratepayer's point of view.—The CLERK then read a long statement in which he set f .rth the reasons why he applied for the appointment of an assistant clerk. He based his claims for the allowance upon the increase in his work from the period of the revision of his salary eight years ago, and upon the new work, not then considered, which had fallen upon his department. He also pointed out that he had been deprived of the pay- ment for work which he no longer did, such as that in connection with the annual elections, and considered that it would only be fair that he should be remunerated for the additional work he had now to do. He likewise read letters he had received from clerks of other unions in which assistant clerks were appointed in all of which the appointments had worked satisfaztorily.—Mr HARRISON quoted the saying that success greatly depended upon the art of putting things. He did not think that anybody would venture to say that their Clerk had put his case before them in such a way as to jeopardise his interests at all. He (Mr. Harrl,on) thought Mr. Sutton had given them a most elaborate account of his duties, and the only thing which it led one to infer was that Mr. Sutton must have thought that his chances of obtaining the required increase were desperate to have rendered it necessary to inflict upon them more than an hour's sp6ech. —(lt was here, however, pointed out, amid some laughter, that the clock in the room by which Mr. Harrison had been guided was standing, and that the Board had not been sit- ting quite an hour, and some preliminary business had been transacted before Mr. Sutton commenced to speak.)—Let that be as it may, Mr. Harrison continued, be wanted the Clerk to be good enough to read the resolution empowering the committee to deal with the question of salaries.—The CLERK said he bad not brought the minute book with him, but he would send for it.—Some discussion took place as to the exact form of the minute referred to by Mr. Harrison, several guardians expressing the opinion that they under- stood the committee was appointed to consider the question of appointing a deputy clerk as well as to eonsider as to the increases of salary.—Mr. HARRISON said he believed he was right in saying that the committee were only empowered to consider the application for increases of salaries. They had travelled out of the scope of their duties by go- ing into the question of creating a new office .with a salary attached. It was a matter they were not ern-

div.p: PRESCOL

_ PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was to have been held on Monday evening, bat as there was not a quorum of members no meeting took place. The only members present were Messrs. T. P. Hewitt and W. Goldsworth.

TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—The usual fortnightly meeting of the Church of England Temperance Society was held on Monday evening last in the Houghton-street schools, the vicar (the Rev. H. A. Macnaghten) presiding. The pro- gramme, which was well rendered and duly appreciated by the audience, was as follows :—Pianoforte duet, Messrs J. and W. Eaton; pianoforte solo, Mr. J. Eaton; song, " Bay of Biscay," Mr. J. Berry; song, "0 gently breathe," Miss Spencer; and a dialogue in two parts called "John Bull's ticket-of-leave."
CHARGE OF PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS.

Before Messrs A. Gladstone and T. Pilkington, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Edward Rogers, land- lord of the Wellington Hotel, Kemble-street, Prescot, was summoned for permitting drunkenness on the 20th ult. The defendant was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens. From the evidence of P.S. Bull and P. S. Ma- -1 gle, it appeared that at a quarter to four o'clock on the date named they visited the defendant's house, and on going in- to the vaults they saw the defendant behind the bar. In the vaults were Ellen Cramer, a prostitute, a convicted thief named Green, and another man named James Orford. Green was badly drunk and could not stand without &ippon. Rogers informed the officers that he had not served Green with any drink, but the woman Cramer said she had let Green have a drink of her beer. Green was locked up.— For the defence Mr. Swift submitted that though it was a fact there was a man under the influence of drink in the house he maintained that the defendant Rogers had not sup- plied any drink to the man Green. Green had only entered the house two or three minutes before the officers entered ; no drink was served to him. Mr. Swift added that the de- fendant Rogers had kept the house for four years without complaint, and he thought it was not likely that the defen- dant would commit such an offence as he was charged with in broad daylight —The defendant was then called and stated that when the man Green entered his house he (the defendant) advised him to leave and go home; and immediately afterwards the officers entered. The man Green had only been in the house two minutes, and he would swear no drink was sup- plied to him. James Orford was also called, and deposed that the man Green had not been served with anything. He had only just entered when the police followed.—Mrs. Rogers (wife of the defendant) gave corroborative evidence. —John Green, a labourer, residing near Market-place, Pres- ent, deposed that he was locked up by the police for being drunk on Roger.' premises on the date in question. He was afterwards brought up before the Bench, and was fined ss. and costs, a sum which he paid. He did not get "a tooth- ml of drink" in Rogers's house that day--The Bench im- posed a fine of 20s and costs.—Superintendent Barker asked that the license might be endorsed, as there had been pre- vious convictions against the house.—Mr. Swift said the defendant had not been previously convicted, and there had not been any conviction against the house for the last seven years, while the Licensing Act fixed the limitation at five years.—The Chairman said the Bench would not endorse the license.—James Mulloy, landlord of the Shamrock beer- house Tea-street, Prescot, was summoned for permitting drunkenness on the 27th nit., and also with selling intoxicating liquors to a drunken man on the same date.—Police Sergeant Dingley deposed that at a quarter to six on the night of the 27th ult be en- tered the defendant's house and in the kitchen found six men with jugs of beer before them. A man named Walsh was amongst them and he was helplessly drunk. He told

the landlady that Walsh was drunk, and she replied, "Well, if he is drunk he must go out." She added that no drink had been supplied to him, and Mulloy himself said no drink had been supplied to him. Witness had previously seen the man Walsh staggering along the road with the assist- ance of two other men.—P.C. Dyson, stationed at Whiston, stated that he accompanied the last witness to Mulloy's house, and corroborated his evidence.—Superintendent Bar- ker was sworn and stated that he was driving in his trap and saw the man Walsh very drunk in the road, in charge of two men. He subsequently instructed P.C. Dyson to search the public-houses, as, he thought it possible the men might have entered one of them.—Mr. Swift, for the defence, called a number of witnesses who stated that the man Walsh was net supplied with any drink in Mulloy's house, and that he had only just entered when the police came in.— The Chairman remarked that the evidence was conflicting and the Bench had decided to dismiss both cases against the defendant Mulloy.

EARLESTOWN. BLACKBERRY.—No shopkeeper should be without W. P. Hartley's Blackberry with Apple Jelly. May be had whole- sale from E. H. Monks, 78,Scholes, Wigan. In 31bs., 21bs., and 11b. jars.—Advt. GOOD TEMPIARY. —At a meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars on Mon- day evening Brother George Warburton, P.W.C.T., pre- sided in the absence of the W.C.T. After one candidate had been initiated a number of the members of the Ashton Ex- celsior Lodge gave a capital selection of songs, recitations, Fec.

THE BITMLARIES AT EARLEVOWN AND NEWTON.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Day, the young man named George Eckersley, who was apprehended and committed for trial on charges arising out of a series of burglaries at Earlestown, Newton, and Sutton, en the 2nd, sth, and Bth inst., was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment with hard labour. THE EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.—During the week special religious services have been conducted in the Primitive Methodist chapel and schools, Legh-street, Earlestown. They were commenced on Sunday, when ad- dresses were given by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin (resident minister), Messrs T. Clark, J. Bagnall, J. Wood, and T. Jackson. On the evenings of Monday and Tuesday the services were conducted in the sbhoolroom by the Rev. S. Griffiths (returned missionary fro.n Africa), who on Wed- nesday evening gave a very enjoyable address on his mis- sionary experience in Fernando Po, West Africa. On Thurs- day evening a special service for coildren was held. ANOTHER FOOTBALL ACCIDENT NEAR EARLESTOWN.— Another accident, by which a young man named William Ashton had a leg broken, occurred at Lowton, near Newton, on Saturday afternoon. Ashton was a prominent member of the Lowton Football Club (an organisation playing under Rugby rules), and last Saturday the Lowton team was play- ing the Widnes Club on the Lowton ground. In the course of the game Ashton seized the ball and was running with it at full speed, when he slipped and twisted his leg, with the result that the bone immediately snapped below the knee. Dr. Dobb, of Golborne, who was in the vicinity, was imme- diately called, and that gentleman set the broken limb. The injured player was subsequently conveyed to his home at Lawton. Besides being a capital footballer Asht)n was a well-known sprint racer. THE EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCROOL.—On Thursday evening a well-attended gathering was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Cross-lane, Earlestown, when the inaugural meeting of a temperance society for adult per- sons was held. Hitherto there has been a Band of Hope for juveniles, and the formation of a similar society for the adults is expected to prove of advantage to the Sunday school. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. H. Graham ; and in the course of the evening Mr. Slater, the new town's missionary for Earlestown, delivered an address. A pro- gramme of songs, &c., was gone through, including Lan- cashire readings, " Owd Fogey," by Mr. T. Jones; and" Our Sailor," by Mr. 0. Pickett ; recitation, " Where there's drink there's danger," Master J. Pickett ; song, "Carry Lea," Mr. J. Broster ; duet, " Far Away," Miss Clare and Master T. Clam ; a song by Mr. Nuttal, and a selec- tion on a dulcimer by Mr. Brown. The proceedings were of an enjoyable character. CROW-LANE BAND or HOPE.—On Wednesday even- ing a very interesting meeting was held at the Congrega- tional Infant Reom, through the kindness of the Juvenile Good Templars, and their conductor, who presided. After a hymn and prayer by Mr. Jones, the president of the so- ciety, the following programme was ably gone through : Recitation. Master R. Walton, "Jack and his big lump :" reading. Mr. Birnett, "Blind Harry ;" song, Clara Greaves, "The old house by the Linden ;" recitation, Master W. Thompson," Lazy bones ;" violin solo, Master Trip ; reci- tation, Miss Lizzy Barnett," Band of Hope melody ;" read- ing, Mr. Newman, "Why James became a teetotaller ;" re- citation, Master C. Walton, " Brother Fred ;" hymn; reci- tation, Mary Harrison, " Liberty ;" duet by the Misses Clarke, "Mother's love ;" recitatim, Master R. Walton, " Here's a teetotaller ;" song, Mary Harrison, " Johnny Smocker ;" recitation, Master R. Molyneux, "The burial of Sir J. Moore ;" violin solo, Master Trip; concluding with a humourous Lancashire reading by Mr. Geo. Clarke, entitled " Sailing for bacon." THE EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVE CLTIB.—The billiard handicap, open to the members of the Conservative Club, Earle-street, Earlestown, has been proceeded with during the present week. Most of the ties in the second round of the competition have been played, and some good games have been witnessed. The results have been as follows T. Adams (25 start) beat H. J. Durman (40) by 13 points; S. Leather (25) beat F. Jackson (10) by 22; C. Singleton (25) beat G. Slinn (35) by 39; J. Howe (50) beat J. Lowe (40) by 21; P. Bent (10 behind scratch) beat R. Wright (20 start) by 33 ; J. Wrigley (35) beat T. Massey (30) by 19; J. Williams (40) beat R. Goodwin (25) by 9 ; W. Moss (20) beat W. Blair (20) by 19 •, James Whalley (15) beat W. Sutton (35) by 12. On Wednesday the weekly discussion meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. William Maudsley. There was again a good attendance of members, who evinced much interest in the debate. The subject "Fair Trade in comparison with our Sham Free Trade" was resumed in a paper by Mr. George Wright. and in the discussion which ensued Messrs. Haseldine, J. Waddilove, Sutton, R. Roberts, Mal cock, H. Roberts. and Greatholder took part.

EMI' ',MOWN MADESMEN ROBBED.—During the last few weeks several tradesmen of Earlestown hay,' been robbed ley a female who has proceeded about her nefarious work in a very systematic manner. In one case she called upon a shopkeeper and stated that she was the wife of a customer. She asked for the loan of a few shillings on the plea that she had left her purse at home, and she would positively send the money, the same evening. The money, however, never arrived, but on the following day the woman herself again turned up at the tradesman's shop, and as- serted that when she got home on the previous evening she found that she had not left the purse behind but she had lost it. She again appealed to the tradesman for help, but the latter's suspicions were aroused, and he naturally declined to comply with her request. Inquiries which have since been instituted have shown that the woman's statements were entirely false, and that she was not the wife of the customer she had named. It was also gathered that she had repeated the " dodge" with other tradesmen, and consequently the matter was placed in the hands of the police. The woman will shortly figure at the police court.
SUDDEN DEATH OF A NEWTON GENTLEMAN.

The news of the sudden death of Mr. Ge—oilge—lTilic;,.of Newton, an unlooked for event, which occurred at the house of his brother, Edge-lane, Liverpool, on Tuesday morning, cast quite a gloom over Earlestown and Newton. The deceased gentleman was highly respected throughout the Newton township, his long residence therein having secured for him the friendship of all classes. Mr. Hilton was the manager of the extensive firm of Messrs. George McCorquodale and Co., Limited, printers, a position he held for about 34 years. A few years ago he suffered from the rupture of a blood vessel, and was then attended by Dr. Watkins, but latterly he has had slight attacks of pleurisy. Though residing at Willow Bank House, Newton, he has for some time past been in the habit of spending the week end at the house of his brother, at Liverpool, and as was his wont, he proceeded thither on gaturday morning. On the plat- form at Newton Bridge station he complained to a friend of feeling slightly unwell, but nothing at all serious was anti- cipated. On the Monday, however, a communication was received at the Newton works stating that he was too un- well to resume his duties, and this was followed on the next day with a telegram announcing his death. A profound feeling of sorrow and regret at the untimely end of Mr. Hilton was manifested throughout every department of the extensive works, and the large circle of personal friends of the deceased gentleman could scarcely credit the report. In addition to the high office he held under Messrs. McCorquo- dale he was one of the overseers of the Newton township, and in that capacity presided at a meeting of the ratepayers held in the Town Hall on the previous Thursday afternoon in connection with the election of a guardian. He was for- merly captain in the 73rd L.R.V., afterwards the 80th L.R.V. (or Liverpool Press Guards), and for a considerable time past he had ably filled the post of captain of the well. trained fire brigade at Messrs McCorquodale's works. He leaves a widow, two sons, and a daughter to mourn their sudden loss—which many others will feel and regret, not only in Newton, but in Warrington. Liverpool, Glasgow. Leeds, and London, where the deceased in his capacity of manager for Messrs McCorquodale was highly esteemed. The funeral of the deceased tuck place at Toxteth Ceme- tery, Srnithdown-lane, Liverpool, on Thursday afternoon. It had been intended that it should be of a private charac- ter, but a number of gentlemen attended as a token of the respect in which the deceased gentleman was held. The relatives present were Mr. Richard Hilton, brother of the deceased, from whose house the funeral took place, and Mr. W. and Mr. G. H. Hilton, sons of the deceased. The firm of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co., represented by Colonel G. MeCorquedale J.P., Captain J. G. Wood, Messrs. D. David- son, and F. J. Wood (Newton); Messrs. Wighton and Cul- roes (London) ; Mr. Chorley (Leeds); Mr. Totty (Liver- pool) ; and Mr. Hall (Oakenholt). The London and North- Western Railway Company were represented by Messrs. Wilcox, Thompson, Addy, and Hornbv, and the following foremen in the employ of Messrs. McCorquodale also attended :—Messrs. Mayor, Adams, Creuchley, Dick, Len- nox, Wood, Atkins, Shaw, Grace, Devereux, Blything, and Appleton. Many Newton gentleman were also present, amongst whom were Messrs. Bond, Luffman, Bodmer, Hurdle, Gowanlock, Barton, Urquhart, Brierley, Whlmesley, Houghton, Mellor, and Holmes. A large number of wreaths were placed upon the coffin, including one from Messrs. Davidson and Woods, representing the Newton workpeople.

An affectionate Irishman once enlisted in the 75th Regi• ment in order to be near his brother, who was a corporal in the 76th. AN ACCOMMODATING Inisma.N.—An Irishman was re- quested by a lady to do some work for her, and he per- formed it to her complete satisfaction. "Pat," she said, "I'll give you some refreshment." "Heaven bless you, ma'am!" '1 What would you prefer—a pint of beer or a tumbler of grog ?" "Well, ma'am, I don't wish to be troublesome, 80 I'll take the one awhilst you're making the other." "JUST AS GOOD AS DIVORCED."—A well-known Betroit clergyman, who has one of the largest congregations in II town, as well as the largest capacity to annreciate a joke, r relates that one day last week he was called- on to marry a couple. His catechism of the prospective bridegroom was satisfactory, and he then turned his attention to the lady. " Elave you ever been married ?" was assed. "Yes, sir." "Husband dead ?" "No, sir." "Are you divorced ?" • "N.no-not exactly, but I'm just as good as divorced. My husband left me, and besides, vie never paid the minister for marrying vs." In Cooperstown they tell a story of an English joker who once visited Fennimore Cooper. Cooper was then the most eminent man in the little town. One day, while Cooper was dining with the Englishman, he poured out some native wine—wine from grapes raised in his own garden. Taking up a glass, and looking through it with pride Cooper re- marked, "Now, Mr. Stebbings, I call this gcod honest wine." " Yes ' Mr. Cooper, I agree with you. It is honest wine-- poor, but honest." Tian TRADE IN HElRLOOMS.—Connecticut manufacturer: "Busy! I never was driven so hard in my life. REFRESHING HIS MEMORY.—An old, gray, wrinkl;d man sat in a fashionable restaurant. "Excuse me. sah," said a waiter, approaching; "seems to me sah, I's seen you befo' some place." " Yes ; you saw me when I was a young man, full of health and vigour, with bright eyes and raven locks and a keen appetite." "I disremember. sah. Wha' was it?" "Right here. Don't you remember ?" "'Wall, now, sail, at does seem to me like I has a mighty faint recollection ob you. But, you see, salt, I's gettin' ole, an', my memory air" as good es it ust to be." "Perhaps I can tell you a little circumstance that will refresh your memory of me." "What's dat, sah ?" "I ordered my dinner of you, and have been waiting here ever since for it." When musical pitch-forks were first introduced, a certain precentor, thinking he would like one, ordered an Edinburgh ... carrier to obtain one for him. The honest carrier, who never heard of any other pitchfork but that used in the barn-yard, purchased one at least ten feet long. It was late on Eaturday evening before he came home, and, as a message had been left to bring it up when he came to church the next day, he marched into the churchyard before the bell rang, where the master of song was standing among a group of villagers. " Aweel, John, here's the pitchfork you wanted; but I can tell you I ne'er thought muckle ce your singing before, and I'm sair mistaken gin you'll sing onY better now." A TRAGIC STORY.—Many are the stories told by the collier lads of losses and rescues, of escapes in the mine, and dis- appearances never accounted for. A mine is flooded or given up as of "no account ;" the shaft is boarded over, and a notice put up to warn that the spot is dangerous. rn a few years the notice becomes illegible, another generation suc• ceeds, the boards become grass-grown, strong to all appear ance, but really rotten; then some unfortunate wight on a dark night loses his way or takes a short cut, the treacher• ons trap swallows him up, and it may not be for many yearn —until the story of his disappearance has become a tradi‘ lion—that the skeleton of the buried alive is found. A harrowing story of an escape was recently told. A collier - lad, going across a heath, returning from his "turn" one evening, suddenly slipped into a hole, but by some meara managed to grasp the edge, and so held on by his fingers to this treacherous but only safeguard. The evening passed into the dusk, star after star came out, but no moon; hour after hour dragged on, and still the hapless miner gripped with the tenacity of despair the edges of the shaft over which he hang. At last dawn broke slowly, then gray light stole over the.heath, breaking through the morning's mists, I when he saw a party of his mates passing at a distance. He called loudly for help. Guided by the voice, they came. Still more nervously did he cling—in a few moments he might be safe. Then, as two strong hands grasped each of his wrists firmly, he ventured to look down the dreaded , depths. One glance was enough; that one look told him that his feet were within four inches of the bottom. It is stated that in his orisons the collier-lad was not as thankful to Providence as he should have been.

HALF A LIFE IN PRISON. George Wilmott, aged 43, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude at Middlesex Sessions, on Monday, for stealing a scarf pin, value .£3O, from the person of Lord Cardross during the London Lord Mayor's Show. The prisoner had already been 21 years in prison._

- A SHOCKING DEATEL—A wheelwright named Rice wad remanded on Wednesday. at Aston, charged with causing the death of his wife. During a quarrel the prisoner threw a quantity of paraffin oil upon Mrs. Rice, who was standing near the fire, and whose clothes were set ablaze. She died on Tuesday from the burns thus received. MINISTERIAL CHANGES.—The following appointments have received the sanction of Her Majesty :—The Right Hon. G. Shaw-Lefevre, M.P., succeeds the late Mr. Fawcett as Postmaster-General; Sir Thomas Brassey, K.C.8., M.P.. assumes the Secretaryship of the Admiralty in the room of Mr. Campbell-Bannerman; and Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., be- comes Civil Lord of the Admiralty in succession to Sir T. Brassey. THE QUEEN, on Monday, attended the funeral of Willie Blair, her Majesty's favourite Highland fiddler, who died last week at the venerable age of 90 years. The rernaine were interred at the churchyard of Craithie, where a monu- ment will be raised by command of her Majesty to press her appreciation of the personal qualities of tins worthy man. Willie Blair was the oldest resident on the Royal estate.

BAD ACCIDENT AT WlGAN.—Wcrkmen had been engaged 'pulling down an old building in Warrington-lane, Wigan, and on Monday night the outside walls were left standing. These were secured by spars, but it is supposed that during -the night the woodwork must have been carried off by parties seeking firewood, for early on Tuesday, whilst two 'brothers were overhauling the debris, the walls fell upon them, killing William Green, aged about eight, and seriously .injuring his younger brother. MR. JOHN BRIGHT AND THE FAIR TRADERS.—Writing to a member of the Hackney Liberal Association, Mr. Bright -shows anew the fallacy of supposing that fair trade would be any remedy for the present depression. He says: " I have known depression in trade to be much greater than it is now, and the sufferings of the traders and workmen during our time of protection, previous to 1842, when re.. form of our tariff began, were beyond comparison greater than they are now. In foreign countries, where high tariffs exist, say in Russia or France and in the United States, the disturbance and depression of manufacturing industries is far greater at this moment than with us. Their tariffs make it impossible for them to have a large foreign trade. We have a wide field for our exports, which they cannot

enter." MURDER OF WELSH PEOPLE IN AMERICA.—LYNONING ' THE MrraDelasrle.—lntelligence of a distressing occurrence to a Flintshire family 'named Davie, who recently emigra- ted to Tennessee, has just reached the relatives home. Mrs. Davies was called to the door at night when she was Shot -dead. Mr. Jones, a wealthy Welsh emigrant farmer, who happened to be calling, looked out to See what was the matter, when be fell dead riddled with shot. Mr. Davies, husband of the murdered woman, returned to find his wife a corpse and Jones lying dead alongside. The country was scoured, and from suspicion the postmaster of Alpine, named Dorsey, aged 70, and a woman named Wade, eked SO, were arrested. Evidence was produced that Dorsey killed Mrs. Davies from personal jealousy, and shot Jones in mistake for Mr. Davies. The infuriated mob then rushed to the gaol, and Hung both Dorsey and Wade from the same limb and by the same rope.
