- - RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. Sir,-1 see by your last Satarday's issue that an anony- mous writer, " Stonjaheg," has attempted to answee my letter respecting the attendance and sermons at the above church I think " Stonjaheg " must admit tke correctness of my letter, considering he admits seeing it three weeks be- fore answering, but I suppose he must have been waiting Sunday after Sunday to hear a good sermon, and then to lose no time in rushing into print to make it known through your valuable paper. " Stonj shag" complains of my being personal, but he surely forgets that preachers are public men, and are open to criticism quite as much as any other public body. Then " Stonjaheg" says in championing the cause of Church preachers .that he supposes the rev, gentleman in question never did me any harm in his life. I will answer that ques- tion by informing " Stonjaheg that he has not, neither would he do me any good if I sat under him in his official capacity to the eni of time. I quite agree with " Stonjabeg " that people should go to church to hear the Word of God, to confess their sins, and to give thanks for the inercies vouchsafed t 3 them, but he forgets to add that the Word of God should lee expounded intelligibly to all the congrega- tion. Further " Stonjaheg " says he was very pleased to hear in an eloquent extempore sermon, delivered by the Rev. T. M. Armson, last Sunday week, his exhortation to the congregation to concentrate their thoughts upon the services of the church, and not upon distant objects or triviali- ties. I fear the preacher must have felt his position some- what just then, knowing as he does that good sermons from our resident curates is a thing of the past. In conclusion, if it should be information to " Stonjaheg," I consider that the Church (through her inferior preachers) is doing more to disestablish herself than any Liberation Society in existence.—Apologizing for again troubling von, yours atc., A CHURCHMAN.

THE PARISH CHURCH CHOIR. Sir,—Kindly allow me a few lines in reply to "A former C. W.," though it will be the first time in my life I have stooped to answer an anonymous correspondent, and I do so now for obvious reasons. Who is "C. W. ?" What is he? What does "C. W." mean? Creeping worm? If so, I wish your correspond- ent had a better name. Bat than how many ef those in favour with the reverend individual he so feebly champions might not come under the same cognomen? Bur, "A former C. W." Has this worm given over creeping? If so, when? or is this flowery effusion his final effort in that direction ? Pity he is not a snail, that by the more marked character of his slime I might track him and bring him out of his shell. What is my offence? "C. W." says "he is not going .to dispute any of the points raised." Good. Can ha? I trow not, no, not even under rectorial inspiration. But what 1113 my offence? I have been for five long years victimised more than any infatuated curate of all the legion who have bsen beguiled by a glittering advertisement ; and because, In mere self-defence, I honestly point out "spiritual wickedress in high places," and that only in the shape of hard facts, " C. W." says lain" ungentlemanly," and that I have" betrayed confidence." Well, if to fearlessly point out wrong doing is" ungentlemanly" and to put in print for wider circulation what was already known to the (com- parative) few, and what was never stated in confidence, then I own the soft impeachment. But I should be loth to learn what is gentlemanly from "A former C. W." He evidently thinks it " gentlemanly "to attack me under a nom de plume, and call me names, in defence of one wham he all but admits he cannot defend. "C. W." says I "bays shared the rector's liberal hospitality." I admit I have, and, underrtbe same circumstances again, should have no alternative but to do likewise, unless I gave offence. All the same, I ehoald have preferred less hospitality, or none at all, and a more adequate remuneration for services ren- dered, and something approaching to a just fulfilment of promises made. Will " A former C. W." be good enough to state how, and for what, the rector " has shared " with me " his private purse ?" On this point specially I pause for a reply. Talk not to me such platitudes with reference to the opinion of "friends," for it is one of the " sweet uses of ad- versity " to find out those who are entitled to the sacred name, and I am thankful to say I am honoured with the friendship of those who approve every step I have taken in this matter, and who have sufficient independence and roan- linens of character to have the courage of their opinions openly. One word more, and I have done with" A former C. W." Let him not try to draw a moral out of that which is im- moral, and if he writes again, let him sign his name, but perhaps that would have less weight even than such a poor nom de plume as "A former C. W."—Yours truly, C. E. ROWLEY.
Central Chambers, Warrington, Nov. 19,1884. [The correspondence on this subject, to which we have accorded considerable space, must close with this letter.— ED., Ex]
THE CONDUCT OF THE MAYOR.

Sir,—Wilt you kindly -allow me a little space to notice that most unkind and unjustifiable letter rsflecting upon the conduct of the Mayor which appeared in your issue of last Saturday. With the political part of the question I have nothing whatever to do more than to express my extreme regret that party prejudice is so often allowed to overstep the bounds of common courtesy and to outrage the feelings of those who are not its slaves. In as far as the letter to which I have referred charges the Mayor with partiality in religious matters, I wish to enter my protest against it, and to state that in my opinion it errs most grievously. In no one of his predecessors has more uniform kindness and courtesy been displayed than in his Worship, and I have never yet heard of a single instance in which he has refused to help any religious denomination, when such help as has been in his power to render has been sought. In conclusion allow me to congratulate my fellow-towns- men upon the re-election to office of a Mayor upon whom •' the mantle of neutrality " sits so gracefully as it does upon Alderman liarrison.—l am, yours, &c., W. MULES.
Emmanuel Church, Warrington, Nov. 21st, 1884.
THE MAYOR'S DINNER AND THE "TOAST LIST."

Sir,—Averse as I am (at present), to entering into a news- paper controversy, I really cannot resist the temptation of askiag you to allow me a very brief reply to your corres- pondent's letter signed "A Disgusted Liberal," which ap- peared in your last Saturday's issue.

But I wish to say in the first place, that I quite agree I with him in one thing, viz., that the health of the honour- able member fur Warrington, J. G. McMlnnies, Esq., ought to have been one of the principal toasts of the evening, and I will go further, and add, one of the earliest ; and its ac- cidental omission, through tne absence of a formal "Toast List;' (tor which lam alone responsible), will effectually remove all doubts which I may have hitherto entertained, as to the policy of dispensing with what I shall hencefor- ward regard as an indispensable adjunct to a successful public dinner; but I cannot imagiue such a thing, as any member of the Town Council being guilty of wilful dis- courtesy towards Mr. McMinnies. He is far too much re- spected by both political sections of that body, and deser- vedly so too •, therefore such an idea may be dismissed as quite unworthy of notice, but I take the entire blame on myself, for the reason already given, and sincerely do I re- gret it. The following extract, however, from your cor- respondent's rancorous letter, I cannot permit to pass un- challenged. "It was also noticeable, that whereas the imi- tations were ostensibly only to include the numbers of the Council and Corporation offictals, they were so extended as .to bring in a few Tory outsiders, but not a single Liberal of note, or Dissenting minister was honoured." My reply to the above unfounded statement is, that the invitations were (with one solitary exception) confined to members of the Town Council and officials : the member and ox-member of the borough ; the ex mayors and borough magistrates ; the membeca of the "Museum, Library, and Arts Commit- tee," who are not members ef the Council (as has been cus- lomary) and the "reporters." It is qeite true there were no Dissenting ministers invited, nor were there (I may say in extenuation) any clergymen of the "Church of England" invited, except the" rector" (the chaplain). I only wish the contrary had been practicable, but what will be thought of the veracity of your correspondent, when in reply to his rash statement that "Net a single Liberal of note was hon- oured," I inform you that the following gentlemen were invited, but for various good reasons, were unable to attend: —the member, 4. G. McMinnies, Esq., Peter Rylands, Esq., M.P., as an ex-mayor, T. G. Rylands, Esq., as an el-mayor, William Neild, Esq., as an ex-mayor, Dr. Jos. Smith, as an ex-mayor; George Crosfield, Esq., as a bor- ough magistrate, John Rylande, Esq., as a borough magis- trate, Samuel Rigby, Esq ,as a borough magistrate, Ziba Armitage, Esq ,as a borough magistrate, Holbrook Gaskell, Esq., as a borough magistrate. If these gentlemen are not in the estimation of your correspondent "Liberals of -note," -where, I would ask him, are they to be found with- in the Parliamentary borough of Warrington ? I will re- /rain from farther comment, with a parting word to your correspondent, in the shape of a friendly suggestion, that when a man puts forward statements that are inaccurate, and suggests conclusions that are unjust, his duty under such circumstances is obvious. He should promptly avow his error, and tender a fitting apology. Such confessions of fallibility are net pleasant, I admit, but unpleasantness .should be endured rs,ther than caade the due discharge of .2111 honourable ohligation.-1 ars, sir, your obedient servant, Warrington, 18th Nay., 1834. JOSEPH HARRISON.

THE SHIP CANAL RATE. Sir,—There is a class of persona who "rush in where angels dear to tread." A writer to a contemporary, in a rambling letter and with confusing iteration—taking thirty- two lines to deal with the point—denies that the Man- chester Corporation have been called upon by the Local Go- vernment Board to justify their proposal to contribute by rate la promotion of a Ship Canal. What are the facts ? Briefly these : that the Manchester Town Council has re- ported its resolutions en the subject to the Board ; that a number of in.fluential ratepayers have petitioned the Board not to approve such resolutions; and that, in consequence, the Local Government Board have asked the Town Council for reasons in support of its proposal, and in answer to the Opposing petition. This action of the Board I described as calling upon the Corporation to justify its proposal no thinking person would take exception to the description. The Latin motto, "Truth is mighty and shall ultimately prevail," is a good one, but where is truth in this contro- versy ? Not necessarily with tee majority. An intolerant ;majority i 9 usually wrong. A majority with truth on its A

side does not need to shout down a minority. It is pleasant to sail with the stream no doubt, but those who prefer truth to popularity, and are loyal to conscience at the risk of being misunderstood and misrepresented. can wait with patience and with confidence the vindication they believe time will ultimately and surely bring them. For, and ever the truth comes uppermost, And ever Is Justice done. The Local Government Board will decide whether the pro- posed Ship Canal is "necessary for tlfe promotion or pro- tection of the interests of the inhabitants" of Warrington, as it is required to decide by section 2 of the Borough Funds Act ; it will also decide whether or not our Corporation shall vote away money over the actual spending of which it would have no control. Whatever may be the decision of the Local Government 'Board on these points, those who deny the right of majori- ties to force minorities to contribute to a purely private and speculative venture, and who perceive the unwisclom of the growing tendency to restrict the freedom of the citizen by reducing the part of his earnings which be has hitherto been allowed to spend as he liked, on the plea that govern- ment or society his the right to take as much as it chooses from the individual so long as it spends it for what it con- siders the general good—all such persons will continue to pretest and struggle against the unwise and insidious pro- positions of the promoters of a Ship Canal rate. Those ac- quainted with the state of affairs which preceded the French Revolution know that that terrible calamity resulted from unnecessary and excessive interferences with the details of men's every actions, and from the enormous drafting away of the products of their labour for the maintenance of the regulating organisations, and for the doing of things for the citizen which he would have done better for himself. The individual does not exist for the government, but the go- vernment mainly for the protection of the individual, and when government, either local or imperial, steps outside its proper sphere, when it assumes that majorities may do what seems them good, and that minorities have no inalienable rights, it is on dangerous ground, and disaster is at hand.— LIBRA.

November 21st. 1884. P.B.—ln my last week's letter in speaking of the neces- sary supply of water for the proposed canal, by a printer's error I am'made to say re2//s. That this question of the supply of water for the canal is a serious one, anyone read- lag to•day's Manchester papers will find. The supply is running so short that the Waterworks Committee have de- cided from Monday next to curtail the consumption br do- mestic and manufacturing purposes, and are urging the householders to the utmost economy in its use. The un- answered question remains: Whence, and, if at all, at what cost can the enormous quantity of suitable water required for Ship Canal purposes at Manchester, and from there to Warrington, be bad?

div.head: SHIP CANAL,7•A REJOINDER..
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL,7•A REJOINDER..

- - Sir,—Your correspondent " Civis " made a slight mistake in his allusions to myself. Neither I nor "some people " are so simple as Is imagine for a moment that the making of the Ship Canal will " take away all the ills that the British working-man is heir to." lam strongly in favour of the Franchise Bill becoming law, not because I think the mere possession of a vote will better the agricultural Labourer's position. I look upon it as a means to an end. The making of the Canal will in the first place put some millions of money into circulation, money, if I read the re- ports of money articles aright, now lying idle. In the next place it will cause a demand for lab mr, so increasing the value of the labourer's capital, viz., his thews and sinews. In another direction it will, if wisely carried out, increase the means of conveying to and fro the raw material and the mansfactured article, and so give to manufacturers a means of escaping out of the hands of what is now virtually a monopoly, viz., the railway companies. Ido not assume that the Canal, when made, " will put our manufacturers in a position to compete successfully with foreign manufac- turers." It will do a little towards it. I recognise that there are a thousand and one causes for the present depres- sion. I wish to remove one. Enable manufacturers to make good use of what nature has placed almost ready made to their hands, and they will have less cause to harrass their workmen. . .

"Civia " seems to be altogether up in a balloon on the whole of the question he writes about. In an indistinct manner he makes reference as to what foreign protection. ista will do. Well. I cannot say what they will do, but I am not to be frightened out of my free trade opinions by the speculations of "Civis." I hold that the prohibitive tariffs adopted by foreign nations work to their disadvantage ; the answer of Earl Granville to Earl Dunraven's speech I give as proof, sufficient to my satisfaction at least. As to the question of "superior skill and improved appli- ances " enabling our manufacturers to successfully com- pete with foreigners. I wish to say a few wotds. Superior skill on the part of English workmen I allow; improved ap- pliances I very much question. I have just read a most interesting lecture, delivered by Mr. Swire Smith, at New Mills. Tnis gentleman, one of the members of the Royal , Commission on Technical Education, points out how de- sirable it is for Englishmen to know that foreign nations are making use of every power within their reach to oust us out of the world's markets ; that Continental youths are being trained in a very much superior fashion to our own. At Antwerp 38 English students were enjoying all the pri- vileges of the Academy on the anne terms as the people of Antwerp themselves, because they were unable to obtain such facilities for tuition in England. " The Commission visited in one instance the designing establishment of one of the largest Lancashire firms actually located in Paris, at a cost of several thousands a year, in order to obtain the best talent at the fountain head." As for mechanical appliances, "Civis" must know that our machinists have for years been sending, to all parts of the world, the very best ma- chinery they could turn out. Have we not invited the foreign manufacturer to visit our exhibitions and our work- shops to there see and be told all that was necessary to make them independent of us? Have not our best shops been selected in which to place German youths to gain the practical knowledge that is now troubling us so much ? I " Civis " will see that he is leaning upon broken reeds if he expects superior skill and improved appliances to keep us in the future what we have been in the past. What we need to do is this : at once clear the deck of all useless expenses. First, there are charges falling upon all em- ployers in the shape of exorbitant rents, rates, and taxes ; rents that go towards swelling the rent rolls of those who toil not, neither do they spin; " unearned incre- ment "so far as the receiver is concerned, reduced wages so far as the labourer is concerned ; rates and taxes that seem to be collected for no other purpose than to give town councillors an opportunity to give their friends a lift. To get into office under the Corporation seems to be the only position whereby a man has a right to expect his salary to be raised each November. When these points are attended to, we must anxiously look farther afield. What is now going on amongst the Skye Crofters carries with it a real significance for us in Lancashire. 'Tis the land question, above all others, that must be attended to. The land is not

bearing its share of the national burdens. Land-grabbers, on all sides, have for years been buying up all they could possibly get hold of; taking fron. the farmers something they call rent, but which I call the labourers wages, driv- ing the agricultural poor into the towns, and what is the consequence ? A dozen men for every job; a fearful com- petition amongst workmen going on for the mere right to earn a living; a large portion of the urban population living from hand to mouth, and helping to swell corporate expenses, but, mind you, leaving our manufacturers who live in the country without a tithe of the expenses, com- paratively, that come against those living in the town. It must not be supposed that I am one of those who fancy that England is "going to the dogs;" not by any means. Depressions in trade seem to have a method in their mad. ness. And the Fair Trader always mounts his hobby horse at these times. During the reign of Lord Beaconsfield we had one of these panics. Soup kitchens became an institu- tion. Wiredrawers wages were reduced, and it was sud- denly found out that British interests lay in forcing the British army into every nook and crevice on the earth's fair surface. We are now paving for the Jingo madness, and it requires all the coolness possible to keep our hobby horse riders from making things very much worse: England's future welfare depends very much on the position Capital and Labour assume towards each other. It they forget that it is to their mutual interest to work together, hard times are before us. If workmen depend upon worn-out trade union notions, and employers think of nothing but how much per cent. they may get for invested capital,why then we may look Out for the Decline and Fall of the British Empire. CLIFFORD DIX.

FATAL QUARREL AT OLDHAM.—At Oldham on Thursday James Robinson, cabman, was remanded on a charge of causing the death of Robert Shaw Burns. On Saturday the two men were quarrelling in the street, when the prisoner called Burns a liar, at the same time knocking him down and_cansing_injuries from which be died.

llitwens'-WeoEs ow WEST Letscasmue.—A large and influential meeting of the West Lancashire Coe!owners' As- sociation was held at the North Western Hotel, Liverpool, on Monday, to consider a letter from Mr. Thomas Ashton, miners' secretary, requesting that a meeting of the coal pro- prietors of West Lancashire might be called to meet a depu- tation of the miners, who would be prepared with a pro- posed sliding scale to submit to such meeting, in accordance with a resolution passed at a conference at the Miners' Hall, Wigan, on the 29th October. which was to the effect that a sliding scale should be established. It was unanimously re- solved :—" That it is desirable to accept the invitation of the miners and to endeavour to form a sliding scale to regu- late miners' wages in South-West Lancashire." A repre- sentative committee of the Association was appointed, with full powers to negotiate and arrange a sliding scale for the future regolation of wages in the district. It was further resolved that the secretary of the Association (Mr. Mao hell W. CROFT.

A WINTER STRAWBERRIt.—On the 12th instant Mr. Isaac Maines, landlord of the Horse Shoe Inn, gathered a remarkably fine ripe strawberry from his garden. There were several others in the same bed in an unripe condi- tion. MEMORIAL TO A SUNDAY SCHOOL Scar:lwo:L.—On Sunday last a memorial in the form of a small marble stand with the following inscription cut en it, "Thy will be done," and on which was plated a beautiful wreath of china, represent- ing roses and jessamine, and covered by a glass shade, was placed on the grave of John Green, in the churchyard, pre- sented by ths scholars, members of the band, choir, and friends at Croft, out of respect for the deceased, who was buried last Saturday week. The deceased was the second son of Mr. John Green, of Heath-lane, Croft, and was 13 years of age. He was also one of the side drummers in the Croft Drum and Fife Band, and a Sunday scholar attend- ing the Croft Church Sunday School, and was greatly es- teemed. The deceased died from diptheria, and his little brother, aged four years, had only been buried a short time before. FUNERAL OF A CHRIST CHURCH CHORISTER.—On Sun- day afternoon a funeral took place at Croft which attracted considerable attention, especially among the Sunday school scholars and members of the choir and congregation of the above church. The remains of Miss Margaret Green, who was the principal soprano in the choir, and also a Sunday school teacher, and who was very highly respected by all who knew her, were interred in the churchyard of the above church in the presence of a large number of people. The deceased was the second daughter of Mr. Isaac Green, of Heath-lane, Croft. The churchyard was crowded with spec- tators, as was also the church. The burial service was con- ducted by the rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, M.A. A large number of relatives and friends remained to take a last look at the grava after the burial service, the coffin being completely covered with beautiful wreaths and crosses presented by the relatives, members of the choir, and friends of the deceased. The deceased had not enjoyed very good hgalth for some time, but was in her usual piece in the choir at both services a fortnight ago, having only been confined to the house for a week with diptheria, which is prevailing in the district at present. Her youngest brother died only a few days before from the same complaint, and was buried on Friday last. The deceased was 17 years of age. It is proposed by the membera of the choir and their friends to place a memorial on the grave of the deceased.

div.head: GARMOYLE BREACH OF
div.p: THE GARMOYLE BREACH OF
PROMISE CASE. DAMAGES £lO,OOO.

In the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court ef Justice, London, on Thursday, the case of Finney v. Cairns (Garmoyle) came before Mr. Justice Manisty and a special jury. This was an action brought by the plaintiff, Miss Finney, known in the theatrical world as Miss Fortescue, against the defendant, Lord Garmoyle, to recover damages for a breach of promise of marriage. Mr. C. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Winch appeared for the plaintiff; and the Attorney-General and Mr. R. S. Wright appeared for the defendant. The defendant in his pleadings admitted the breach of promise, and towards meeting his liability had paid 40s into court. At half-past ten o'clock, the time fixed for commencing the business, the court was exceedingly crowded.

Mr. Russell, in opening the case, said the promise to marry had not been disputed, and he should show that that promise had been unjustifiably broken. The sole question, therefore, was as to the amount of damages. Miss Finney was a young lady who was born in 1859, and was the daughter of a gentleman who was once in a very good posi- tion commercially in London. He was a member of a firm of coal merchants, and the plaintiff was the elder of two girls, and a few years ago as her father had to go into liquidation, she became the main support of her younger sister and her mother. She was educated as a lady, and in 1880 obtained an introduction to several well-known theatrical managers in London. She afterwards appeared at the Savoy Theatre in "Patience," which, as was well known, was the work of Mr. Gilbert, the music of the libretto being written by Sir A. Sullivan. At first her salary was not very large, being only three guineas a week, but it was subsequently increased to six guineas. It was during this engagement that Lord Garmovle became acquainted with her, and upon the 11th July, 1883, he pro- posed to her, and was accepted. The plaintiff at once men- tioned the matter to her mother, who pressed on Lord Gar- moyle the necessity of his mentioning his intentions to his father and mother. He at once assented to the propriety of that course, and it appeared he did make the communi- cation personally to Lady Cairns, who expressed approval, and on the 18th July wrote to 'Dear Miss Fortescue—a name by which you will shortly not be known." In that letter Lady Cairns expressed her anxiety for the happiness of her beloved son, and hoped that this union would tend to promo`e that happiness. In reply to that letter Miss Fortescue wrote to "Dear Lady Cairns," thanking her for her good wishes, and saying that her only wish was to make Lord Garmoyle happy. In the following August the defendant explained to Miss Fortescue that his people had strong views as to the profession she had adopted ; that I they considered it not only frivolous, but even ungodly, al- though he cbcl not share in those views himself. Upon that , statement she agreed to give up her career upon the stage, and, more than that, she caused her younger sister 1 who bad bees preparing for the same profession, to i relinquish it. After this, on the sth August, 1883, she visited Lady Cairns, who talked to and advised her in the kindest possible way, and finally led her into the library, where she was received by Lord Cairns in a similar way. So matters went on until the plaintiff paid a visit to Lord 'Cairns at his shooting box in Perth, where a large company had assembled, the engagement being a recognised thing. A discussion took place with Lady Cairns and Lord Gar- moyle as to when the wedding should take place, and Lady Cairns suggested that as Lord Garmoyle had passed one examination at Sandhurst he should have the army as a profession, and that he had better return to Sandhurst and complete his examination before he married. Whilst at Sandhurst Lord Garmoyle sent the plaintiff a very hand- some present, in acknowledging which she addressed him as "Dear sweetheart," and said she had worn the pre- sent at dinner. She, however, said that she did not require such tokens of his affections, for they must know that although they were a loving lad and lassie, they were also a man and woman, and jewels, and toys were not required. The letter then called him " Dear old boy," and it went on to say that he had heavy expenses to bear, that she wee a "loving woman and not a brainless doll," and she desired to continue so in the future; and the letter concluded by an expression of appreciation of the sweet thoughts which had prompted the present in January, 1884. She was under a promise visit with Lord and Lady Cairns at Bournemouth, hut upon the 3rd of that month she re- ceived from Lord Garmoyle a letter requesting her to put off the visit, as both his father and mother were unwell. She agreed to do so, and went with her mother and sister to Brighton, where they stayed some days. Whilst there Lord Garmoyle paid a visit to the plaintiff, and re- mained at Brighton until the 21st of January, which was the last visit he ever paid to her, and up to that time letters full of affectionate respect and , love had over and over again been received. On the 21st January Lord Garmoyle left her without giving 1 the slightest intimation that his feelings had changed. He continued his professions of love and regard so to that day, and then he at once wrote a letter breaking off the engage- ment. He even then still professed the sane lave and ad- miration, bnt he said in his letter that she would not be I accepted by his friends and relations in consequence of the profession she had followed, and that acting in the interest and on the suggestions of others he must break off the i match. He had already said that not only the plaintiff but her sister left the stage is consequence of the representation made, and it was te the plaintiff that the mother and sister still looked for support. She might have been idle, and have come into the court saying that the stage was closed to her, but she was a courageous woman, and had returned to her profession. Under the circumstances it would be for them to say what damages she was entitled to. The Attorney-General said he wished to interpose here, and to at once say that Miss Fortescue was amply justi- fied in bringing this action; and although Lord Garmoyle had always been desirous to make compensation she was justified in bringing the case into court. Taking that view Lord Garmoyle desired to say that compensation should be given to the amount of £lO,OOO, which he trusted would be considered fair. He wished tfa go further, and say that Lord Garmoyle was desirous it should be stated that from his first acquaintance With Miss Fortescue, and throughout the whole time he had known her, there was 'nothing in the course of her conduct but what was becoming a high- minded English lady. He was also desirous to state that in breaking off this engagement it resulted in no way from any action of hers, bat was affected out of considera- tions applicable to himself only. He really had no other answer to make to the just claim which had been made.

.... ..... Thejury then, under the direction of his Lordship, gave their assent formally to a verdict for £lO,OOO. The Law Journal says the £lO,OOO awarded to the plaintiff in " Finney v. Cairns " (otherwise Garmoyle) is probably the largest amount of damages ever recorded in this country in an action for breach of promise of marriage.

A telegram from New York of Friday's date says that ad- vices from Mexico report popular disorder. The Duke of Argyll dined with the Queen at Windsor last evening. He will return .to London to-day. The British force in Egypt new numbers 16,000 men, and of this considerable army more than 9,000 are at or south of Assouan.

A very heavy north-easterly gale prevailed at Yarmouth yesterday, and many casualties to fishing boats and craft have been reported. The ice in Lake Ladoga has commenced to move into the ,Neva. The thermornetor registers five degrees of frost, and sleighing has commenced.
, It wa—s resolved at a large meeting of crofters at Ui to carry on the agitation as hitherto until the grievances com- plained of shall have been redressed.

During a gale off the Lincolnshire coast on Friday morn- ing, the Donna Nook lifeboat pat off to a vessel in distress, which is supposed to have foundered. A Madrid despatch says the students were detained OR Thursday night for causing disturbances in provoking an anti-clerical demonstration, and severe measures are threat,ned.

OUTBREAK OF CATTLE DISEAS,.—On Friday morning the Clerk of the Peace for Lancashire was informed that pleuro•nneumonia has broken out at the shippons of Mr. Richard Neild, Prescot, near Liverpool. Two animals had been slaughtered. There are no cases of foot-and-mouth disease in Lancashire.

SHOCKING FATALITY.—Very early on Friday morning Police-constable Farrow, of the Durham county force, was found to have fallen int) a quarry at Pittingtou in the course of his beat, during the prevalence of a severe gale. He was alive when discovered, but died shortly afterwaids. He • leaves a widow and two or three children. THE APPLICATION OF THE " CAT."—Michael Jordan (20), wire drawer, and John Davitt (19), metal roller, convicted at Warwick assizes of robbery and personal violence at Bir- mingham, sentenced to seven years' penal servitude, and ordered to receive twenty-four strokes with the "cat," in two instalments, on Friday morning received the first por- tion of thnir castigation within the walls of Warwick Gaol. They howled loudly during the infliction of the last half dozen lashes.

THE CHARGE AGAINST LORD MARCCS BERESEORD.—At Middlesex Sessions, on Friday, Lord Marcus Beresford sur- rendered to his bail on the charge of having assaulted Mr. Bowles, editor of Vanity Fair.—Nir. Bowles deposed to the circumstances of the assault, and was cross-examined at considerable length by Mr. Montagu Williams in reference to other libel cases in which he had been the defendant. Witness said he was always ready to apologise if he made mistakes.—Lord Egmont and other witnesses repeated the evidence given by them before the magistrate, and the case for the prosecution then closed.—Mr. Williams, for the de- fence, contended tnat this was one of the most paltry cases ever brought before a British jury. He could offer no ins- tidcation for a man breaking the law, but he could not help thinking that if Mr. Bowles was assaulted it served him right.—Witnesses were then called to prove that Lord Marcus Beresford was himself seriously assaulted by the plaintiff and a number of men in his employ.—The jury re- tired at five o'clock, and after an absence of forty minutes, returned into court with a verdict of not guilty, and dis- charged defendant from custody amidst applause. EXTRAORDINARY LIBEL CASE.—The libel action Adams v. Coleridge commenced in the Queen's Bench on Friday, before Justice Manisty and a special jury. The plaintiff claims £lO,OOO damages for an alleged libel contained in a letter written by the defendant (the Hon. Berpard Coleridge) I to his sister, Miss Coleridge, to whom the plaintiff was en- gaged to be married.—The plaintiff, who conducted his OWR case, in his opening statement, said he could not expect any barrister to undertake the case, because it would mean pro- fessional ruin to interfere in a case in which the Lord Chief Justice had already taken up the cudgels for the de- fendant. With undignified vehemence, his lordship had turned his daughter out of doors, and struck her name out of his will. Plaintiff then read defendant's letter, which charged him with eloping with a young lady, whom he after- wards made miserable, and with being without character or principle. Other charges were insinuated against the plain- tiff and Miss Coleridge was urged to break off her acquain- tance with him. Plaintiff declared that the statements in the letter were tissues of falsehoods.—Mr. Justice Manisty hinted to the plaintiff that a letter from brother to sister was privileged, but plaintiff continued his speech, and had not concluded when the court adjourned.

div.head: MURDER NEAR TORQUAY,.
div.p: THE MURDER NEAR TORQUAY,.

The adjourned inquest on the body of Miss Keyes was resumed in St. Mary's Church Town Hall, on Friday morn- ing. Before half-past ten o'clock the hall was half filled, and persons continued to pour in until the court was most unpleasantly crowded. The prisoner, John Lee, was brought up in a cab by two police officers. He was pale, but jumped nimbly out, and ran lightly up the steps. It will be remembered that the prisoner is stated to have been wearing a collar when first seen on Saturday morning, the ' presumption being that he had not been in bed. A collar has been found near the residence of Colonel Mac- lean, whither the prisoner was sent with intelli- gence of the fire, search being made in consequence of intelli- gence riven by a local photographer, who states he dreamt that the collar would be found there.— In opening the inquiry the coroner said he should call four witnesses and again adjourn. He had been in communica- tion with the Home Secretary, who had instructed Dr. Stevenson to examine the weapons found and the clothing of the deceased and the prisoner, but he had not yet finished his investigations.—W. Bowen, surveyor, Mary Church Local Board, produced a plan of the house.—Constable Much said that on Saturday, about 4-30 a.m., he went to Babbicombe Glen. Eliza Neck, one of the old servants, told him that Miss Keyse had been burnt to death. He saw the prisoner there with both hands bloody. He asked him how he accounted for the blood on his bands, and he replied that he had smashed the dining-room window to let out the smoke. The prisoner went upstairs with him and tore down a lace curtain in the " honeysuckle-room."—The Inquiry was adjourned.

Penis, FRIDAY.-A telegram received here from Shan- ghai of to-dav's date states that the Chinese ironclad cruisers Cho Lung and Yung Wei have arrived there. It le reported that they intend to try and face the blockade of Formosa. THE WEST AFRICAN CONFERENCE.

BERLIN, FRIDLY.—At yesterday's sitting of the Com- mittee of the West African Conference the members settled the mode of procedure to be observed and deliberated upon the mode of dealing with the material before them. The sitting closed at half-past three o'clock. The committee will meet again at one o'clock this afternoon.

_ Earl GRANVILLE, replying to Lord Zouche. said the French Minister at Tangiers had denied the truth of the accusations reported in Gaulois against Sir John Drummond Hay, British Minister at Morocco. CONDITION OF THE SCOTCH CROFTERS.—The Duke Of ARGYLL drew attention to the report of the Royal Commis- sion on the Scotch crofters. The noble Duke denied the existence of dire distress amongst the crofters as in great industrial centres in England. During the last twenty years the condition of the crofters had improved, and High- land proprietors had anticipated many of the recommenda- tions of the Commission for still bettering their condition. He adversely criticised the report, which was founded on imperfect evidence, and did not afford means for carrying out their recommendations with regard to the farther divi- sion of allotments. Recent disturbances were fomented by professional agitators in London, the crofters being law- abiding people when undeisturbed.—Lord NAPIER and ErrnicK believed that local grievances must be met by local remedies.—The subject then dropped, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FAIDAS. The House met at four o'clock.

BRISSEY, replying to Mr. Holdswortb, said the recognition of Congo as a free state bad been notified by the United States.

div.head: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

On the motion to go into Committee of Supply, Mr. LABOUCJIERE moved " That in view of the fact that the Conservative party is able, and has for rainy years been able through its permanent majority in the House of Lords, to alter, defeat, or delay legislation, although that legislation had been re- commended by the responsible advisers of the Crown, and approved of by the nation through its elected representa- tives, it was desirable to make such alterations in the rela- tions of the two Houses of Parliament as would effect a remedy for this state of things." He considered the present House of Lords as one sot in accordance with the times, as it represented only the owners of lands. He did not think it possible that a more absurdly composed assembly could by any means be got together than the present House of Lords, and the sooner it was reformed the better. Its pre- sent object appeared to be to mar useful legislation, and, re- ferring to the action the House of Lords had pursued with regard to the Franchise Bill, he said it had controlled the action of the most powerful Prime Minister that ever existed, and practically had deprived the House of Com- mons of he freedom. The House of Lords was in opposition to the feelings of the great body, and in his opinion the sooner a change took place in its constitution the better.—Sir W. Lawsole seconded the reso- lution. He contended that hereditary legislation was ab- surd, unconstitutional, and injurious to the public interests. —Mr. GLADSTONE said he did not share in the opinion that there • was anything humiliating. to the House of Com- mons in the communications that had taken place with regard to the Franchise Bill. He admitted that the proposal submitted was a serious one, and pointed out that the hereditary principle was to be judged not merely by its principle but also by its relative merits. If there was only one House of Parliament, peers would have to be eligible for election as members of that House, and they would no doubt be returned in such numbers as would

secure a larger portion of representation than their numbers bore to the bulk of the population. They were then asking the House of Lords to do a great Liberal act, and under such circumstances he did not think the present a happy moment to bring forward the present subject. Mr. Laboucbere's resolution was then rejected by 145 to 71. THE INDUSTRIES OF IRELAND.--SiT E. WILMOT op- pealed to the Government to appoint a Select Committee to inquire into the present condition of manufacturing and. productive industries in Ireland.—Mr. A. MOORE sup- ported, and Mr. TREVELYAN said if the committee was mgved for next February the Government would not oppose it.— Mr. E. GRAY thought a Royal Commission would be better than a Select Committee.—After further discussion the sub- ject dropped.

WESTMINSTER ABBEY.—Mr. CAVENDISH BENTINCE cu- led attention to the present condition of the fabric of West- minster Abbey, and asked if the Government had granted money to the Dean and Chapter for repairs'of the Abbey and the renovating of the north transept. The CHANCEL- LOR of the EXCHEQUER announced the intention of the Government, at the beginning of the sitting after Christ- mas, to bring in a Bill providing that capitular bodies, in- stead of depending upon the management of estates, for the payment of their officers and maintenance of ecclesias- tical buildings, should receive a fixed sum from the Eccle- siastical Commissioners.

MISCELLANEOUS.—In Committee a vote of £2,000,490 out of the Consolidated Fund was agreed to.—On the motion for the second reading of the Income Tax Bill, Mr. RYLANDS complained of the increased expenditure of the Government, and said it was due to their drifting policy in Egypt.—Sir W. 13ARTELLOT believed that the Nile and Becuanaland ex- peditions, increasing the navy and defence of our coaling station, would demand at least £10,000,000, and he objec- ted to the whole of that vast sum being cast on the income tax. He did not think that an increase of income tax of 2d in the £ for six months ought to be allowed to pass without observation.—After a further discussion the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said that he believed two mil- lion and a quarter would be quite sufficient for present ex- penditurn.—The Bill was read a second time. The House was then counted and 40 members not being present, the House adjourned at twenty minutes past eleven.

Although the motion against the House of Lords was re- jected by 145 votes against 71, the largeness of the minority caused some surprise. Amongst those who voted in the minority with Mr. Labouchere and Sir Wilfrid Lawson were—Sir G. Campbell, Messrs. Cameron, Anderson, Gour- ley, Firth, A. Arnold, Mclntosh, Armitage, Mason, Roe, Peddie, Jno. Morley,Woodhall, Williamson, Borlase, Storey, Webster, P. Edwards, Farquharson, Summers, Albert Grey, W. E. Briggs, Richard Picton, Barran, Bryce. Cowen, Broadhurst, Rylands, and 12 members of Mr. Parnell's party. Neither Mr. Chamberlain nor Sir Charles Dilke took part in the division, but several members of the Government voted in the majority, including Mr. Gladstone, Lord Hartington, Sir W. Harcourt, Messrs. Childers, Trevelyan, Courtney, Campbell, Bannerman, Mundella, and Sir T. Brassey, The front Opposition Bench was represented in the lobby against ' the motion by Sir S. Northcote, Mr. W. H. Smith, Lord JllO. Manners, kc.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS AND ITS
div.p: THE HOUSE OF LORDS AND ITS
ENEMIES.

On Wednesday evening an address on the " House of Lords and its enemies" was delivered in the Assembly- room of the Conservative Club, by Mr. F. G. Leslie, of Liverpool. The chair, in the absence of Sir Gilbert Green- all, who had been announced to attend, was taken by Capt. Reynolds. There were also on the platform tbe Mayor (Alderman Harrison), the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Dr. Mackie, Councillors Burgess and Sutton, Mr. John Roberts, Mr. Adams. There was a good attendance. The CHAIRMAN said he felt sure they would be disappointed in not seeing Sir Gilbert Greenall there that night, but he had caught a cold on Saturday and did not think it wise to come out that evening. They woald be wrong in asking him to endan- ger his health, for, as they knew, they should want him to fight their battle in Warrington very soon. Therefore they must ask him to keep his health as well as he could for that battle. Referring to the House of Lords, he said he should no doubt be expressing their views if he said that if every man in England was to be asked whether they should abolish the Huse of Lords or not there would be a very large majority in favour of keeping up that old part of our constitution. (Hear, hear.) There had been some very hot and hard language used against the House of Lords, but if it were wished by the people that it should be abolished they would not cnly hear that language in the great Radical centres of this country, but they would hear from all classes—beginning with a faint voice possibly but increasing until they heard such a roar that they would at once understand that the people wished the House to be abolished. But they had heard nothing of that sort, and therefore he did not think the House of Lords should be abolished. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. LESLIE, who was received with applause, proceeded to correct what he said was the not uncommon error of supposing that the House of Lords was a mere modern institution than the House of Com- mons. He also argued that the House of Lords had done much to secure!and protect the liberty of the English people even when the representative House was ready to sacrifice it. He claimed that nearly every considerable measure of land and law reform during the present generation had pro- ceeded in the first instance from the House of Lords, and that that House had protected the interests of the people on social questions, and were the true benefactors of the people, whose interests they had always had at heart. One accusa- tion brought against the Upper House was that it had some unworthy members. That was an absurd accusation, for there was no body of men without members who were un- worthy of their positions, and they might as well cast from them the benefits of their religion, because some of the ministers of that religion might have disgraced their sacred calling. (Applause.) Another charge was that the House of Lords was always Conservative. Granting that to be so it was a startling fact, because since 1830 the Liberal prime ministers had created enough Liberal peers to swamp any opposition of the House of Lords. Evidently so long as a Liberal in the House of Commons had any reward to look to he voted with the party most likely to give it him, MA when he got into the House of Lords, and had no further reward to expect, he exercised his own feelings and voted with the Conservatives. (Cheers and laughter.) It was well that there should be a Conservative leaning in the House of Lords, for, while the Radical House of Commons I was eager for change for change's sake, the other House was intent upon saying that a change should not be a change for the worae. (Cheers.) The object of having two legislative chambers was that the bias, influences, Prejudices, and interests brought to bear upon the one, might be counteracted by the other. With regard to the objections to hereditary principles, he contended that such principles pervaded our whole social system, as men born to wealth and position had naturally an advantage over those who were not. A man who had inherited wealth, or whose father had given him a good education and placed him in a good position, had twenty years start in life of the man who had no such advantages. In the beginning of the 17th century the first Sir Wilfred Lawson was created, and he was member for the county of Cumberland, and nearly every succeeding Lawson had been member for Cumberland or the city of Carlisle. He ventured to say that the "chances of birth" had given them—and would continue to give—as many able men as the chances of the ballot box. He denied that the House of Lords opposed the will of the people, and upheld their action respecting the Franchise Bill. After tour months of squabbling on that question, the Government had said that they would give in and disclose what their redistribution was going to be rather than make an appeal to the country. The Conservative party was con- tent with that, which was what they had all along been striving for. If the House of Lords during the past four months had been opposing the wishes of the people, Mr. Glad- stone himself was now doing the same, for he was acceding to a demand which he had declared the people would disapprove of. The House of Lords had only opposed the will of an ex- treme section of the Radical party. Continuing, he said that they knew too much of what the Liberal Government had done and had left undone, to desire its return to power. They knew what it had done in Egypt ;'had done and left undone in the Soudan; the muddle that it had made in South Africa, and everywhere else. Four years ago they took office with a clap-trap flourish of trumpets about Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform. Peace! He did not believe that since Mr. Gladstone took office there had passed a single day en which England had Hot been at war. Re- trenchment! He should like to hear Mr. Gladstone, logician and casuist as he was, prove that retrenchment was compassed by putting an additional penny on to the income tax. What had it reformed? The only thing it might have reformed and had not done was itself. (Laugh- ter.)—A vote of thanks to the lecturer was moved by Dr. Mackie, seconded by Councillor Burgess, and carried by ac- clamation; a similar compliment,on the motion of Council- lor Sutton, seconded by Mr. Isherwood, was paid to the chairman. The meeting then terminated.
The Gaiety Theatre, Southampton, at which the usual performance took place on Tuesday night, was burnt .down at an early hour on Wednesday morning.

The Earl of Stair was on Thursday declared duly elected Chancellor of Glasgow University. The Marquis of Bute had withdrawn his candidature. Dr. Alexander Bain was elected Lord Rector of Aberdeen University on Saturday. Lord Randolph Churchill carried the Angus nation by a majority of 24, but Dr. Bain won in all the other nations. Mrs. Fawcett desires to offer earnest thanks on behalf of herself and her daughter for the messages of grief and sym• pathy which have reached them from every part of the ocuntry, from abroad, and from India.

HOLY TRINITY CHunog.—Sermons were on Sunday preached at Holy Trinity Church, Warrington, in aid of ' the curates' fond; in the morning by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (vicar), and in the evening by the Rev. Morley Stevenson, M.A. The congregations at both cervices were large.

I DESPERATE STRUGGLE BETWEEN A PRISONER AND A CONSTABLE—On Thursday Constable Royle, of the Che- shire Constabulary, apprehended James Mullins, 30, farm labourer, in an isolated place between Moore and Stockton Heath, near Warrington, for a criminal attack on a girl named Hannah Fleetwood, now living at Runcorn. Several desperate struggles ensued between the policeman and Mul- lins, who is a daring character, before reaching the police station, two miles away, which was accomplished in a little short of three hours. Both men suffered much in the Bght. Mullins was remanded on Thursday on two charges.

IN PARLIAMENT. SESSION 1885. RUNCORN GAB. (Additional Capital. Application of Funds. Consolidation of , Capital, Additional Lands, Construction of New and Maintenance of Old Works, Manufacture and Storage of Gas and Residuals on old and new sites, Limits of Sup- ply, Sale of Lands, Breaking up of Streets. Supply of Gas Meters, Stoves, &c., Price of Gas and Dividends, Sliding Scale, Purity. Quality, and Pressure of Gas, Public Lighting. New Provisions respecting Regulation of Company, Rates, Rents, and Charges, Patent Rights, Incorporation and Amendment of Acts.) NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that application is in- tended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing year, by the Runcorn Gas Company (hereinafter called "the Com- pany"), for leave to bring in a Bill (hereinafter called "the Bill ") for all or some of the ',following amongst other p in- poses, that is to say, To authorize the Company to raise, for the purposes of the Bill and the general purposes of their undertaking, additional capital by the creation and issue of new.ordinary and prefer- ence shares and stock, and by borrowing and by the creation and issue of debenture stock, or by any of such methods, and to attach"to any such shares, stocks, or loans any pre. ference or pdority of dividend or interest, and to apply to the purposes aforesaid any capital, funds, or money now belonging to or authorized to be raised or borrowed by the Company, and to consolidate and arrange the shares and stacks of the Company. To authorize the Company to purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire by agreement, and to hold and use for the purposes of their undertaking, and in addition to the lands which they are empowered to purchase and bold by the Runcorn Gas Act. 1847 (hereinafter called "the Act of 1847 "), the following lands (that is to say) : First. A piece of land, containing 4 acres 19 perches or there- abouts, known as Culvert Meadow, situate In the township of Runcorn, in the parish of Runcorn. in the County of Chester, and lying on the south side of and adjoining the Bridgewater Canal, and bounded on the north or ncrth west aide thereof by the said canal and property belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Bridgewater Navigation Company. Limited; on the west side thereof by property belonging, or reputed to beloog, to the trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater; on the south side thereof by the public highway known as the Halton-road, leading from Runcorn to Warrington; and on the east side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the execu- tors of the late William Henry uckleston. Secondly. A piece of land containing 2 rcods and 12 perches or thereabouts, with the building thereon, known as Highfield House, situate in the said township of Runcorn, and parish of Noncom, and county of Chester, and lying on the north side of the said Bridgewater Canal; and bounded on the south side thereof by the road adjoining the towing path of the said canal, and leading from Canal-street, Runcorn, to Bate's Bridge, Halton; on the west side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of the Duke of Bridge- water ; and on the north and east sides thereof by land belong- ing, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of Mrs. Eliza Ann Kirkham. And to authorize the Company on those lands, or part or parts thereof, to erect, construct, make, and maintain and on the lands hereinafter described as the site of the Company's existing gas works, to maintain and continue, and as regards all such lands from time to time extend, enlarge, and Improve gas works, and works for the manufacture, distribu- tion, storage, and supply of gas, and for the manufacture. con- version, utilization, storage and distribution of materials used in and about the manufacture of gas and of residual products resulting from such manufacture, and to empower the Corn pany on and from all such lands to manufacture, store, and supply gas, and to manufacture, convert, utilize, distribute, and store such materials and residual products as aforesaid, and to extend and make applicable to, and to enable the Com- pany to exercise,' in respect of the before-mentioned lands, and of the supply of gas therefrom all or some of the provi- sions of the Act of 1847 as altered, amended, or enlarged by the Bill. The site of the Company's existing Gas Works consists of the pieces of land hereinafter described, that is to say : First.—A piece of land containing 1,785 square yards or there- abouts, situate in the said township and parish of Runcorn, in the county of Chester, on the east side of Gas-street, and bounded on the westerly side thereof by that street, on the southerly, or south-easterly side thereof by the towing path of the Bridgewater Canal, on the easterly side thereof by a street known as Stone-street, and on the northerly side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Marquis of Chol- mondeley Becondly.—A piece of land containing 2,609 square yards, or thereabouts, situate in the said township and parish ot Run- corn, on the west side of Gas-street, and bounded on the north side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the said Marquis of Cholmondeley, on the east side thereof by Gas-street, on the south_ side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Runcorn Smelting Company, and on the west side thereof in part by Sutherland-street, and on the remaining parts by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Trustees of the United Methodist Free Church, and by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater respectively. To amend or repeal section 7 of the Act of 1847, and to alter and define the limits within which the Company may supply gas, such limits to include the town of Runcorn, otherwise called Higher and Lower Runcorn, the township of Runcorn, and the townships or hamlets of Halton, Astmore, otherwise Astmore-wlth-Halton. Norton, Weston, Weston Point. and Clifton, otherwise Clifton-with R tcksavage, in the County of Chester, or such of them, or such parts thereof as may be speci- fied in the Bill. To empower the Company, from time to time, to sell, ex- change, let on lease, or otherwise to dispose of any lands at the time belonging to them, which they may not require for the purposes of their undertaking. To give power to the Company within their limits of supply to lay down, maintain. um, alter, and renew mains, pipes, and other conveniences for the distrthution, supply, and disposal of gas and residual products' ant to open, break up, and inter- fere with streets, roads, highways, midges, railways, canals, sewers, drains, and other passages add places, and gas and water, telegraphic, telephonic, and other pipes, wires, and apparatus. To authorize the Company to manufacture, purchase, hire, sell, let, supply, and deal In, and to fix, alter, remove and refix gas meters, fittings, gas engines, stoves, ranges, pipes, and other appliances and apparatus for lighting, he•ting, motive power, ventilating, cooking, and other purposes for whish gas may be used, and to empower the Company to supply gas for any such purposes, and to manufacture, buy, sell, and deal in coal, lime, coke, tar, ammoniacal liquor, chemicals, and other materials used in or resulting from the manufacture of gas, and to carry on any business usually carried on by a Gas Company. To regulate the price to be charged by the Company for gas, and the rate of eividends which they may divide, and, if thought fit, to provide for the variation of the rate of divi- dends according to the price charged for gas, and to make provision for the maintenanse asid formation of insurance and reserve funds to meet deficiencies in divL ends and accidents, strikes or other extraordinary claims and circum- stance,. To make provision with respect to the purity, quality, and pressure of gas to be supplied by the Company, and the testing of gas and meters, the supply of gas and lamps for public light- ing, and the erection, cleaning, lighting, extinguishing, and repairing of such lamps. To amend or repeal the provisions of the Act of 1847, with respect to the time of ordinary meetings, the scale of voting by shareholders, the number and quorum of directors, the number of directors to constitute, and the quorum of com- mittees, the holding of proxies, the remuneration of directors, and such other matters relating to the regulation and manage- ment of the Company as may be dealt with in the Bill ;' and to make other and further provisions in respect thereto, and to alter and fix the period of the year up to which the annual ac- counts of the Compsny shall be made up. To vary and extinguish any rights and privileges connected with any lands, streets, roads, highways, canals sewers, dtains, pipes, wires, and other apparatus and properly to be acquired or interfered with by the Company, and any other rights and privileges wbich would Interfere with the objects and purposes of the Bill, and to confer all such rights and pri- vileges as may be necessary or convenient for effecting such objects and purposes. To authorize the Company to demand, levy, and recover rates, rents, and charges for the supply of gas and other mat- ters and things supplied, and services rendered by them, and to alter rates, rents, and charges, and to confer, vary, or ex- tinguish exemptions from the payment of rates, rents, and charges, and to provide for the allowance of discounts. To authorize the Company to purchase, hold, and use patent rights or licenses for the use of inventions, relative to the manufacture and supply of gas, meters, fittings, apparatus, engines, stoves, ranges, pipes, and other apparatus and ap- pliances. To incorporate with and apply to the Bill (so far as may be "applicable, and except so far as exprestly varied thereby), all or some of the provisions of the Companies Clauses Osnsolida- tion Act, 1845, the Companies Clauses Act, 1863, and the Com- panies Clauses Act, 1809; the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts, 1815, 1860, and 1889, the Gas Works Clauses Act, 1847, and the Gas Works Clauses Act, 1871, with such variations or modifications ss may be thought expedient, or may be provided for by the Bill, and to make all or some of the provisions of the last-mentioned Act apply to the existing undertaking of the Company, and to amend, alter, or repeal, so far as may be necessary for the purposes of the Bill, all or some of the pro- visions of the Act of 1847, and any other Acts relating to the Company, the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852, and any other Act relating to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, and any other Act affected by the Bill. Printed copies of the Bill will be deposited in the Private BM Office of the House of Commons on or before the Twentieth day of December next Dated this Vourteenth day of November, 1884. ROBERT DAVIES, SHARP, & iIRKOONNEL, ' Market-place, Warrington, Solicitors for the Bill. GRAHAMES, CURREY, At SPE/fB, 30, Great George-street, Westminster, Parliamentary Agents.

Middle- ton, half-backs; Barnes, Winne, Findlay, Croyton, Motley, McKeown, Blackburn, Hall, and Wilson. forwards. EARLESTOWN v. BIRKENHEAD. The first team of the Birkenhead club (an organisation of some note in the Liverpool district) visited Earlestown on Saturday after- noon, and for the first time met the silver medallists of last season's Liverpool and District Cup Competition. Unfor- tanately for the Birkenhead team, however, they turned up one man short, their captain being left behind at Lime' street, while he was securing the tickets for the team. The result was that the visitors only placed ten men in the field, while Earlestown was represented by its full streegth. The game was of a very one sided character, the Earlestonians having matters entirely their own way. The Birkenhead team won the toss, and for the first half chose to play down hill with the wind in their favour. Dagnall kicked off for Earlestown, passing the leather to the left wing where Sint's secured it. Sims immediately shot for goal, and Ellison rushing up sent it through the uprights in less than half a minute from the commencement amid loud cheers. The visitors disputed the point on a ciaim of hands" and the leather was ultimately kicked from the goal. The Earlestonians pressed their opponents and in three minutes Ogden scored amid applause. The remain- der of the first half was in favour of the home team, who pressed their opponents, but though some capital shots were sent in, they were unable to increase their lead. Ends were changed with the score at one goal to noae in favour of the home team, who afterwards had the ground in their favour. On the game being recommenced the Earlestonians quickly assumed the aggressive 4 and the Birkenhead team was severely pressed. In quick succes- sion Sims scored a second and third goal, Ellison the fourth, Ogden the fifth, and Dagnall the sixth, while two other goals were disallowed for offside play. The visi- tors never had a chance of scoring, and had it not been for the splendid defensive play of Owens, and the good play of the goalkeeper, their defeat would have been more severe. When time was called the Earlestonians retired the victors by six goals to none. Teams :-'-Earlestown: J. Appleton, goal ; R. Green and J. Green. backs; R. Hawker, J. Duxbury, and J. Whalley, half-backs ; W. Rich and J. Ellison, right wing ; A. W. Dagnall. centre ; J. Sims and J. Ogden, left wing. Birkenhead : Hartley, goal; Owens and Beynon, backs; Bowering and McMillan, half- backs; Crellin, Turner, Bradshaw, Stevenson, and Hay- hurst, forwards.

THE EXAMINE R. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1884.

ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRlD.93.—Before Alderman Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair. MISCELLANECUS.—The following persons were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness :—John Jones, Margaret Gerard, John Grimes, Michael McGrath, Joseph Appleton, Thomas Barlow, John Ratchford ; Margaret Ramsdale, who appeared for the 21st time, was fined 10s and costs for a similar offence. Thomas Fallon, of Sutton. and Patrick Donald were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting, and they were bound over for their good beha- viour. ASSAULT.—James Flynn summoned John Brady, of Ec- cleston, for assaulting him by striking and kicking him in Liverpool-road, on the previous Tuesday evening.—As the defendant did not appear the Bench imposed a fine of 20s an costs. MoNnAv.—Before Messrs. W. W. Pilkington and T. Pilkington. DnusgENNEss.—The following persons were fined the amounts stated for being drunk and disorderly :—James Kelly, Pollard-street, Windle' Saturday night, 5s and costs 9 ; John Millington, Windle gaturday night, 5s and costs ; Mary Ann Burns, Windte, Saturday night, 5s and costs; Thomas Derbyshire, 5s and costs. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—Frank Grundy, a young I man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and as- saulting P.C. Richard Walsh, on Saturday night.—The constable stated that the prisoner was cursing his wife and beating her in Sindlield Crescent, Eccleston. He was under the influence of drink, and the constable said he would re- port him, after which the prisoner struck him in the face. The prisoner had been three times previously convicted, and the Bench imposed a fins of 5s and costs for the drunk- enness and a like amount for the assault. BEGGING.—Robert Halstead was charged with begging from foot passengers in Bridge-street. Windle, on the 'Pre- vious afternoon, and was committed to prison for seven days.

For the first time for two years the public were allowed to approach the train at Aberdeen, and a large crowd cheered the Royal travellers. DEATH IN THE FOOTBALL FIELD. While a number of studends at St. Thomas's Hospital were playing football in the Archbishop's grounds at Lambeth, on Saturday, one of the players was seen to stagger and fall *town dead. The body was conveyed to the hospital mortuary, where it waif identified as that of Mr. Rowe, aged 23 years, one of the senior students. THE CHINESE AND GENERAL GORDON.—A Hong Kong telegram says :—On the announcement reaching Canton that General Gordon had been killed in the Soudan, the Viceroy paraded the garrison, who fired volleys, as if over his grave. The squadron in the river lowered their flags to half•mast, and fired minute guns in honour of the hero who had done so much for China, and who is still remembered with gratitude. FATAL ACCIDENTS AT HAYDOCK.—Tiro sad fatalities have lag recently occurred near Haydock. On Friday afternoon Jacob Prior. 40 years of age, a collier employed in the Old Boston Pit, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and CO., was engaged taking "props " from under a portion of the roof, when a large quantity of stones and dirt fell from over- head. Prior was covered with the debris, and it was found that he was quite dead when the body was recovered about three hours later.—Nancy Taylor 83 years of age, residing at Billings, died on Saturday from injuries received by be- ing burned. Some time previously she was placing the kettle on the fire in the house when her clothes ignited and she sustained injuries which caused her death as stated. v„.
